NUCLEAR REGULATORY COMMISSION

10 CFR Part 52

[NRC-2026-2377]
RIN 3150-AL70


AP1000 Design Certification Renewal

AGENCY: Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

ACTION: Proposed rule and environmental assessment.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) is proposing to 
amend its regulations to renew the AP1000 design certification and 
incorporate Revision 20 of the AP1000 design control document. The 
purpose of this rulemaking action is to update the AP1000 design to be 
consistent with changes made to the design during the



licensing, construction, and operation of Vogtle Electric Generating 
Plant, Units 3 and 4. This rulemaking incorporates AP1000 design 
control document Revision 20, which includes updates made to the AP1000 
design to represent a current, construction-validated design. The NRC 
also proposes to issue an environmental assessment supporting this 
rule.

DATES: Submit comments by November 13, 2026.

ADDRESSES: Submit your comments, identified by Docket ID NRC-2026-2377, 
at https://www.regulations.gov. If your material cannot be submitted 
using https://www.regulations.gov, call or email the individual listed 
in the FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT section of this document for 
alternate instructions.
    Do not include any personally identifiable information (such as 
name, address, or other contact information) or confidential business 
information that you do not want publicly disclosed. All comments are 
public records; they are publicly displayed exactly as received, and 
will not be deleted, modified, or redacted. Comments may be submitted 
anonymously.
    Follow the search instructions on https://www.regulations.gov to 
view public comments.
    You can read a plain language description of this proposed rule at 
https://www.regulations.gov/docket/NRC-2026-2377. For additional 
direction on obtaining information and submitting comments, see 
``Obtaining Information and Submitting Comments'' in the SUPPLEMENTARY 
INFORMATION section of this document.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Jason Carneal, Office of the Chief 
Information Officer, U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Washington, DC 
20555-0001; telephone: 301-415-1451, email: [email protected].

I. Obtaining Information and Submitting Comments

A. Obtaining Information

    Please refer to Docket ID NRC-2026-2377 when contacting the NRC 
about the availability of information for this action. You may obtain

following methods:

     NRC's Agencywide Documents Access and Management System 
(ADAMS): You may obtain publicly available documents online in the 
ADAMS Public Documents collection at https://www.nrc.gov/reading-rm/adams.html. To begin the search, select ``Begin ADAMS Public Search.'' 
For problems with ADAMS, please contact the NRC's Public Document Room

[email protected]. For the convenience of the reader, instructions

     NRC's PDR: The PDR, where you may examine and order copies

[email protected] or call 1-800-397-4209 or 301-415-4737, between 8 
a.m. and 4 p.m. eastern time, Monday through Friday, except Federal 
holidays.

B. Submitting Comments

    The NRC encourages electronic comment submission through the 
Federal Rulemaking Website (https://www.regulations.gov). Please 
include Docket ID NRC-2026-2377 in your comment submission.
    The NRC cautions you not to include identifying or contact 
information that you do not want to be publicly disclosed in your 
comment submission. The NRC will post all comment submissions at 
https://www.regulations.gov as well as enter the comment submissions 
into ADAMS. The NRC does not routinely edit comment submissions to 
remove identifying or contact information.
    If you are requesting or aggregating comments from other persons 
for submission to the NRC, then you should inform those persons not to 
include identifying or contact information that they do not want to be 
publicly disclosed in their comment submission. Your request should 
state that the NRC does not routinely edit comment submissions to 
remove such information before making the comment submissions available 
to the public or entering the comment into ADAMS.

II. Rulemaking Procedure

    Because the NRC considers this action to be non-controversial, the 
NRC is publishing this proposed rule concurrently with a direct final 
rule in the Rules and Regulations section of this issue of the Federal 
Register. The direct final rule will become effective on December 28, 
2026. However, if the NRC receives significant adverse comments by 
November 13, 2026, then the NRC will publish a document that withdraws 
the direct final rule. If the direct final rule is withdrawn, the NRC 
will address the comments in a subsequent final rule. Absent 
significant modifications to the proposed revisions requiring 
republication, the NRC will not initiate a second comment period on 
this action in the event the direct final rule is withdrawn.
    A significant adverse comment is a comment where the commenter 
explains why the rule would be inappropriate, including challenges to 
the rule's underlying premise or approach, or would be ineffective or 
unacceptable without a change. A comment is adverse and significant if:
    (1) The comment opposes the rule and provides a reason sufficient 
to require a substantive response in a notice-and-comment process. For 
example, a substantive response is required when:
    (a) The comment causes the NRC to reevaluate (or reconsider) its 
position or conduct additional analysis;
    (b) The comment raises an issue serious enough to warrant a 
substantive response to clarify or complete the record; or
    (c) The comment raises a relevant issue that was not previously 
addressed or considered by the NRC.
    (2) The comment proposes a change or an addition to the rule, and 
it is apparent that the rule would be ineffective or unacceptable 
without incorporation of the change or addition.
    (3) The comment causes the NRC to make a change (other than 
editorial) to the rule.
    For procedural information and the regulatory analysis, see the 
direct final rule published in the Rules and Regulations section of 
this issue of the Federal Register.

III. Background

    The NRC originally approved the AP1000 design certification in a 
final rule published on January 27, 2006 (71 FR 4464). On December 30, 
2011 (76 FR 82079), the NRC published a final rule amending appendix D, 
``Design Certification Rule for the AP1000 Design,'' to part 52, 
``Licenses, Certifications, and Approvals for



Nuclear Power Plants,'' of title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations 
(10 CFR) to incorporate AP1000 Design Control Document (DCD), Revision 
19, APP-GW-GL-702, dated June 13, 2011. On September 22, 2021 (86 FR 
52593), the NRC published a direct final rule extending the duration of 
the AP1000 design certification by five years, with an effective date 
of December 6, 2021.
    On July 2, 2025 (90 FR 28869), the NRC amended its regulations to 
replace the 15-year duration of design certifications with a 40-year 
duration, both for existing design certifications currently in effect 
and generically for future design certifications, including renewals. 
The NRC did not change the date of issuance or renewal for existing 
design certifications but changed their expiration dates based on the 
most recent date of issuance or renewal. The current AP1000 design 
certification expires on February 27, 2046.
    On February 10, 2012, the NRC issued combined licenses (COLs) to 
Southern Nuclear Operating Company (SNC) for the Vogtle Electric 
Generating Plant (VEGP) Units 3 and 4 (COLs NPF-91 and NPF-92). During 
the licensing, construction, and operation of VEGP Units 3 and 4, SNC 
submitted over 180 license amendment requests (LARs) to the NRC 
addressing design changes, construction-discovered issues, and 
operational refinements. The NRC reviewed and approved these LARs 
through safety evaluations for each approved amendment. In addition, 
SNC implemented numerous Tier 2 departures under the section VIII.B.5 
of appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 change process that did not require 
prior NRC approval. The VEGP licensing process also resolved the COL 
action items identified in DCD Revision 19 with site-specific design 
details, operational program descriptions, and as-built information. 
The VEGP Unit 3 entered commercial operation on July 31, 2023, and Unit 
4 did so on April 29, 2024.
    In SECY-26-0034, ``NRC Regulatory Pathways and Licensing Readiness 
for Near Term Large Light-Water Reactor Deployment,'' dated March 9, 
2026, the NRC staff informed the Commission, among other things, that 
it anticipated submission of the Westinghouse Electric Company LLC 
(Westinghouse) application to update and renew the AP1000 design 
certification. The NRC staff also informed the Commission of its plan 
to incorporate the as-built changes incorporated into VEGP Units 3 and 
4, previously approved safety findings, and lessons learned into a 
revised AP1000 design certification. The NRC's verification review 
determined that no new changes were incorporated into AP1000 DCD 
Revision 20 that require additional technical review, and that all 
changes incorporated into the AP1000 DCD Revision 20 were either 
previously reviewed and approved by the NRC or were incorporated using 
a process that does not require NRC approval. Therefore, the NRC is 
using the direct final rule process to update appendix D to 10 CFR part 
52 to include AP1000 DCD Revision 20. This renewal would improve 
regulatory clarity, avoid unnecessary re-review, and streamline future 
AP1000 licensing activities by providing applicants with an updated, 
standardized design basis. The NRC is amending appendix D to 10 CFR 
part 52 to include AP1000 DCD Revision 20. The NRC is also retaining 
the incorporation by reference of AP1000 DCD Revision 19 in appendix D 
to 10 CFR part 52 because several combined license holders were 
licensed to AP1000 Revision 19 and the incorporation of the AP1000 DCD 
Revision 19 in appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 remains part of the 
licensing basis for those combined license holders. Applicants could 
reference either revision in future applications.
    While 10 CFR 52.63(a) imposes restrictive limits on the types of 
changes that may be made while a design certification rule is in 
effect, 10 CFR 52.59(c) allows a design certification renewal applicant 
greater flexibility in seeking changes to the design certification. 
Thus, a design certification renewal application that includes 
amendments to a certified design is not required to address the 
criteria in 10 CFR 52.63, ``Finality of standard design 
certifications.'' However, if the amendment request entails such an 
extensive change to the design certification that an essentially new 
standard design is being proposed, 10 CFR 52.59(c) provides that an 
application for a design certification must be filed. The AP1000 
amendment request does not propose an essentially new standard design.
    The NRC is amending the design certification for the AP1000 
standard plant design to renew the AP1000 design certification for 40 
years from the effective date of the direct final rule. The NRC 
determined the submitted application for incorporation by reference of 
DCD Revision 20 into appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 is acceptable. 
Further, the Commission granted an exemption from 10 CFR 52.57(a) to 
allow renewal more than 36 months before expiration of the current 
design certification rule (91 FR 40596; July 2, 2026). The requirements 
of 10 CFR 52.55, ``Duration of certification,'' govern the duration of 
a design certification and the effect of timely renewal. The AP1000 
design certification rule does not expire until 2046.
    The NRC is amending section VIII.B.6 of appendix D to 10 CFR part 
52 to incorporate the alternative change process that was previously 
reviewed and approved for Vogtle Units 3 and 4 into appendix D to 10 
CFR part 52. The license amendments and exemptions included in AP1000 
DCD Revision 20 include a previously reviewed and approved change 
process for Tier 2* information. On December 21, 2017, SNC submitted 
LAR-17-037, and an associated exemption request, seeking changes to the 
Vogtle Units 3 and 4 COLs to add a license condition that would apply 
the change process for Tier 2 information for a proposed departure from 
Tier 2* information provided that specific criteria are not met. If one 
of the criteria were met for the proposed departure, then the proposed 
departure would continue to require prior NRC approval. On September 
20, 2018, the NRC granted the amendments and exemptions to Vogtle Units 
3 and 4 that effectively replaced the Tier 2* change process with an 
alternative process (reflected in a license condition) that applied the 
Tier 2 change process along with nine additional criteria to determine 
whether a license amendment was required. Inclusion of this change 
process in section VIII.B.6 of appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 promotes 
regulatory efficiency by eliminating the need for unnecessary licensing 
actions for applicants referencing either AP1000 DCD Revision 19 or 
AP1000 DCD Revision 20.

IV. Plain Writing

    The Plain Writing Act of 2010 (Pub. L. 111-274) requires Federal 
agencies to write documents in a clear, concise, and well-organized 
manner. The NRC has written this document to be consistent with the 
Plain Writing Act as well as the Presidential Memorandum, ``Plain 
Language in Government Writing,'' published June 10, 1998 (63 FR 
31885). The NRC requests comment on this proposed rule with respect to 
clarity and effectiveness of the language used.

V. National Environmental Policy Act: Environmental Assessment and 
Proposed Finding of No Significant Impact

    The NRC has determined under the National Environmental Policy Act 
of 1969, as amended (NEPA), and the NRC's regulations in subpart A, 
``National Environmental Policy Act--Regulations Implementing Section 
102(2),'' of 10 CFR part 51,



``Environmental Protection Regulations for Domestic Licensing and 
Related Regulatory Functions,'' that this proposed rule, if issued, 
would not be a major Federal action significantly affecting the quality 
of the human environment and, therefore, an environmental impact 
statement is not required. The NRC's generic determination in this 
regard, reflected in 10 CFR 51.32(b)(1), is based upon the following 
considerations: (1) A design certification rule does not authorize the 
siting, construction, or operation of a facility referencing any 
particular design, but only codifies a standard design certification in 
a rule (extending the AP1000 design certification and incorporating 
changes to the design in this case); (2) the NRC will evaluate the 
environmental impacts and issue an environmental finding in a Record of 
Decision as appropriate under NEPA as part of the application for the 
construction and operation of a facility referencing any particular 
design certification rule; and (3) comments on the environmental 
assessment will be limited to the consideration of severe accident 
mitigation design alternatives as required by 10 CFR 51.30(d). The 
environmental assessment is available in the companion direct final 
rule published in the Rules and Regulations section of this issue of 
the Federal Register. In keeping with Commission policy, that 
environmental assessment also updates the agency's consideration of 
severe accident mitigation design alternatives.

VI. Paperwork Reduction Act

    This proposed rule does not contain any new or amended collections 
of information subject to the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (44 
U.S.C. 3501 et seq.). Existing collections of information were approved 
by the Office of Management and Budget, control number 3150-0151.

Public Protection Notification

    The NRC may not conduct or sponsor, and a person is not required to 
respond to, a collection of information unless the document requesting 
or requiring the collection displays a currently valid Office of 
Management and Budget control number.

VII. Executive Orders

    The following are Executive orders that are related to this 
proposed rule:

A. Executive Order 12866: Regulatory Planning and Review (as amended by 
E.O. 14215, Ensuring Accountability for All Agencies)

    The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) has 
determined that this direct final rule is not a significant regulatory 
action.

B. Executive Order 14154: Unleashing American Energy

    The NRC has examined this proposed rule and has determined that it 
is consistent with the policies and directives outlined in E.O. 14154.

C. Executive Order 14192: Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation

    This action is determined to be a deregulatory action as defined by 
E.O. 14192. The AP1000 renewal and amendments will facilitate future 
reactor licensing by resolving design issues generically, which will 
lead to shorter and more efficient reviews yielding savings to the 
agency and future applicants.

D. Executive Order 14267: Reducing Anti-Competitive Regulatory Barriers

    E.O. 14267 requires the NRC to identify anti-competitive 
regulations for recission or modification. The purpose of a design 
certification rule is to facilitate the licensing process for future 
applicants that reference the certified design. Therefore, there are no 
anti-competitive regulatory barriers associated with this rule.

E. Executive Order 14270: Zero-Based Regulatory Budgeting To Unleash 
American Energy

    E.O. 14270, ``Zero-Based Regulatory Budgeting to Unleash American 
Energy,'' requires the NRC to insert a conditional sunset date into all 
new or amended NRC regulations provided the regulations are (1) 
promulgated under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, as amended (AEA), the 
Energy Reorganization Act of 1974, as amended (ERA), or the Nuclear 
Waste Policy Act of 1982, as amended (NWPA); (2) not statutorily 
required; and (3) not part of the NRC's permitting regime. The NRC 
determined that the regulatory changes proposed in this rule are part 
of the NRC permitting regime as future licensing applicants may 
reference the AP1000 certified design to obtain operating licenses. 
Therefore, the NRC views this rulemaking to be outside the scope of 
E.O. 14270 and did not insert conditional sunset dates for the 
regulatory changes in this direct final rule.

III. Background

    The NRC originally approved the AP1000 design certification in a 
final rule published on January 27, 2006 (71 FR 4464). On December 30, 
2011 (76 FR 82079), the NRC published a final rule amending appendix D, 
``Design Certification Rule for the AP1000 Design,'' to part 52, 
``Licenses, Certifications, and Approvals for Nuclear Power Plants,'' 
of title 10 of the Code of Federal Regulations (10 CFR) to incorporate 
AP1000 Design Control Document (DCD), Revision 19, APP-GW-GL-702, dated 
June 13, 2011. On September 22, 2021 (86 FR 52593), the NRC published a 
direct final rule extending the duration of the AP1000 design 
certification by five years, with an effective date of December 6, 
2021.
    On July 2, 2025 (90 FR 28869), the NRC amended its regulations to 
replace the 15-year duration of design certifications with a 40-year 
duration, both for existing design certifications currently in effect 
and generically for



future design certifications, including renewals. The NRC did not 
change the date of issuance or renewal for existing design 
certifications but changed their expiration dates based on the most 
recent date of issuance or renewal. The current AP1000 design 
certification expires on February 27, 2046.
    On February 10, 2012, the NRC issued combined licenses (COLs) to 
Southern Nuclear Operating Company (SNC) for the Vogtle Electric 
Generating Plant (VEGP) Units 3 and 4 (COLs NPF-91 and NPF-92). During 
the licensing, construction, and operation of VEGP Units 3 and 4, SNC 
submitted over 180 license amendment requests (LARs) to the NRC 
addressing design changes, construction-discovered issues, and 
operational refinements. The NRC reviewed and approved these LARs 
through safety evaluations for each approved amendment. In addition, 
SNC implemented numerous Tier 2 departures under the section VIII.B.5 
of appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 change process that did not require 
prior NRC approval. The VEGP licensing process also resolved the COL 
action items identified in DCD Revision 19 with site-specific design 
details, operational program descriptions, and as-built information. 
The VEGP Unit 3 entered commercial operation on July 31, 2023, and Unit 
4 did so on April 29, 2024.
    In SECY-26-0034, ``NRC Regulatory Pathways and Licensing Readiness 
for Near Term Large Light-Water Reactor Deployment,'' dated March 9, 
2026, the NRC staff informed the Commission, among other things, that 
it anticipated submission of the Westinghouse Electric Company LLC 
(Westinghouse) application to update and renew the AP1000 design 
certification. The NRC staff also informed the Commission of its plan 
to incorporate the as-built changes incorporated into VEGP Units 3 and 
4, previously approved safety findings, and lessons learned into a 
revised AP1000 design certification. The NRC's verification review 
determined that no new changes were incorporated into AP1000 DCD 
Revision 20 that require additional technical review, and that all 
changes incorporated into the AP1000 DCD Revision 20 were either 
previously reviewed and approved by the NRC or were incorporated using 
a process that does not require NRC approval. Therefore, the NRC is 
using the direct final rule process to update appendix D to 10 CFR part 
52 to include AP1000 DCD Revision 20. This renewal would improve 
regulatory clarity, avoid unnecessary re-review, and streamline future 
AP1000 licensing activities by providing applicants with an updated, 
standardized design basis. The NRC is amending appendix D to 10 CFR 
part 52 to include AP1000 DCD Revision 20. The NRC is also retaining 
the incorporation by reference of AP1000 DCD Revision 19 in appendix D 
to 10 CFR part 52 because several combined license holders were 
licensed to AP1000 Revision 19 and the incorporation of the AP1000 DCD 
Revision 19 in appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 remains part of the 
licensing basis for those combined license holders. Applicants could 
reference either revision in future applications.
    While 10 CFR 52.63(a) imposes restrictive limits on the types of 
changes that may be made while a design certification rule is in 
effect, 10 CFR 52.59(c) allows a design certification renewal applicant 
greater flexibility in seeking changes to the design certification. 
Thus, a design certification renewal application that includes 
amendments to a certified design is not required to address the 
criteria in 10 CFR 52.63, ``Finality of standard design 
certifications.'' However, if the amendment request entails such an 
extensive change to the design certification that an essentially new 
standard design is being proposed, 10 CFR 52.59(c) provides that an 
application for a design certification must be filed. The AP1000 
amendment request does not propose an essentially new standard design.
    The NRC is amending the design certification for the AP1000 
standard plant design to renew the AP1000 design certification for 40 
years from the effective date of this direct final rule. The NRC 
determined the submitted application for incorporation by reference of 
DCD Revision 20 into appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 is acceptable. 
Further, the Commission granted an exemption from 10 CFR 52.57(a) to 
allow renewal more than 36 months before expiration of the current 
design certification rule (91 FR 40596; July 2, 2026). The requirements 
of 10 CFR 52.55, ``Duration of certification,'' govern the duration of 
a design certification and the effect of timely renewal. The AP1000 
design certification rule does not expire until 2046.
    The NRC is amending section VIII.B.6 of appendix D to 10 CFR part 
52 to incorporate the alternative change process that was previously 
reviewed and approved for Vogtle Units 3 and 4 into appendix D to 10 
CFR part 52. The license amendments and exemptions included in AP1000 
DCD Revision 20 include a previously reviewed and approved change 
process for Tier 2* information. On December 21, 2017, SNC submitted 
LAR-17-037, and an associated exemption request, seeking changes to the 
Vogtle Units 3 and 4 COLs to add a license condition that would apply 
the change process for Tier 2 information for a proposed departure from 
Tier 2* information provided that specific criteria are not met. If one 
of the criteria were met for the proposed departure, then the proposed 
departure would continue to require prior NRC approval. On September 
20, 2018, the NRC granted the amendments and exemptions to Vogtle Units 
3 and 4 that effectively replaced the Tier 2* change process with an 
alternative process (reflected in a license condition) that applied the 
Tier 2 change process along with nine additional criteria to determine 
whether a license amendment was required. Inclusion of this change 
process in section VIII.B.6 of appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 promotes 
regulatory efficiency by eliminating the need for unnecessary licensing 
actions for applicants referencing either AP1000 DCD Revision 19 or 
AP1000 DCD Revision 20.

VI. Regulatory Flexibility Certification

    Under the Regulatory Flexibility Act (5 U.S.C. 605(b)), the NRC 
certifies that this direct final rule does not have a significant 
economic impact on a substantial number of small entities. This direct 
final rule affects only the licensing and operation of large nuclear 
power plants. The companies that own these plants or would apply to own 
such a plant do not fall within the scope of the definition of ``small 
entities'' set forth in the Regulatory Flexibility Act or the size 
standards established by the NRC (10 CFR 2.810).

VII. Regulatory Analysis

    The NRC has not prepared a regulatory analysis for this direct 
final rule. The NRC prepares regulatory analyses for rulemakings that 
establish generic regulatory requirements applicable to all licensees. 
Design certifications are not generic rulemakings in the sense that 
design certifications do not establish standards or requirements with 
which all licensees must comply. Rather, design certifications are NRC 
approvals of specific nuclear power plant designs by rulemaking, which 
then may be voluntarily referenced by applicants for combined licenses 
or construction permits. For these reasons, the NRC concludes that 
preparation of a regulatory analysis is neither required nor 
appropriate.

constitute backfitting as defined in 10 CFR 50.109, ``Backfitting,''

does not constitute backfitting because it does not impose new or 
changed requirements on any previously issued licenses that incorporate

section III of this document, the NRC does not need to address the 
finality criteria in 10 CFR 52.63.

X. National Environmental Policy Act: Environmental Assessment and 
Final Finding of No Significant Impact

A. Introduction

    The NRC is renewing the design certification for the AP1000 
standard plant design for 40 years from the effective date of this 
direct final rule. The NRC also is updating the design certification to 
reflect changes provided by Westinghouse, by letter dated March 27, 
2026. The NRC issues design certification rules as appendices to 10 CFR 
part 52. The purpose of this amendment is to renew the period that the 
AP1000 design certification is valid for referencing by an applicant 
and includes incorporation of VEGP Units 3 and 4 license amendment 
approvals under their respective COLs. Specifically, Revision 20 of the 
AP1000 DCD incorporates the issuance of Amendments 142 and 141 for VEGP 
Units 3 and 4 granting changes to the Tier 2* departure evaluation 
process with a 10 CFR 51.22(c)(9) categorical exclusion determination 
and is incorporated by reference into this NEPA evaluation. This rule 
amends Section VIII.B.6 of appendix D to 10 CFR part 52 to include 
changes to the Tier 2* departure evaluation process for the AP1000 
design. With the renewal approval, the AP1000 design certification rule 
would remain valid for referencing until 40 years after the effective 
date of this direct final rule.
    The NRC developed in section X, ``National Environmental Policy 
Act: Environmental Assessment and Final Finding of No Significant 
Impact,'' of this document containing this evaluation of the 
environmental impacts of the renewal request. The NRC has documented 
its finding of no significant impact in accordance with the 
requirements of 10 CFR 51.21, ``Criteria for and identification of 
licensing and regulatory actions requiring environmental assessments''; 
10 CFR 51.31, ``Determinations based on environmental assessment''; and 
the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969, as amended (NEPA). This 
evaluation also addresses the severe accident mitigation design 
alternatives (SAMDAs) that the NRC has previously evaluated for the 
Westinghouse AP1000 design in the environmental assessment (EA) dated 
September 1, 2021. The evaluation does not address the site-specific 
environmental impacts of constructing and operating any facility that 
references the AP1000 design certification at a particular site. The



SAMDA analysis completed as part of this direct final rule can be 
incorporated by reference into the environmental determination related 
to an application for siting, construction, or operation of a nuclear 
plant that references the AP1000 standard design. The NRC would 
evaluate those impacts as part of any application(s) for the siting, 
construction, or operation of such a facility.
    As discussed later in this section of this direct final rule, the 
NRC has determined that issuing the subject renewal does not constitute 
a major Federal action significantly affecting the quality of the human 
environment. This determination is based on the generic finding made in 
10 CFR 51.32(b)(2) that there is no significant environmental impact 
associated with this renewal of the AP1000 design certification. This 
renewal does not authorize the siting, construction, or operation of a 
facility referencing the AP1000 design; it only codifies an extension 
of the period an applicant can reference the AP1000 design in a COL 
application. Furthermore, because the certification and update of the 
design constitute a rule change rather than a physical action, it does 
not involve the commitment of any resources that have alternative uses. 
The 10 CFR 51.32(b)(2) generic finding of no significant impact is, 
essentially, the legal equivalent of a categorical exclusion (72 FR 
49427; August 28, 2007). Therefore, the NRC has not prepared an 
environmental impact statement (EIS) for this direct final rule.
    Under 10 CFR 51.30(d), an EA for an amendment, of which a renewal 
is, to a design certification is limited to the consideration of 
whether the design change that is the subject of the proposed amendment 
renders a SAMDA previously rejected in the earlier EA to become cost 
beneficial, or results in the identification of new SAMDAs, in which 
case, the costs and benefits of new SAMDAs and the bases for not 
incorporating new SAMDAs in the design certification must be addressed.
    This amendment renewal request brings the AP1000 design 
certification up to date. Revision 20 to the DCD includes construction 
and operating experience from current AP1000 nuclear power plants 
operating in the U.S. today (i.e., Vogtle Units 3 and 4) and will allow 
for consistency and standardization in future AP1000 plant 
applications. Although DCD Revision 20 does not affect the overall risk 
profile for the AP1000 design (i.e., Revision 20 to the AP1000 DCD does 
not change the risk insights and conclusions of the AP1000 design 
certification or COL probabilistic risk assessments), as discussed in 
this section of the direct final rule, the NRC updated its SAMDA 
evaluation and performed sensitivity analyses in section X.B.2 of this 
document to determine whether any SAMDAs previously rejected in the 
earlier AP1000 design certification EAs could become cost beneficial 
due to updated cost parameter information.

B. Severe Accident Mitigation Design Alternative Evaluation

    Consistent with the objectives of standardization and early 
resolution of design issues, the Commission decided to evaluate SAMDAs 
as part of the original design certification for the AP1000 design. In 
its ``Policy Statement on Severe Reactor Accidents Regarding Future 
Designs and Existing Plants'' (50 FR 32138; August 8, 1985), the 
Commission defined the term ``severe accident'' as an event that is 
``beyond the substantial coverage of design-basis events (DBEs),'' 
including events where there is substantial damage to the reactor core 
(whether or not there are serious offsite consequences). These DBEs are 
analyzed in accordance with NUREG-0800, ``Standard Review Plan for the 
Review of Safety Analysis Reports for Nuclear Power Plants: LWR 
Edition,'' and documented in several chapters of the AP1000 DCD, such 
as Chapters 2, 3, 15, and 19.
B.1 Westinghouse's DCD Revision 20 Assessments of SAMDAs
    In the transmittal letter for the AP1000 renewal, Westinghouse 
states that Appendix 1B of the AP1000 DCD Revision 19 fulfills this 
requirement and addresses the costs and benefits of 15 SAMDAs that are 
not included in the AP1000 plant design. Revision 19 Appendix 1B has 
been retained in AP1000 DCD Revision 20. Westinghouse continues to find 
that the previously considered SAMDAs, which were deemed to be non-cost 
beneficial, remain non-cost beneficial and that no new design 
alternatives were identified. Their evaluation concludes that the SAMDA 
review performed in AP1000 DCD Revision 19 with regard to the viability 
of the proposed SAMDAs remains valid and applicable to the AP1000 plant 
design presented in AP1000 DCD Revision 20.
B.2 NRC Evaluation
    The NRC conducted an audit of Appendix 1B as part of its DCD 
Revision 20 application review. During that review, the NRC found that 
Westinghouse did not evaluate the effect of applying current dollar 
values to the cost analysis in Appendix 1B of Revision 20 of the AP1000 
DCD. An environmental evaluation considers the present conditions at 
the time of the application submission and this would include cost 
evaluations related to SAMDAs. Several recent new reactor construction 
permit applications have used appropriate current cost values in their 
initial SAMDA evaluations. For example, these applicants applied the 
updated dollar-per-person-rem value in accordance with NUREG-1530, 
``Reassessment of NRC's Dollar per Person-Rem Conversion Factor 
Policy,'' Revision 1, issued February 2022. These new reactor 
applicants also applied current dollar inflation adjustments to 
undiscounted dollar parameter values in the cost formulas in Section 
5.7 as directed in Section 5.8 of NUREG/BR-0184, ``Regulatory Analysis 
Technical Evaluation Handbook,'' published in January 1997.
    The NRC uses the dollar-per-person-rem value to monetize the impact 
of a potential severe accident, which the agency then compares to the 
costs of a mitigation measure to determine if it is cost beneficial. 
Significantly, the agency published the revised dollar-per-person-rem 
values in 2022, after the agency reviewed Revision 19 of the AP1000 
DCD, but before Westinghouse submitted Revision 20. Thus, consideration 
of this new information could change the agency's determination on 
whether any of the proposed SAMDAs are cost beneficial.
    Similarly, Westinghouse did not provide a discussion on adjusting 
for inflation for undiscounted cost parameters as recommended in 
Section 5.8 of NUREG/BR-0184. Therefore, the NRC conducted a review of 
Appendix 1B to DCD Revision 20 to determine if the Westinghouse SAMDA 
conclusion is still valid when applying the noted updated monetary 
values.
    The NRC reviewed the information in Appendix 1B to Tier 2, Chapter 
1, of the AP1000 DCD, Revision 20, and in the EAs issued for the 
original AP1000 design certification rule in January 2006, for the 
amendment to the AP1000 design certification in January 2011, and for 
the amendment to extend the design certification in September 2021. Due 
to the intervening time between when Westinghouse originally developed 
Appendix 1B and the submission of Revision 20, the NRC examined, with 
respect to the guidance in Section 5.8 of NUREG/BR-0184 and Revision 1 
of NUREG-1530, whether the revised dollar values have the potential to 
change the cost-benefit conclusions for any of the SAMDAs. The NRC 
evaluated new cost information on updates to a dollar-per-person-rem 
value of $7,300



consistent with guidance in NUREG-1530, Revision 1, and inflated to 
2026 dollars the previously undiscounted cost parameters used in the 
maximum benefit valuation formulas of NUREG/BR-0184. Based on the 
updated maximum benefit valuation with sensitivity analyses, the NRC 
concluded that the new cost information would not change the 
conclusions reached in the EAs issued for the original, amended AP1000 
design certification rules and the renewal AP1000.
    For any future application referencing the AP1000 design 
certification, the inflation of cost parameters (e.g., the dollar-per-
person-rem value) and revised cost-benefit guidance should be 
considered in determining the subsequent AP1000 applicability of the 
SAMDA conclusions previously described. This clarification for future 
AP1000 applications is noted in paragraph VI.7 of appendix D of 10 CFR 
part 52.

C. Summary of the Environmental Impacts of the Direct Final Rule

    On the basis of 10 CFR 51.32(b) and the evaluation in section X.B 
of this document, the NRC concludes that the direct final rule will not 
have a significant effect on the quality of the human environment. 
Accordingly, the NRC is not required to prepare an EIS for this direct 
final rule.
    Since no physical changes would occur in the human environment, the 
agency action (rulemaking) would not affect any threatened or 
endangered species or historic properties. Accordingly, the NRC finds 
that the direct final rule would have no significant environmental 
impact.

D. Finding of No Significant Impact

    The NRC has prepared this evaluation to determine the environmental 
effects of the agency action (rulemaking). This rule is primarily 
administrative or procedural in nature and therefore would not have any 
physical environmental effect. As explained in sections X.A through C 
of this document, the NRC has determined that the rulemaking would not 
change the conclusions in Appendix 1B of Revision 20 to the AP1000 DCD 
and would result in no new or different environmental effects. 
Therefore, the NRC concludes that the rule's action would not have a 
significant effect on the quality of the human environment. Based on 
this conclusion, the NRC has determined there is no need to prepare an 
environmental impact statement. Accordingly, the NRC finds the direct 
final rule would have no significant environmental impact. This 
environmental assessment and finding of no significant impact can be 
tracked with identification number NEPA ID EAXX-429-00-000-1784080234.

XI. Paperwork Reduction Act

    This direct final rule does not contain any new or amended 
collections of information subject to the Paperwork Reduction Act of 
1995 (44 U.S.C. 3501 et seq.). Existing collections of information were 
approved by the Office of Management and Budget, approval number 3150-
0151.

Public Protection Notification

    The NRC may not conduct or sponsor, and a person is not required to 
respond to, a collection of information unless the document requesting 
or requiring the collection displays a currently valid Office of 
Management and Budget control number.

XII. Executive Orders

    The following are Executive orders that are related to this direct 
final rule:

A. Executive Order 12866: Regulatory Planning and Review (as amended by 
E.O. 14215, Ensuring Accountability for All Agencies)

    The Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs (OIRA) has 
determined that this direct final rule is not a significant regulatory 
action.

B. Executive Order 14154: Unleashing American Energy

    The NRC has examined this direct final rule and has determined that 
it is consistent with the policies and directives outlined in E.O. 
14154.

C. Executive Order 14192: Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation

    This action is determined to be a deregulatory action as defined by 
E.O. 14192. The AP1000 renewal and amendments will facilitate future 
reactor licensing by resolving design issues generically, which will 
lead to shorter and more efficient reviews yielding savings to the 
agency and future applicants.

D. Executive Order 14267: Reducing Anti-Competitive Regulatory Barriers

    E.O. 14267 requires the NRC to identify anti-competitive 
regulations for recission or modification. The purpose of a design 
certification rule is to facilitate the licensing process for future 
applicants that reference the certified design. Therefore, there are no 
anti-competitive regulatory barriers associated with this rule.

E. Executive Order 14270: Zero-Based Regulatory Budgeting To Unleash 
American Energy

    E.O. 14270, ``Zero-Based Regulatory Budgeting to Unleash American 
Energy,'' requires the NRC to insert a conditional sunset date into all 
new or amended NRC regulations provided the regulations are (1) 
promulgated under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, as amended (AEA), the 
Energy Reorganization Act of 1974, as amended (ERA), or the Nuclear 
Waste Policy Act of 1982, as amended (NWPA); (2) not statutorily 
required; and (3) not part of the NRC's permitting regime. The NRC 
determined that the regulatory changes in this rule are part of the NRC 
permitting regime as future licensing applicants may reference the 
AP1000 certified design to obtain operating licenses. Therefore, the 
NRC views this rulemaking to be outside the scope of E.O. 14270 and did 
not insert conditional sunset dates for the regulatory changes in this 
direct final rule.

XIII. Congressional Review Act

    This direct final rule is a rule as defined in the Congressional 
Review Act (5 U.S.C. 801-808). However, the Office of Management and 
Budget has found that it does not meet the criteria at 5 U.S.C. 804(2).

XIV. Compatibility of Agreement State Regulations

    Under the ``Agreement State Program Policy Statement'' approved by 
the Commission on October 2, 2017, and published in the Federal 
Register (82 FR 48535; October 18, 2017), this rule is classified as 
compatibility ``NRC.'' Category NRC consists of program elements over 
which the NRC cannot discontinue its regulatory authority pursuant to 
the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 (AEA), as amended, or provisions of 10 
CFR. Under the Policy Statement, a program element means any component 
or function of a radiation control regulatory program, including 
regulations and other legally binding requirements imposed on regulated 
persons, which contributes to the implementation of that program. The 
NRC maintains regulatory authority over program elements classified as 
category NRC and the Agreement States must not adopt these NRC program 
elements. However, an Agreement State may inform its licensees of these 
NRC requirements through a mechanism under the State's administrative 
procedure laws, as long as the State adopts these provisions solely for 
the purposes of notification, and does not



exercise any regulatory authority as a result.

XV. Voluntary Consensus Standards

    The National Technology Transfer and Advancement Act of 1995, 
Public Law 104-113, requires that Federal agencies use technical 
standards that are developed or adopted by voluntary consensus 
standards bodies unless the use of such a standard is inconsistent with 
applicable law or otherwise impractical. Design certifications are not 
generic rulemakings establishing a generally applicable standard with 
which all 10 CFR parts 50 and 52 nuclear power plant licensees must 
comply. Design certifications are Commission approvals of specific 
nuclear power plant designs by rulemaking. Furthermore, design 
certifications are initiated by an applicant for rulemaking, rather 
than by the NRC. This action does not constitute the establishment of a 
standard that contains generally applicable requirements.

XVII. Procedures for Access to Proprietary and Security-Related 
Information for Preparation of Comments on the Direct Final Rule

    This section contains instructions regarding how the non-publicly 
available documents related to this rule, and specifically the 
information contained in Enclosure 2 of the March 27, 2026, letter from 
Westinghouse, ``AP1000 Design Certification Renewal Request,'' may be 
accessed by interested persons who wish to comment on the design 
certification renewal. These documents contain proprietary information 
and security-related information.
    Interested persons who desire access to proprietary information or 
security-related information on the AP1000 design certification 
extension should first request access to that information from 
Westinghouse Electric Company LLC, the design certification applicant. 
A request for access should be submitted to the NRC if the applicant 
does not either grant or deny access by the 10-day deadline described 
in the following section.

Submitting a Request to the NRC for Access

    Within 10 days after publication of this direct final rule, any 
individual or entity who believes access to proprietary information or 
security-related information is necessary in order to submit comments 
on this rule may request access to such information. Requests for 
access to proprietary information or security-related information 
submitted more than 10 days after publication of this document will not 
be considered absent a showing of good cause for the late filing 
explaining why the request could not have been filed earlier.
    The requestor shall submit a letter requesting permission to access 
proprietary information or security-related information to the Office 
of the Secretary, U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Attention: 
Rulemakings and Adjudications Staff, Washington, DC 20555-0001. The 
email address for the Office of the Secretary is 
[email protected]. The requestor must send a copy of the 
request to the design certification applicant at the same time as the 
original transmission to the NRC using the same method of transmission. 
Requests to the applicant must be sent to Zachary S. Harper, Manager, 
Licensing Engineering, Westinghouse Electric Company LLC, 1000 
Westinghouse Drive, Cranberry Township, Pennsylvania 16066.
    The request must include the following information:
    (1) The name of this design certification, AP1000 Design 
Certification; the rulemaking identification number, RIN 3150-AL70; the 
rulemaking docket number, NRC-2026-2377; and the Federal Register 
citation for this rule.
    (2) The name, address, and email of the requestor.
    (3) The identity of the individual(s) to whom access is to be 
provided, including the identity of any expert, consultant, or 
assistant who will aid the requestor in evaluating the information.
    (4) The requestor's need for the proprietary information or 
security-related information in order to prepare meaningful comments on 
the design certification extension must be demonstrated. Each of the 
following areas must be addressed with specificity:
    (a) The specific issue or subject matter on which the requestor 
wishes to comment.
    (b) An explanation why information which is publicly available is 
insufficient to provide the basis for developing meaningful comment on 
the AP1000 design certification extension rule with respect to the 
issue or subject matter described in paragraph 4.a. of this section.
    (c) The technical competence (demonstrable knowledge, skill, 
training or education) of the requestor to effectively utilize the 
requested information to provide the basis for meaningful comment. 
Technical competence may be shown by reliance on a qualified expert, 
consultant, or assistant who satisfies these criteria.
    (d) A chronology and discussion of the requestor's attempts to 
obtain the information from the design certification applicant, and the 
final communication from the requestor to the applicant and the 
applicant's response, if any was provided, with respect to the request 
for access to proprietary information or security-related information 
must be submitted.
    Based on an evaluation of the information submitted under paragraph 
(4) of this section, as applicable, the NRC will determine within 10 
days of receipt of the request whether the requestor has established a 
legitimate need for access to proprietary information or security-
related information.

Determination of Legitimate Need for Access

    If the NRC determines that the requestor has established a 
legitimate need for access to proprietary information or security-
related information, the NRC will notify the requestor in writing that 
access to proprietary information or security-related information has 
been granted. The written notification will contain instructions on how 
the requestor may obtain copies of the requested documents and any 
other conditions that may apply to access to those documents. These 
conditions may include, but are not limited to, the signing of a Non-
Disclosure Agreement or Affidavit by each individual who will be 
granted access.

Filing of Comments on the AP1000 Design Certification Renewal Rule 
Based on Non-Public Information

    Any comments on this final rule that are based upon the disclosed 
proprietary information or security-related information must be filed 
by the requestor no later than 25 days after receipt of (or access to) 
that information, or the close of the public comment period, whichever 
is later. The commenter must comply with all NRC requirements regarding 
the submission of proprietary information and security-related 
information to the NRC when submitting comments to the NRC (including 
marking and transmission requirements).

Review of Denials of Access

    If the request for access to proprietary information or security-
related information is denied by the NRC after a determination on 
requisite need, the NRC staff shall immediately notify the requestor in 
writing, briefly stating the reason or reasons for the denial.
    The requestor may challenge the NRC staff's adverse determination 
by filing a challenge within five days of receipt of that determination 
with the NRC's Executive Director for Operations under 10 CFR 9.29(d).

XVIII. Incorporation by Reference--Reasonable Availability to 
Interested Parties

    The NRC is incorporating by reference a document submitted by 
Westinghouse that updates the AP1000 design certification to Revision 
20. As discussed in the ``Discussion'' section of this document, DCD 
Revision 20 includes updates made to the AP1000 design to represent a 
current,



construction-validated design. The NRC is required by law to obtain 
approval for incorporation by reference from the Office of the Federal 
Register.
    The Office of the Federal Register's requirements for incorporation 
by reference are set forth in 1 CFR part 51. These regulations require 
an agency to include in a direct final rule a discussion of the ways 
that the materials the agency incorporates by reference are reasonably 
available to interested parties or how it worked to make those 
materials reasonably available to interested parties. The discussion in 
this section complies with the requirement for direct final rules as 
set forth in 1 CFR 51.5(b)(2).
    The NRC considers ``interested parties'' to include all potential 
NRC stakeholders, not only the individuals and entities regulated or 
otherwise subject to the NRC's regulatory oversight. These NRC 
stakeholders are not a homogeneous group but vary with respect to the 
considerations for determining reasonable availability. Therefore, the 
NRC distinguishes between different classes of interested parties for 
the purposes of determining whether the material is ``reasonably 
available.'' The NRC considers the following to be classes of 
interested parties in NRC rulemakings with regard to the material to be 
incorporated by reference:
     Individuals and small entities regulated or otherwise 
subject to the NRC's regulatory oversight (this class also includes 
applicants and potential applicants for licenses and other NRC 
regulatory approvals) and who are subject to the material to be 
incorporated by reference by rulemaking. In this context, ``small 
entities'' has the same meaning as a ``small entity'' under 10 CFR 
2.810.
     Large entities otherwise subject to the NRC's regulatory 
oversight (this class also includes applicants and potential applicants 
for licenses and other NRC regulatory approvals) and who are subject to 
the material to be incorporated by reference by rulemaking. In this 
context, ``large entities'' are those that do not qualify as a ``small 
entity'' under 10 CFR 2.810.
     Non-governmental organizations with institutional 
interests in the matters regulated by the NRC.
     Other Federal agencies, States, local governmental bodies 
(within the meaning of 10 CFR 2.315(c)).
     Federally-recognized and State-recognized \2\ Indian 
Tribes.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \2\ State-recognized Indian Tribes are not within the scope of 
10 CFR 2.315(c). However, for purposes of the NRC's compliance with 
1 CFR 51.5, ``interested parties'' includes a broad set of 
stakeholders, including State-recognized Indian Tribes.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

     Members of the general public (i.e., individual, 
unaffiliated members of the public who are not regulated or otherwise 
subject to the NRC's regulatory oversight) who may wish to gain access 
to the materials which the NRC incorporates by reference by rulemaking 
in order to participate in the rulemaking process.
    The NRC makes the materials incorporated by reference available for 
inspection to all interested parties, by appointment, at the NRC 
Technical Library, which is located at Two White Flint North, 11545 
Rockville Pike, Rockville, Maryland 20852; telephone: 301-415-7000; 
email: [email protected]. In addition, as described in the 
``Availability of Documents'' section of this document, documents 
related to this direct final rule are available online in the NRC's 
Agencywide Documents Access and Management System (ADAMS) Public 
Documents collection at https://www.nrc.gov/reading-rm/adams.html.
    The NRC concludes that the materials the NRC is incorporating by 
reference in this final rule are reasonably available to all interested 
parties because the materials are available to all interested parties 
in multiple ways and in a manner consistent with their interest in the 
materials.

AGENCY: U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (``ICE''), Department 
of Homeland Security (``DHS''); Executive Office for Immigration Review 
(``EOIR''), Department of Justice (``DOJ'').

ACTION: Final rule.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: On June 27, 2025, the Departments issued an interim final rule 
(``IFR'') to streamline assessment of civil penalties under the 
Immigration and Nationality Act (``INA'') for aliens who fail to depart 
during a voluntary departure period, willfully fail or refuse to depart 
after a final removal order and certain other proscribed activities, or 
are apprehended while improperly entering or attempting to enter the 
United States. This final rule addresses comments and finalizes the IFR 
with one change: it permits acceptance of a late-filed appeal based on 
documented mail delivery delays that ICE finds were beyond the alien's 
control.

DATES: The effective date of this final rule is October 14, 2026.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: 
    For DHS: Office of the Principal Legal Advisor, Regulatory Affairs 
Unit, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Department of Homeland 
Security, 500 12th Street SW, Washington, DC 20536; telephone (202) 
732-6960.
    For DOJ: Jamee E. Comans, Assistant Director, Office of Policy, 
Executive Office for Immigration Review, 5107 Leesburg Pike, Suite

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

I. Background

A. Basis and Purpose of the IFR

    On January 20, 2025, President Trump issued Executive Order 
(``E.O.'') 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion. E.O. 
14159, 90 FR 8443 (Jan. 29, 2025). In Section 2 of that E.O., President

removable aliens'' and ``to achieve the total and efficient enforcement 
of those laws, including through lawful incentives and detention 
capabilities.'' 90 FR 8443. Section 8 of E.O. 14159 directs the 
Secretary of Homeland Security, in coordination with the Secretary of 
the Treasury, to ``take all appropriate action to ensure the assessment 
and collection of all fines and penalties that the Secretary of 
Homeland Security is authorized by law to assess and collect from 
aliens unlawfully present in the United States, including aliens who 
unlawfully entered or unlawfully attempted to enter the United 
States.'' 90 FR 8444-45. Section 12 of E.O. 14159 directs the Secretary 
of Homeland Security, in coordination with the Secretary of State and 
the Attorney General, ``to take all appropriate action . . . to adopt 
policies and procedures to encourage aliens unlawfully in the United 
States to voluntarily depart as soon as possible, including through 
enhanced usage of the provisions of section 240B of the INA (8 U.S.C. 
1229c), international agreements or assistance, or any other measures 
that encourage aliens unlawfully in the United States to depart as 
promptly as possible''. 90 FR 8445. In Section 2 of E.O. 14165, 
Securing Our Borders, President Trump directed the Departments to 
``take all appropriate action to secure the borders of our Nation,'' 
including by ``[d]eterring and preventing the entry of illegal aliens 
into the United States'' and by ``[o]btaining complete operational 
control of the borders of the United States.'' E.O. 14165, 90 FR 8467 
(Jan. 30, 2025). In Proclamation 10935, President Trump established 
Project Homecoming to ``present illegal aliens with a choice: either 
leave the United States voluntarily, with the support and financial 
assistance of the Federal-government, or face the consequences.'' 
Establishing Project Homecoming, 90 FR 20357 (May 14, 2025).
    On June 27, 2025, the Departments issued an IFR, effective on the 
same date, to streamline how DHS assesses certain civil monetary 
penalties that Congress has long authorized under the INA. See 
Imposition and Collection of Civil Penalties for Certain Immigration-
Related Violations, 90 FR 27439 (June 27, 2025). The IFR applies to 
three categories of illegal aliens: (1) aliens who willfully fail or 
refuse to depart the United States pursuant to a final order of removal 
or take certain actions to thwart their departure or removal, INA 
274D(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1324d(a)(1); (2) aliens who voluntarily fail to 
depart the United States within the time period specified pursuant to a 
voluntary departure order, INA 240B(d)(1)(A)-(B), 8 U.S.C. 
1229c(d)(1)(A)-(B); \1\ and (3) aliens apprehended while entering (or 
attempting to enter) the United States unlawfully, INA 275(b)(1), 8 
U.S.C. 1325(b)(1). See also 8 CFR 281.1(a) (scope of the IFR). The IFR 
revised the Departments' civil monetary penalty procedures for these 
categories of aliens so that DHS can more efficiently and effectively 
promote compliance with Immigration Court orders and support border 
security. See 90 FR 27442. The IFR partially implements Section 8 of 
E.O. 14159 and supports DHS's efforts, as directed by the President, to 
faithfully execute the immigration laws, to achieve total and efficient 
enforcement of those laws, and to secure the borders of the United 
States. See 90 FR 27446-47. The IFR also advances the purpose of 
Proclamation 10935, Establishing Project Homecoming, by reinforcing 
that aliens must either voluntarily depart the United States, with 
Federal support as applicable, or face statutorily authorized 
consequences for failing to comply with removal or departure orders.

    As the IFR explains, the revised procedures are needed to 
complement DHS's efforts to address the large number of aliens who 
remain in the United States despite having final removal or voluntary 
departure orders. See 90 FR 27446. Prior to the issuance of the IFR, 
there were approximately 1.5 million aliens on ICE's non-detained 
docket with final orders of removal, including those who failed to 
depart after being granted voluntary departure pursuant to INA 240B, 8 
U.S.C. 1229c. For example, as discussed in the IFR, in FY 2024 alone, 
EOIR issued more than 282,000 final removal orders, but DHS data 
indicate that only about 10 percent of those orders were executed. 90 
FR 27445. In the same year, EOIR granted approximately 8,800 voluntary 
departure orders, yet only about 50 percent of those aliens confirmed 
their departure. Id. Moreover, as a result of the prior 
Administration's policies, including its border policies, the



Immigration Court caseload has dramatically increased in recent 
years.\2\ In the third quarter of FY 2026, there were over 3.4 million 
pending Immigration Court cases, a large percentage of which, if 
consistent with previous years, will result in removal or voluntary 
departure orders once adjudicated.\3\ Thus, without the IFR's 
intervention, the number of aliens who remain in the United States 
despite final removal and voluntary departure orders would have been 
likely to increase in the coming years. Id.

    An Immigration Court's order of an alien's removal, unless reversed 
or vacated on appeal, is binding on all parties, including aliens. See 
8 CFR 1240.1(a)(1)(i), 1240.41, 1241.1. Aliens subject to final 
executable orders of removal \4\ remain legally obligated to comply 
with Immigration Court orders to depart the United States, regardless 
of prior DHS policies that did not prioritize all such aliens for 
apprehension, detention, and removal. The large number of unexecuted 
removal orders and the growth of DHS's non-detained docket demonstrate, 
however, that many aliens do not comply with this obligation.\5\ This 
pattern of large-scale noncompliance risks further encouraging aliens 
to disregard such orders under the belief that they can remain in the 
United States without consequence. See 90 FR 27446. Such noncompliance, 
in turn, undermines the integrity of the immigration system, weakens 
the authority of Immigration Courts, and raises fairness concerns for 
aliens who do comply with removal and departure requirements. See id.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \4\ The term ``final executable removal order'' describes a 
situation where there is no legal impediment to the alien's removal. 
As discussed in Section III of this preamble, DHS does not issue 
failure to depart penalties to aliens for whom there is no final 
executable removal order because, for example, they have a stay of 
removal or other forms of protection, including Temporary Protected 
Status, withholding of removal, or protection under the regulations 
implementing the Convention Against Torture when no alternative 
country of removal is available, or have a DHS approved reason for 
remaining in the United States including an affirmative grant of 
deferred action. (For aliens who have protection under the 
regulations implementing the Convention Against Torture but for whom 
there is an alternative country of removal, the final order of 
removal may still be executable to that alternative country.) For 
ease of reading in this preamble, the Departments use the term 
``removal order'' to mean a ``final executable removal order'' when 
discussing civil penalties for failure to depart.
    \5\ Section 241(a) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1231(a), governs the 
detention and removal of aliens who have already been ordered 
removed. It directs DHS to remove an alien within a 90-day removal 
period. The statute provides: during the removal period, DHS shall 
detain the alien and ``[u]nder no circumstance during the removal 
period shall the [Secretary] release an alien who has been found 
[removable on certain criminal and national-security grounds].'' See 
INA 241(a)(1), 1231(a)(1). The prior Administration did not 
prioritize the apprehension, detention, and removal of all aliens 
with final removal orders. See United States v. Texas, 599 U.S. 670, 
715 (2023) (Alito, J. dissenting) (discussing enforcement priorities 
memoranda issued by DHS and ICE in 2021). Instead, many simply 
remained in the United States without consequence. Congress, 
however, has not absolved such aliens of their obligation to depart 
the United States if they were not removed, were never detained, or 
were released during the removal period. Indeed, section 241 of the 
INA, 8 U.S.C. 1231, expressly contemplates that even aliens who were 
never detained during the 90-day removal period have an independent 
obligation to leave the United States. See INA 241(a)(3), 8 U.S.C. 
1231(a)(3) (providing that DHS may impose conditions of supervision 
on the alien ``[i]f the alien does not leave or is not removed 
within the removal period.'' Moreover, Congress has specifically 
authorized DHS to impose civil monetary penalties on aliens who 
willfully remain in the United States after a removal order which 
demonstrates that aliens have an independent obligation to leave the 
United States even if ICE did not take action to physically remove 
the alien or the alien was released after the expiration of the 
removal period. See INA 274d(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1324(d)(a)(1).

    The IFR was also intended to complement DHS's efforts to maintain 
border security. Under the prior Administration, more than 8 million 
aliens were encountered along the southern border of the United States. 
90 FR 8334. In FY 2024 alone, DHS estimates that approximately 1.5 
million aliens entered or attempted to enter unlawfully between ports 
of entry. 90 FR 27445. Although encounters have since declined in 
connection with this Administration's policies, these prior high 
encounter levels demonstrate the need for DHS to use all statutorily 
authorized tools to maintain border security and reduce incentives for 
unlawful entry. Id.
    When such large numbers of aliens enter unlawfully between POEs, as 
occurred under the last Administration, DHS's capacity to apprehend, 
process, detain, and swiftly remove all such aliens diminishes.\8\ As a 
result, under the prior Administration, millions of aliens were 
released into communities nationwide, many of whom were subject to but 
not processed under expedited removal as envisioned by the statutory 
framework, imposing substantial costs on the States and encouraging 
additional migration by unlawful aliens who believed they would likely 
be released into the United States while awaiting removal proceedings 
that often



take years to resolve.\9\ When U.S. Border Patrol (``USBP'') officers 
are diverted from patrol duties to process large groups of migrants and 
conduct detention-related activities, criminal organizations and 
smugglers can exploit the diversion of resources to move illegal drugs, 
weapons, contraband, and aliens into the United States. See E.O. 14165, 
90 FR 8467 (Jan. 20, 2025). Elevated levels of unlawful border 
crossings also strain ICE's detention resources and impede ICE's 
ability to detain other aliens, including those with final removal 
orders. See 90 FR 45397, 45397. In combination, the prior 
Administration's policies and resulting incentives for unlawful entry 
hindered the effective operation of immigration laws designed to 
protect U.S. sovereignty and prevent the unlawful entry of illicit 
contraband, criminals, and illegal aliens.

    Additionally, elevated border crossings can severely inhibit the 
effective functioning of the Immigration Courts. Under the prior 
Administration, the record numbers of aliens encountered across the 
southern border overwhelmed DHS's capacity to process such aliens 
through expedited removal as envisioned by the statutory framework of 
the Act. 89 FR 81158. Instead, DHS was forced to place aliens into 
section 240 removal proceedings at a rate that outpaced EOIR's capacity 
to complete such cases in a timely manner and led to extensive delays 
in Immigration Court proceedings. Id. Under this Administration, the 
Departments have taken significant efforts to disrupt aliens' 
expectations of lengthy Immigration Court delays, including more robust 
utilization of expedited removal where available and a renewed focus on 
EOIR operational efficiency. Accordingly, EOIR has seen a precipitous 
drop in initial receipts of charging documents to initiate proceedings 
between FY 2024 and FY 2025, and has been continually increasing the 
total number of case completions.\10\ However, considering the 
challenges experienced under the prior administration at the southern 
border and the resulting consequences, the Departments have a need to 
use all available measures to prevent such a situation from 
reoccurring.
