    For these reasons, and consistent with this Administration's 
policies, DHS believes that it must employ all immigration enforcement 
authorities that Congress has provided in order to both maintain border 
security, including to discourage large numbers of aliens from crossing 
the southern border and overwhelming the Departments' abilities to 
effectively process and remove such aliens as occurred under the last 
administration, and to address the large number of aliens with removal 
and voluntary departure orders who have violated U.S. immigration law 
by remaining in the United States in contravention of such orders.
    One such authority is civil monetary penalties. As explained in 
more detail in the IFR, Congress has authorized DHS to impose civil 
penalties on: (1) aliens who willfully fail or refuse to depart the 
United States after a final order of removal or take other action to 
thwart removal; (2) aliens who fail to comply with a voluntary 
departure order; and (3) aliens who are apprehended entering or 
attempting to enter the United States unlawfully (``unlawful entry 
penalties''). See INA 274D(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1324d(a)(1); INA 
240B(d)(1)(A), 8 U.S.C. 1229c(d)(1)(A); INA 275(b)(1), 8 U.S.C. 
1325(b)(1). Congress has also specified the authorized range of penalty 
amounts, which DHS has adjusted for inflation. For ``unlawful entry,'' 
the penalty amounts range from $100 to $500 per entry or attempted 
entry. See INA 275(b)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1325(b)(1); 8 CFR 280.53(b)(14). For 
failure to comply with voluntary departure conditions, the penalty is 
set by an Immigration Judge or the Board of Immigration Appeals 
(``BIA'') and may range from $1,992 to $9,970 after inflation 
adjustments, but the general default amount is $3,000. See INA 
240B(d)(1)(A), 8 U.S.C. 1229c(d)(1)(A); 8 CFR 280.53(b)(3), 1240.26(l). 
For aliens ordered removed who remain in the United States, DHS may 
impose a penalty of up to $998 for each day the alien willfully fails 
to comply with the order. See INA 274D(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1324d(a)(1); 8 
CFR 280.53(b)(14). As the IFR explains, DHS believes that robust 
application of these civil penalties will deter future unlawful entries 
and encourage greater compliance with removal and voluntary departure 
orders, in line with Congress's intent and this Administration's focus 
on securing the border and restoring integrity to the immigration 
system. See 90 FR 27439-40, 27442.
    Prior to the IFR, however, DHS was required to use the general 
civil penalty procedures at 8 CFR part 280 to impose these penalties. 
These procedures were promulgated by the former Immigration and 
Naturalization Service (``INS'') decades before Congress authorized the 
specific failure-to-depart and unlawful entry penalties covered by the 
IFR. See 90 FR 27440-41. Those regulations were designed primarily for 
penalties imposed on airlines and other carriers that violate INA 
provisions governing the transport of aliens into the United States, 
rather than for penalties against individual aliens for failure-to-
depart or unlawful entry. Id. Under those regulations, DHS had to 
provide a written notice of intent to fine (``NIF''), served in person 
or by certified mail, and then wait at least 30 days for a response. 
Id. If the alien did not respond or did not contest the fine, a DHS 
officer could issue a final decision imposing the penalty. Id. If the 
alien contested the fine, the alien could request an in-person 
interview or submit a sworn written response; a supervisory immigration 
officer would then issue a written decision; the alien could seek 
reconsideration within DHS; after exhausting DHS procedures, the alien 
could appeal to the BIA. Id. As discussed in the IFR, these procedures 
are lengthy, resource intensive, and not tailored to the failure-to-
depart and unlawful entry penalties that Congress later authorized. See 
90 FR 27444-46.
    The IFR streamlined and simplified the process DHS uses to impose 
civil penalties for failure-to-depart and unlawful entry and eliminated 
unnecessary procedures that are not required by statute. See 90 FR 
27449-52. The IFR changed only the way DHS issues and adjudicates civil 
monetary penalties and the way an alien may contest such penalties for 
these specific fines. 90 FR 27454. The IFR did not require the 
imposition of any new penalties or otherwise change the substantive 
criteria for issuing civil penalties. Id.
    Under the IFR, the new 8 CFR 281 allows a DHS immigration officer 
to initiate the penalty process by issuing a written decision and order 
imposing the civil monetary penalty. 8 CFR 281.1(b), (c). The decision 
and order must identify the statutory basis for the penalty, state the 
type and amount of the penalty, and provide a brief



explanation of the reasons for the decision. 8 CFR 281.1(c)(1). The 
decision and order must also advise the alien of the right to appeal; 
the process for filing an appeal; the right to be represented by 
counsel at no expense to the government; and the opportunity to submit 
written arguments and supporting documentation challenging the penalty. 
8 CFR 281.1(c)(2). The alien may file a written defense and supporting 
evidence or may simply submit a written notice of appeal. 8 CFR 
281.1(c)(2), (e)(1). DHS may serve the decision and order in person or 
by regular mail. 8 CFR 281.1(d).
    The IFR also replaced the elaborate review process before DHS set 
forth in 8 CFR part 280 and appeal process before EOIR set forth at 8 
CFR 1280.1 \11\ for these three specific civil penalties with an appeal 
process that takes place solely before DHS. Under the IFR, an alien 
must file a notice of appeal within 15 business days of service of the 
initial decision and order. 8 CFR 281.1(e)(1). If the alien does not 
file a timely appeal with DHS, the initial decision and order become 
final. 8 CFR 281.1(f)(3). If the alien files a timely appeal with DHS, 
a supervisory immigration officer who did not issue the initial 
decision and order will review the appeal. 8 CFR 281.1(e)(2). The 
supervisory officer will review the appeal within 10 days of receipt 
and may, in his or her discretion, request additional written briefing 
or documentation, which the alien must provide within 15 days of 
receiving the request. Id. At the alien's request, the supervisory 
officer will generally provide copies of pertinent documents and 
records relevant to the penalty. 8 CFR 281.1(e)(3). The supervisory 
officer will decide the appeal on the written record; the IFR does not 
provide for in-person interviews. Id. The record must include the 
initial decision and order, evidence in DHS's administrative files, and 
any timely written submissions, briefs, documentary evidence, or other 
relevant materials submitted by the alien. Id. The supervisory officer 
will review this record de novo, including the initial decision and 
order and any written arguments and evidence submitted by the alien, 
and will issue a final decision within 45 days. 8 CFR 281.1(e)(2). That 
officer's decision constitutes the final agency action, subject only to 
discretionary review by the Secretary of Homeland Security, and the 
alien may not appeal the decision to the BIA. 8 CFR 281.1(e)(4), 
(f)(1)-(3). However, the IFR allows DHS to reopen a decision, in its 
sole discretion (i.e., sua sponte), at any time to reconsider the 
decision and reduce or rescind the fine. 8 CFR 281.1(f)(1).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \11\ Any cases appealed to the BIA would add to the BIA's 
pending caseload and be subject to the same case management 
framework as all other appeals. See 8 CFR 1003.1. To address an 
unprecedented caseload and an urgent need to improve the efficiency 
of BIA procedures, the Department has reconsidered the Board's role 
as an appellate tribunal and issued an IFR to streamline BIA 
procedures. See generally Appellate Procedures for the Board of 
Immigration Appeals, 91 FR 5267 (Feb. 6, 2026) (partially set aside 
on procedural grounds Amica Ctr. for Immigrant Rts. v. EOIR, No. CV 
26-696 (RDM), 2026 WL 662494, at *34 (D.D.C. Mar. 8, 2026)). 
Divesting the BIA of responsibility over DHS imposition and 
enforcement of civil fines and penalties, an area where there is no 
statutory requirement for EOIR review and where the BIA has no 
unique adjudicatory expertise, is consistent with BIA efforts to 
create operational efficiencies.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    As explained in the IFR, the Departments reasoned that these 
updated procedures will allow DHS to impose these civil penalties more 
swiftly on more aliens who unlawfully enter the United States and on 
those who disregard removal and voluntary departure orders. See 90 FR 
27442. In turn, this will help support DHS's efforts to maintain border 
security and enforce immigration laws by deterring unlawful entries and 
encouraging compliance with removal and departure orders. See 90 FR 
27445-46. Compared to the general procedures in 8 CFR part 280, the 
revised process reduces unnecessary administrative burdens and allows 
DHS to reach final decisions more quickly while at the same time 
reducing unnecessary burdens on the BIA's caseload. See 90 FR 27444-45. 
The IFR explained that these changes are needed to ensure that DHS can 
efficiently employ these statutory penalties while continuing to 
prioritize, without diverting resources away from, border security and 
the apprehension, detention, and removal of aliens who have violated 
the Nation's immigration laws, consistent with this Administration's 
policy objectives and the President's direction. See 90 FR 27444-46.
    To further advance the IFR's goal of encouraging compliance with 
removal and departure orders, DHS has announced that it will rescind 
most failure to depart fines if an alien uses the U.S. Customs and 
Border Protection (``CBP'') Home app to arrange and complete self-
departure from the United States.\12\ This policy, coupled with DHS's 
expanded use of these civil penalties, is intended to provide an 
additional clear incentive for aliens to comply with removal and 
departure orders and avoid civil monetary penalties by doing what the 
law requires: departing the United States as ordered.\13\

    At the same time, the Departments determined that the revised 
procedures are consistent with due process. For the reasons discussed 
more fully in the IFR and in response to comments in Section III of 
this preamble, the Departments have concluded that a shortened appeal 
period, removal of in-person interviews, and the shift from BIA review 
to internal DHS review are appropriate and consistent with due process 
given that these civil penalties typically turn on routine and 
straightforward factual and legal determinations and aliens have 
limited grounds to contest them. 90 FR 27451-55. In addition, ICE will 
now also permit acceptance of a late-filed appeal based on documented 
mail delivery delays that ICE finds were beyond the alien's control.
    First, INA 275(b), 8 U.S.C. 1325(b), authorizes DHS to impose a 
civil penalty on any alien who is apprehended while entering or 
attempting to enter the United States at an improper place or time. 
Aliens apprehended while entering unlawfully have, by definition, 
violated INA 275(b), 8 U.S.C. 1325(b), and the documented encounter 
provides the only fact necessary to impose these penalties. 
Additionally, when USBP agents apprehend an alien entering unlawfully, 
the agents prepare a Form I-213, Record of Deportable/Inadmissible 
Alien, which documents the apprehension and is sufficient to 
demonstrate liability for these penalties. See 90 FR 27442. As a matter 
of practice, USBP issues these penalties at the time that it apprehends 
the alien. In these circumstances, the Departments do not believe that 
a lengthy, multi-step appeal process is necessary. See id. The IFR's 
appeal structure preserves an alien's meaningful ability to contest an 
unlawful entry penalty if the alien believes a penalty was issued 
erroneously.
    Second, the nature of the failure to depart penalties also supports 
the IFR's changes. Congress has authorized DHS to impose civil monetary 
penalties on aliens for failure to depart, subject to the general 
federal statute of limitations, 28



U.S.C. 2462, if two elements have been satisfied: (1) the alien is 
subject to a final order of removal or was granted voluntary departure 
and (2) the alien willfully fails or refuses to depart under a removal 
order or voluntarily fails to comply with a voluntary departure order. 
INA 274D(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1324d(a)(1); INA 240B(d)(1)(A), 8 U.S.C. 
1229c(d)(1)(A). DHS maintains records of an alien's immigration 
history, including removal and voluntary departure orders, and has 
ready access to information about any pending appeals needed to verify 
that the alien is subject to a final removal or departure order. 90 FR 
27442-43. Before issuing a penalty, ICE guidance requires the 
immigration officer to verify that there are no DHS records of the 
alien's departure from the United States and reviews the alien's 
immigration records for information suggesting that the alien's failure 
to depart was not willful or voluntary. This includes information 
about: automatic stays resulting from motions to reopen; certain 
immigration benefits under the Violence Against Women Act (``VAWA'') 
that stay the alien's removal; for aliens on an order of supervision, 
efforts the alien has made to secure travel documents at DHS's request; 
whether DHS has affirmatively approved the alien for deferred action; 
whether the Immigration Courts, DHS, or a federal court has granted a 
stay of removal; and whether DHS or EOIR has granted the alien 
protection that excuses the alien's failure to depart while the alien 
maintains that protection, including temporary protected status 
(``TPS''), protection under the Convention Against Torture (``CAT''), 
and withholding of removal under INA 241(b)(3), 8 U.S.C. 1231(b)(3) 
when no alternative country of removal is available.
    Absent evidence in records accessible to DHS showing that the alien 
is permitted to remain in the United States, or that the alien has 
departed, DHS believes the statutory prerequisites to issue a penalty 
will have been met where an alien ordered removed or granted voluntary 
departure is physically present in the United States beyond the time 
frame specified by the Immigration Judge. As the IFR explains, civil 
penalties for failure to depart are generally issued after completion 
of section 240 removal proceedings that resulted in a final order 
requiring the alien's departure from the United States immediately or 
within a certain time frame specified by the Immigration Judge. See 90 
FR 27440. These aliens have received due process through section 240 
removal proceedings where they had an opportunity to contest the 
charges against them, to seek relief, and to be informed by an 
Immigration Judge of their obligation to depart and of the consequences 
of failing to do so. Id. Aliens granted voluntary departure prior to 
the conclusion of section 240 removal proceedings have already agreed 
to forgo challenging removal or seeking relief in exchange for being 
allowed to depart voluntarily. Id. In these circumstances, and when DHS 
records show the removal order is executable, the Departments reasoned 
that an alien's continued presence in the United States is generally 
sufficient to establish liability for these civil penalties, absent the 
alien providing evidence on appeal \14\ to demonstrate otherwise. See 
90 FR 27442-43.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \14\ The Departments determined that such appeal should take 
place before DHS, and not the BIA, given the straightforward and 
readily determinable requirements for imposing and enforcing such 
penalties based on information within DHS's and the alien's 
possession. 90 FR 27444.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    In addition, Immigration Judges are required by law to inform 
aliens of their departure obligations and the consequences for failing 
to comply. Under INA 240(c)(5), 8 U.S.C. 1229(a)(5), when an 
Immigration Judge orders removal, the Immigration Judge must inform the 
alien of the consequences for failure to depart under the order of 
removal, including civil penalties described at sections INA 274D, 8 
U.S.C. 1324(d). See 8 CFR 1240.13(d). Likewise, for voluntary 
departure, the INA requires that an Immigration Judge ``shall inform 
the alien of the penalties'' that will apply if the alien voluntarily 
fails to depart within the time allowed, including civil monetary 
penalties and ineligibility for certain forms of relief. INA 
240B(d)(3), 8 U.S.C. 1229c(d)(3). These advisals are mandatory 
components of 240 removal proceedings, not discretionary steps.
    These statutory and regulatory requirements are directly relevant 
to the willfulness and voluntariness elements in the civil penalty 
statutes. Before DHS considers imposing a failure to depart penalty, 
the alien will ordinarily have been advised, on the record, that the 
law requires the alien to depart the United States and that failure to 
do so may result in civil fines and other adverse consequences. When an 
alien remains in the United States after such clear, legally required 
notice, his or her continued presence strongly supports the conclusion 
that the alien has ``willfully fail[ed] or refuse[d]'' to depart under 
a removal order or ``voluntarily'' failed to comply with a voluntary 
departure order, as required by the failure to depart civil penalty 
statutes. In making this assessment, DHS also relies on the presumption 
of regularity that attaches to official acts of government officers, 
including Immigration Judges. See United States Postal Serv. v. 
Gregory, 534 U.S. 1, 10 (2001). Under this presumption, DHS may 
reasonably assume that Immigration Judges complied with their legal 
obligations under the INA and implementing regulations and provided the 
required advisals concerning departure obligations and the consequences 
of noncompliance, absent specific evidence to the contrary in the 
record. In all cases, ICE considers the willfulness of an alien's 
violation in determining whether to impose a penalty.
    Taken together--(1) the procedural protections provided in section 
240 removal proceedings, (2) the mandatory Immigration Judge advisals 
of departure obligations and penalties, (3) the presumption of 
regularity applicable to those advisals, and (4) DHS's careful review 
of U.S. Government records to confirm that the alien is subject to a 
final, executable order and lacks lawful permission to remain--DHS 
concludes that an alien's continued presence in the United States is 
generally sufficient to establish the willful or voluntary failure to 
depart required to impose these civil penalties, absent evidence 
provided by the alien on appeal to demonstrate that the alien is not 
liable. Therefore, the Departments reasoned that streamlining the 
issuance and adjudication of these civil penalties, and the associated 
appeals process, aligns more closely with the nature and intent of 
these straightforward civil penalties. While in most cases, DHS records 
sufficiently establish the facts necessary to demonstrate that the 
alien is subject to these civil penalties, the alien retains the right 
to contest them on limited grounds. See 90 FR 27442-46.
    To the extent an alien believes that DHS issued a penalty 
erroneously--for example, because the alien is not subject to a removal 
order, is legally permitted to remain in the United States, or did not 
willfully or voluntarily fail to depart--the Departments determined 
that the IFR provides sufficient notice and an opportunity to contest 
the decision before DHS, and that further review before EOIR is 
unnecessary. See 90 FR 27451-55. Under the IFR, a DHS immigration 
officer must issue a written decision that sets forth the statutory and 
factual basis for the penalty and informs the alien of the requirements 
and deadlines for filing an appeal. See Mullane v. Cent. Hanover Bank & 
Tr. Co., 339 U.S. 306, 314 (1950) (stating



that notice under due process must be of a sufficient nature as to 
reasonably convey the required information). The revised appeal process 
also preserves an alien's opportunity to contest a civil penalty. Under 
the IFR's procedures, the alien has 15 business days to appeal using 
the DHS-developed Form 281, Notice and Violation of Order, and a 
supervisory immigration officer who did not issue the initial decision 
will review the record de novo and may request additional evidence 
before making a final determination. See 90 FR 27452-54.
    As explained in the IFR and in response to comments in Section III 
of this preamble, the Departments believe that additional procedures, 
beyond those contained in the IFR, would not enhance the accuracy, 
fairness, or reliability of the process given the straightforward 
nature of these penalties and the limited grounds that an alien may 
have to contest them. See id. Thus, for the reasons discussed in the 
IFR and in response to comments in Section III of this preamble, the 
Departments believe that the revised procedure preserves an alien's 
ability to contest the fine while better ensuring that the BIA does not 
unnecessarily expend resources in areas where DHS is better positioned 
to review such determinations, and that DHS can reach final decisions 
efficiently and apply these statutory penalties swiftly and at the 
scale necessary to address the large number of aliens who have entered 
or remain unlawfully in the United States. Accordingly, after carefully 
considering comments received on the IFR, the Departments are 
finalizing this rule with one change discussed in more detail below to 
account for U.S. postal delays.

B. The Departments' Experience With the IFR

    The IFR is working as intended. As a result of the IFR, DHS has 
been able to issue a significantly greater number of civil penalties 
compared to the pre-IFR process under 8 CFR part 280. From March 26, 
2025, through June 26, 2025, ICE issued 12,135 civil penalties under 
the pre-IFR process.\15\ From June 27, 2025, after the IFR took effect, 
through September 14, 2026, ICE issued approximately 110,000 failure to 
depart civil penalties, and CBP issued an additional 66,000 civil 
penalties for unlawful entry. Thus, DHS increased the number of civil 
penalties issued from approximately 930 per week under the pre-IFR 
process to nearly 2,800 per week under the IFR process.\16\ 
Accordingly, the IFR has allowed DHS to impose more civil penalties 
more quickly on a greater scale, while retaining procedural safeguards 
designed to promote accurate penalty assessments without diverting 
resources away from border security, and the apprehension, detention, 
and removal of aliens who have violated our immigration laws.

    \15\ See Office of Homeland Security Statistics analysis of 
Alien Departures by Civil Fine, DHS Enforcement, and EOIR Case 
Outcomes (Oct. 7, 2026).
    \16\ Id.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Second, DHS's robust use of civil penalties appears to be shifting 
incentives for aliens with removal and departure orders who might 
otherwise remain unlawfully in the United States. DHS data indicates 
that over 82,000 aliens with removal orders and voluntary departures

issuing civil penalties in March 2025 through September 14, 2026.\17\ 
In that same period, over 7,700 aliens have self-departed after 
receiving a civil penalty.\18\ Further, the number of aliens with 
removal orders or voluntary departure orders who have self-departed 
since the IFR took effect has increased significantly, as has the 
number of aliens who have departed after receiving a civil penalty. In 
the pre-IFR period from March 26, 2025, through June 26, 2025, 
approximately 8,600 aliens with removal or voluntary departure orders 
self-departed, and approximately 540 aliens self-departed the United 
States after receiving a civil penalty during this period.\19\ In the 
post-IFR period from June 27, 2025, through September 14, 2026, over 
74,000 aliens with removal orders or voluntary departure orders self-
departed in total, and approximately 7,180 aliens self-departed after 
receiving a civil penalty during this period. This data indicates that 
DHS's robust use of civil penalties, as facilitated by the IFR's 
streamlined procedures, is encouraging illegally present aliens to 
depart the United States on their own, consistent with the IFR's 
objectives.

    Finally, DHS's experience implementing the civil penalties covered 
by this rule since March 26, 2025, confirms that many pre-IFR

its existing pending caseload to conduct review better addressed by 
DHS. As discussed above, the IFR shortens the appeal period, eliminates

support these changes:
     Under the pre-IFR process, aliens filed written answers 
pursuant to 8 CFR 280.12 contesting failure to depart penalties for

to appeal unlawful entry penalties issued under INA 275(b), 8 U.S.C. 
1325(b), given the even more straightforward nature of those 
penalties.

     Only 4 aliens requested an in-person interview out of the 
222 penalty notices that aliens contested under the pre-IFR process, 
indicating that in-person interviews are generally unnecessary and that 
aliens can adequately contest these decisions through written

     Under the pre-IFR process, only 44 aliens appealed DHS's 
penalty decision to the BIA under 8 CFR part 1003, further supporting 
the Departments' assessment that the legal issues associated with these 
penalties are relatively straightforward and appeals can be handled by 
DHS. As of September 10, 2026, the BIA has issued only two decisions in 
these appeals, including a published decision which



upheld the civil penalty.\21\ This further supports the Departments'

     Aliens have successfully contested penalty decisions under 
the post-IFR processes. Of the appeals that DHS has adjudicated under

clearly demonstrates that the IFR's appeal process is meaningful, and 
DHS can adjudicate these penalties fairly without the need for the 
BIA's review.
    These results support the Departments' conclusion that the IFR's 
streamlined procedures provide appropriate protections while allowing 
DHS to apply statutory penalties efficiently and at scale. DHS believes 
there have been fewer appeals to fines issued under 8 CFR part 281, as 
compared to 8 CFR part 280, because of the straightforward 
determinations of fact associated with fines under part 281. 
Additionally, the appeal process under 8 CFR part 281 discourages

II. Statutory Authority

    The Attorney General and Secretary of Homeland Security issue this 
joint final rule pursuant to their respective authorities. The Homeland 
Security Act of 2002 (``HSA''), Public Law 107-296, 116 Stat. 2135, as 
amended, transferred to the Secretary many functions previously 
exercised by the former INS in implementing and enforcing Federal 
immigration law. The INA, as amended, charges the Secretary ``with the 
administration and enforcement of this chapter and all other laws 
relating to the immigration and naturalization of aliens.'' INA 
103(a)(1); 8 U.S.C. 1103(a)(1). It authorizes the Secretary to take 
actions ``necessary for carrying out'' that responsibility. INA 
103(a)(3); 8 U.S.C. 1103(a)(3). As relevant here, the INA and HSA now 
authorize the Secretary to impose most civil monetary penalties under 
the INA, including those set forth in INA 240B(d), 274D(a), and 275(b); 
8 U.S.C. 1229c(d), 1324d(a), and 1325(b). See INA 103(a)(1); 8 U.S.C. 
1103(a)(1) (reposing in the Secretary the authority to administer and 
enforce the immigration laws except as expressly reserved to the 
President, Attorney General, or Secretary of State) and HSA 402(3), 6 
U.S.C. 202(3) (charging the Secretary with carrying out the immigration 
enforcement functions vested by statute in, or performed by, the 
Commissioner of the former INS).
    Within DHS, the HSA allocated immigration functions and 
responsibilities to CBP, ICE, and U.S. Citizenship and Immigration 
Services (``USCIS''). See HSA 411, 6 U.S.C. 211 (CBP); HSA 442, 6 
U.S.C. 252 (ICE); HSA 451, 6 U.S.C. 271 (USCIS). ICE is generally 
responsible for interior immigration enforcement, and CBP is generally 
responsible for immigration enforcement at ports of entry and along the 
United States border. Both components have authority to administer 
civil monetary penalties relating to certain violations of immigration 
law and Immigration Court orders, including penalties authorized under 
INA 240B(d), 274(D)(a), and 275(b). See, e.g., 8 CFR part 280.
    The Secretary may delegate or re-delegate any authority vested in 
DHS under the immigration laws to any DHS officer, official, or 
employee, including by successive delegations. See INA 103(a)(4), 8 
U.S.C. 1103(a)(4); 8 CFR 2.1; Authority of the Secretary of Homeland 
Security; Immigration Laws, 68 FR 10922 (Mar. 6, 2003). The Secretary 
may delegate his authority in any manner he chooses, including by 
regulation, memorandum, directive, or other method. 8 CFR 2.1. In 
addition, HSA 102(a)(3), 6 U.S.C. 112(a)(3), vests all functions of DHS 
officers, employees, and organizational units in the Secretary.
    The HSA retains in DOJ, under the direction of the Attorney 
General, the functions of EOIR. See HSA 1101, 6 U.S.C. 521, INA 
103(g)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1103(g)(1). Immigration Judges within EOIR conduct 
section 240 removal proceedings and have authority to issue removal 
orders or grant voluntary departure. See INA 240, 240B, 8 U.S.C. 1229a, 
1229b. The INA further provides that the Attorney General's 
determinations on questions of law ``shall be controlling.'' INA 
103(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1103(a)(1). Nothing in this final rule alters 
EOIR's or the Attorney General's authority to conduct or review section 
240 removal proceedings, including the issuance of removal orders or 
grants of voluntary departure.
    DOJ participates in this rulemaking because, prior to the IFR, 
DOJ's regulations established BIA appellate jurisdiction over certain 
DHS-issued civil monetary penalties authorized under the INA, including 
those covered by this rulemaking. The IFR removed that appellate 
authority, which is finalized without further change in this rule. See 
90 FR 27439, 27459. The INA does not require the BIA to review civil 
penalties, and nothing in the statute precludes the Attorney General 
from removing the BIA's appellate jurisdiction over civil monetary 
penalties imposed by another agency. To the contrary, INA 103(g)(1) and 
(g)(2), 8 U.S.C. 1103(g)(1)-(2), authorize the Attorney General to 
issue regulations necessary for carrying out EOIR's responsibilities 
and governing its adjudicatory structure. Consistent with that 
authority, through the IFR, DOJ amended its regulations to eliminate 
the BIA's appellate authority over these DHS-imposed penalties in order 
to focus EOIR's resources on its statutory functions.
    This final rule addresses DHS procedures for imposing civil 
monetary penalties under INA 240B(d), 274D(a)(1), and 275(b), 8 U.S.C. 
1229c(d), 1324d(a), and 1325(b). Those statutory provisions define the 
categories of aliens subject to civil penalties, establish penalty 
amounts, and authorize DHS to impose such penalties, but they do not 
prescribe procedures DHS must follow or require DOJ review of those 
penalties. Similarly, INA 280, 8 U.S.C. 1330, addresses the collection 
of civil monetary penalties but does not specify assessment procedures. 
Accordingly, the INA affords DHS discretion to adopt reasonable 
procedures for assessing and issuing civil monetary penalties. See Vt. 
Yankee Nuclear Power Corp. v. Nat. Res. Def. Council, Inc., 435 U.S. 
519, 543 (1978) (``Absent constitutional constraints or extremely 
compelling circumstances the administrative agencies should be free to 
fashion their own rules of procedure and to pursue methods of inquiry 
capable of permitting them to discharge their multitudinous duties.'') 
(cleaned up).

III. Response to Public Comments on the IFR

    The Departments received a total of 28 public comment submissions 
in response to the IFR. The Departments reviewed all the public 
comments received and have addressed relevant comments in this final 
rule, grouped by subject matter. While some commenters wrote that they 
supported the IFR, the vast majority of commenters opposed all or part 
of it.

A. General Support

    Comment: Several commenters expressed overall support for the IFR. 
These commenters agreed with the use of civil monetary penalties to 
promote compliance with immigration laws. One commenter considered such 
civil penalties necessary to deter unlawful presence, encourage self-
departure, and help offset the costs associated with



enforcing immigration laws and carrying out removals. Another commenter 
recognized the government's interest in recovering some of the costs 
associated with removing aliens. A third commenter expressed general 
support for imposing civil monetary fines to strengthen overall 
immigration enforcement. Collectively, these comments broadly endorsed 
the IFR's underlying policy objective of streamlining the process for 
imposing civil monetary penalties on aliens subject to the violations 
addressed in this rule.
    Response: The Departments agree that promoting compliance with the 
Nation's immigration laws and maintaining border security is critical, 
and this rule is a key part of DHS's efforts to use all statutorily 
available tools to help achieve those objectives consistent with the 
Administration's policies and priorities while also allowing EOIR to 
focus time and resources on completing cases that are more aligned with 
its statutory authorities. See 90 FR 8445-55. Specifically, the 
unprecedented number of aliens entering and remaining in the country 
illegally, in recent years necessitates this rule. See 90 FR 27442 
(quoting 90 FR 8443). Congress has authorized DHS to impose civil 
monetary penalties on aliens who unlawfully enter the United States and 
those who remain after a final removal or voluntary departure order. 
See 90 FR 27439-41. As explained in the IFR, this rule allows DHS to 
preserve due process while more efficiently imposing a greater number 
of these civil penalties on the aliens subject to them. 90 FR 27442. 
The Departments believe that this effort will, in turn, encourage 
greater compliance with removal and voluntary departure orders and 
discourage future unlawful entries. Id.

B. General Opposition

1. Impacts on Aliens, Families, Businesses, and Communities
    Comment: Many commenters opposed the IFR, asserting that it will 
negatively impact aliens and their families. One commenter stated that 
the aliens impacted by this rule could face steep civil monetary fines 
in excess of $1,000,000, causing significant financial distress for 
them and their families. Other commenters echoed this point, stating 
that the rule creates a substantial financial burden on aliens, and 
specifically viewed as particularly egregious the fine of $998-per-day 
for willful failure or refusal to depart after a final removal order 
and certain other proscribed activities. One commenter said the IFR 
directly harms U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents because 
many aliens subject to these civil monetary fines are parents and 
spouses of U.S. citizens and permanent residents. They characterized 
these fines as ``economically catastrophic for the entire household'' 
resulting in ``eviction, bankruptcy, or forced separation.'' This 
commenter also noted that aliens who fail to pay the assessed penalties 
may be subject to additional consequences including garnished wages, 
seizure of assets including homes and vehicles, and long-term financial 
ruin.
    Another commenter reiterated this point and additionally noted the 
potential confiscation of savings and vehicles and imposed additional 
financial planning burden and financial uncertainty. This commenter 
claimed that the Departments' conclusion that the IFR aligns with due 
process was arbitrary and capricious. The commenter said that the IFR 
arbitrarily characterized these penalties as ``modest,'' and claimed 
the Departments overlooked case law recognizing heightened due process 
interests when the government seizes homes, confiscates savings, and 
imposes fines that result in significant economic impacts on families. 
Given the substantial penalty amounts and the collateral consequences 
that can result if an alien fails to pay, the commenter argued that the 
IFR's procedures are constitutionally inadequate.
    Response: As an initial point, Congress, not the Departments, has 
defined both the types of violations and the monetary range for the 
civil penalties covered by the IFR and this rule. These penalties and 
their amounts reflect Congress's judgment that the conduct involved--an 
alien's unlawful entry and failure to depart after a removal or 
voluntary departure order--is serious, and in some cases substantial 
civil fines are necessary to encourage aliens to comply with the 
immigration laws. See 90 FR 27439-40. This rule does not expand the 
scope of these penalties, nor their minimum or maximum dollar amounts. 
Furthermore, the immigration consequences for failing to depart or 
unlawful entry flow from the underlying immigration violation, not from 
the failure to pay the assessed civil monetary penalties. This rule 
merely streamlines the process that DHS applies when imposing civil 
penalties that Congress has already authorized DHS to impose. 
Therefore, to the extent that commenters are objecting to these civil 
monetary penalties and the amounts authorized by Congress, such 
concerns are outside of the scope of this rulemaking.
    DHS often assesses the maximum penalty amount to fulfill the 
enforcement and deterrent objectives of the statute, as intended by 
Congress. These amounts are also consistent with the enforcement 
priorities of the Administration, as reflected in recent Executive 
Orders. See 90 FR 8443, 8443-45; 90 FR 8467, 8467. However, the 
Departments note that, in the voluntary departure context, immigration 
officers follow the civil penalty amounts that will continue to be set 
by EOIR. See 8 CFR 1240.26(l).
    The Departments disagree with commenters' arguments that DHS should 
not streamline the process for imposing these civil penalties because 
of the burdens the penalties create for aliens and their families. The 
Departments acknowledge these concerns but note that financial, 
emotional, and family burdens are also an inherent consequence of 
removal based on an alien's violation of the Nation's immigration laws. 
See e.g., Moctezuma-Reyes v. Garland, 124 F.4th 416, 423 (6th Cir. 
2024) (``[F]inancial and emotional strains are the typical results of 
removal; they aren't rare''); see also Matter of Pilch, 21 I&N Dec. 
627, 631 (BIA 1996) (``[E]motional hardship caused by severing family 
and community ties is a common result of deportation''). The most 
substantial civil fines apply only to aliens who have been ordered 
removed or granted voluntary departure after the conclusion of 
immigration proceedings. These aliens have been warned of the 
consequences for failing to comply with the removal or departure order 
but have willfully ignored their departure obligations. In these 
circumstances, the Departments do not believe that it is unfair to 
impose substantial civil penalties that Congress has authorized for 
these violations even though it may cause additional burdens and 
hardships on aliens and their families.
    To help alleviate the financial burden of civil penalties and 
incentivize compliance, DHS has announced it will reopen and rescind 
most outstanding civil penalties when an alien uses the CBP Home app to 
voluntarily self-depart the United States.\22\ This option allows 
aliens to avoid the civil penalties and attendant consequences that 
commenters have noted. The



Departments recognize that an alien's choice to exercise this option 
may still impose significant personal and family hardships, including 
to U.S. citizen or lawful permanent family members, but the Departments 
note that these hardships are an inherent consequence of a removal 
order and are compounded by the alien's willful failure to depart when 
that order became final and executable. See Morales-Izquierdo v. DHS, 
600 F.3d 1076, 1091 (9th Cir. 2010) (rejecting argument that ``an 
illegal alien with United States citizen family members cannot be 
removed'' because such a proposition ``would radically alter the status 
quo of our immigration law''). Additionally, the Departments believe 
that permitting removable aliens to remain in the United States would 
undermine immigration enforcement, the integrity of the Nation's 
immigration laws, American communities, and public safety.\23\

Establishing Project Homecoming, 90 FR 20357 (May 9, 2025); 90 FR

    \23\ See 90 FR 47445-46 (discussing how an alien's failure to

---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Regarding commenters' concerns that aliens may face collateral 
consequences if they fail to take advantage of this off-ramp and 
further fail to pay these civil fines, the Departments note that the 
IFR and this final rule do not authorize the confiscation of savings, 
garnished wages, or the seizure of assets. Rather, separate statutes 
and regulations govern the U.S. Government's debt collection activities 
and remedies, which are outside the scope of this rule. However, the 
Departments note that only DOJ's Civil Division or another authorized 
litigating component of DOJ, not EOIR and DHS, have authority to obtain 
a judgment on a debt owed to the United States. See 31 CFR 904.1-904.4. 
DOJ's Civil Division or another authorized litigating component must 
bring an action in federal court to obtain a judgment and pursue any 
lien against assets or confiscation of savings, and the alien has an 
opportunity to request a federal court hearing on the enforceability of 
the debt. See, e.g., 28 U.S.C. 3002(3)(B), 3101(d)(1), (d)(2). This 
provides due process before the U.S. Government seeks to obtain a 
judgment on an uncollected debt and before it can confiscate an alien's 
property or savings. Accordingly, nothing in this rule deprives an 
alien of the ability to challenge the imposition of particular civil 
penalty assessments or collection methods that the alien regards as 
disproportionate, excessive, or in violation of due process during a 
federal court hearing.
    Finally, the Departments disagree that the IFR's due process 
analysis fails to consider the full magnitude of the departure 
penalties and the collateral consequences that could result, should an 
alien remain in the United States and fail to pay the civil monetary 
penalty. As an initial matter, contrary to one commenter's claim, the 
Departments did not characterize the penalties covered by this rule as 
``modest.'' Rather, the IFR used that term to contrast the penalty 
amounts associated with the unlawful entry and voluntary departure 
order penalties and the per diem fines Congress has authorized DHS to 
impose on aliens who willfully remain in the United States for many 
years after a removal order. See 90 FR 27541.
    The Departments do, however, acknowledge that the per diem civil 
penalties can result in substantial fines, including sums of over one 
million dollars in certain cases, and that these amounts could impose 
significant economic and emotional burdens on aliens and their 
families. The Departments also note that DHS will cancel most 
outstanding penalties when an alien uses the CBP Home app to depart the 
United States, as discussed above. Similarly, the Departments 
acknowledge the collateral consequences that could result if an alien 
fails to pay a civil penalty or depart the United States, but the 
Departments reiterate that this rule does not authorize DHS or EOIR to 
seize an alien's property, garnish wages, or confiscate savings. That 
authority rests with DOJ's Civil Division or another litigating 
component, and the alien would be able to challenge any action in court 
before any deprivation occurs.
    The Departments, however, also have a weighty interest in ensuring 
that DHS can impose statutorily authorized civil monetary penalties 
efficiently and at scale to create greater incentives for aliens to 
comply with final removal orders and to impose timely consequences on 
those who do not. As the Departments explained in the IFR and Section 
II of this preamble, the need for this rule is demonstrated by the 
sheer number of aliens in the United States with final removal orders 
and the risk that, without additional action, a significant number of 
the millions of aliens currently in Immigration Court proceedings may 
be encouraged to simply ignore final decisions ordering their removal. 
See 90 FR 27445. An alien's failure to comply with a removal order 
risks undermining the overall integrity of the immigration laws and 
processes and imposes significant enforcement costs on DHS. Id; see 
also Section II of this preamble.
    On balance, the Departments believe that the IFR's streamlined 
civil monetary penalty procedures strike an appropriate balance 
between: (1) increasing DHS's ability to impose statutorily authorized 
civil penalties quickly against aliens who have willfully failed to 
comply with removal orders and (2) protecting an alien's interest in 
ensuring that he or she has a meaningful opportunity to contest any 
civil penalty that DHS may have issued erroneously. Based on its 
experience, DHS believes that the risk of imposing these civil fines in 
error is low given the straightforward nature of these civil penalty 
determinations, and that the IFR's procedures provide sufficient due 
process to aliens who contest these penalties. See 90 FR 27451-54.
    Comment: Commenters claimed that these penalties will harm 
businesses and communities. One commenter stated that many aliens 
targeted by this IFR pay taxes and work in ``essential'' sectors such 
as agriculture, healthcare, and construction. Another commenter claimed 
that the threat of high civil penalties will increase fear in 
communities and push people into hiding. The commenter claimed that the 
high penalties would reduce enrollment in schools and healthcare, and 
deter victims and witnesses from reporting crimes, thereby harming 
public safety and communities. Given these claimed impacts, commenters 
argued that the Departments should rescind the IFR.
    Response: The Departments do not dispute the contributions of 
lawful immigrants to United States businesses and communities. The 
purpose of the IFR and this rule, however, is not to harm businesses or 
communities but to allow DHS to more efficiently impose these 
statutorily authorized civil monetary penalties on the large number of 
aliens who violate the Nation's immigration laws by entering or 
remaining in the country unlawfully. Congress has authorized DHS to 
impose civil penalties for these violations and did not create 
exceptions for aliens who pay taxes, work in ``essential sectors'', or 
otherwise ``contribute'' to communities. An alien's engagement in these 
activities does not absolve him or her from complying with the 
immigration laws. Moreover, the Departments note that, with limited 
exceptions, Congress has not authorized



aliens with final executable removal and voluntary departure orders to 
work in the United States. INA 241(a)(7), 8 U.S.C. 1231(a)(7). 
Therefore, the Departments decline to rescind the IFR based on 
commenters' speculation that its procedures for imposing penalties on 
aliens will indirectly ``harm'' businesses or essential sectors. 
Further, the Departments believe that any such indirect impact that the 
penalties themselves may have on businesses would be outweighed by 
their benefits, including benefits to border security, public safety, 
immigration enforcement, and the integrity of the immigration laws. See 
90 FR 27445-46; Section II of this preamble; see also 90 FR 8444-45.
    Regarding comments related to the IFR's potential effects on the 
willingness of aliens to report crimes, while DHS does not dispute that 
illegal aliens might be less willing to report a crime, DHS cannot 
reliably estimate this rule's speculative impact on local policing, 
especially considering that this rule merely provides procedures for 
issuing civil fines that are authorized by statute. For similar 
reasons, the Departments decline to rescind the IFR based on other 
speculative community-level effects described by some commenters. 
Commenters provided no support for their belief that the revised civil 
penalty procedures will discourage eligible individuals from accessing 
education, healthcare, or other community services, or otherwise 
disengaging from their communities. The Departments believe that any 
such indirect impacts are also outweighed by this rule's potential 
benefits, including benefits to border security, public safety, 
immigration enforcement, and the integrity of the immigration laws.
2. Impacts on Specific Populations
    Comment: Commenters broadly suggested that the IFR will have a 
disproportionate impact on vulnerable groups such as minors, aliens 
with limited English proficiency, and aliens fleeing hardships and 
lacking sufficient funds for legal representation. Commenters asserted 
that such aliens may face barriers in understanding or responding to 
civil monetary penalties within the prescribed timeframes and that the 
imposition of fines could create additional hardship or deter some from 
challenging these penalties altogether. One commenter expressed 
particular concern about aliens subject to domestic violence and human 
trafficking. The commenter explained that these aliens may be eligible 
for immigration relief based on this harm, but large civil fines may 
impose a barrier to escaping these situations and obtaining such 
relief. Collectively, these commenters suggested that the IFR's 
streamlined penalty process, including its deadlines, should not apply 
to these groups.
    Response: The procedures established by the IFR are designed to 
ensure efficiency in assessing civil penalties authorized by the INA, 
while maintaining the due process protections required by law. See 90 
FR 27451-53. The rule does not alter eligibility for immigration 
benefits or relief available under other provisions of the INA, 
including protection for victims of trafficking or domestic violence, 
nor does it limit the Departments' existing discretion to consider 
individual circumstances consistent with applicable statutes and 
regulations. Moreover, ICE's guidance to immigration officers instructs 
that aliens with approved (or in some cases tentatively approved) 
applications for VAWA protections, T-visas, and U-visas for aliens who 
are victims of human trafficking or certain crimes should not be issued 
a civil fine. DHS also notes that nothing in this rule prevents 
immigration officers from exercising discretion in individual cases to 
not issue a civil monetary penalty if DHS is aware of such 
circumstances.
    Moreover, the Departments reject commenters arguments that the 
IFR's procedures would have a singular impact on non-English speakers 
or aliens who are unrepresented, low-income, or unfamiliar with the 
law. First, the Departments note that all immigration documents issued 
to aliens by DHS, and all orders, decisions, and notices issued by 
EOIR--including written removal and voluntary departure orders--are in 
English.\24\ Therefore, the Departments do not believe that civil 
penalty decisions issued in English raise any inherent fairness 
concerns for non-English speakers, as a reasonable recipient would be 
on notice that further inquiry is required. See, e.g., Lopez v. 
Garland, 990 F.3d 1000, 1003 (6th Cir. 2021) (recognizing that English 
language notice typically satisfies due process because it alerts the 
alien to make further inquiry and seek help with any language barrier); 
see also Ojeda-Calderon v. Holder, 726 F.3d 669, 675 (5th Cir. 2013) 
(citing Nazarova v. INS, 171 F.3d 478, 483 (7th Cir. 1999)) (explaining 
due process does not require notices to be in a language the alien can 
understand).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

select forms available in other languages. See EOIR, Forms & Fees 
(last visited Oct. 6, 2026), https://www.justice.gov/eoir/eoir-forms

2026), https://www.uscis.gov/forms/all-forms [https://perma.cc/J8A6-UASE]. Regulations require that all documents filed with the EOIR 
Immigration Courts must also be in the English language or 
accompanied by a certified English translation. See 8 CFR 1003.33, 
1003.23(b)(1)(i). DHS regulations also contain English-language 
requirements. E.g., 8 CFR 103.2(b)(3), 204.1(f)(2).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Second, the IFR's procedures provide all aliens with a fair 
opportunity to contest civil penalties. The penalty decision itself 
provides aliens with notice, in plain language about why the alien is 
subject to a civil penalty, see 90 FR 27449, and the Departments 
reiterate that Immigration Judges have already warned aliens subject to 
the failure to depart penalties about the consequences of failing to 
comply with removal and departure orders. See Section II of this 
preamble. The penalty decision also explains, in plain language, what 
an alien must do to contest the penalty. See 90 FR 27449. Indeed, the 
penalty decision, DHS Form 281, Notice of Violation and Order, contains 
a textbox that the alien can use to indicate that he or she is 
contesting the penalty decision and to provide a brief statement of 
reasons for the appeal. Moreover, the IFR simplifies regulatory 
requirements to trigger an appeal compared to the former process at 8 
CFR part 280 that applies when an alien responds to a NIF. See 8 CFR 
280.12 (requiring written answers responding to civil penalties to be 
filed under oath and in triplicate). Finally, under the IFR, an alien's 
appeal suffices to trigger mandatory de novo supervisory review. See 8 
CFR 281.1(e)(2). In these circumstances, the Departments disagree with 
commenters' speculative concerns that the IFR's procedures unfairly 
disadvantage non-English speakers and unrepresented aliens with limited 
financial means. With regard to commenters' concerns about minors, DHS 
notes that ICE guidance to immigration officers is that such penalties 
should not be issued to minors without exceptions.
    Comment: One commenter claimed that the IFR is particularly harmful 
to aliens seeking asylum or protection at the border. The commenter 
stated that, as a result of this IFR, these aliens will now be charged 
a civil fine, which the commenter characterizes as an erosion of their 
right to seek asylum, particularly when paired with other policies 
limiting asylum at the border.
    Response: This rule does not alter or limit any statutory or 
regulatory right to apply for asylum or related protections under the 
INA or the regulations implementing U.S. obligations under the CAT. It 
does not create new grounds of inadmissibility, deportability, or 
ineligibility for relief or protection, and



it does not authorize the imposition of penalties based solely on the 
act of seeking asylum or protection. Rather, the IFR streamlines the 
process for assessing statutorily authorized civil penalties against 
aliens who violate immigration laws by entering the United States 
unlawfully, irrespective of their purpose for doing so. The statute 
does not create an exception for those who enter the United States 
unlawfully for the purpose of seeking asylum or related protection. 
Aliens who present themselves at a port of entry to seek asylum or 
other related protection are not subject to civil penalties under this 
rule.
3. Discrimination and Value-Based Considerations
    Comment: Several commenters characterized the IFR as inconsistent 
with U.S. values and traditions, describing the IFR as ``un-American,'' 
``unjust,'' and ``contrary to national values.'' One commenter 
characterized the IFR as designed to ``punish'' people trying to 
navigate the ``labyrinthian immigration system.'' One commenter 
suggested that the IFR was promulgated for a pretextual political 
purpose rather than a legitimate administrative one. The commenter 
argued that the IFR punishes aliens rather than deterring violations 
and improving compliance with removal obligations or upholding 
statutory requirements. Commenters generally suggested that the 
Administration should pursue policies that focus on humane and fair 
immigration policies, rather than punitive ones.
    Response: The Departments categorically reject commenters' 
characterization of this rule as inhumane, ``un-American,'' ``unjust,'' 
or ``contrary to national values.'' The United States is a nation of 
immigrants and a nation of laws. DHS is charged with administering and 
enforcing those laws, but the number of illegal aliens in the United 
States who are subject to final removal orders has outpaced DHS's 
enforcement resources. See 90 FR 27445; see also Section II of this 
preamble. Further, EOIR statistics indicate that there are over 3.4 
million pending Immigration Court proceedings as of the third quarter 
of FY 2026.\25\ When completed, these cases may result in a substantial 
number of additional removal orders against aliens, and without 
additional action there is a risk that many of these aliens may remain 
in the United States unlawfully. Further, although this Administration 
has made great strides to secure the southern border, DHS is committed 
to maintaining operational control of the border to ensure that DHS has 
sufficient resources to address the public safety and national security 
threats that arise constantly at the border.\26\

2026 (Third Quarter). The term ``pending cases'' includes all

(explaining the impact on DHS resources and the public safety and 
national security concerns that result when there is an influx of 
aliens arriving at the border and entering or attempting to enter 
illegally).

    The Departments believe that these circumstances warrant additional 
action consistent with this Administration's direction to use all 
available statutory immigration enforcement tools including civil 
penalties. See 90 FR 27445-46 and Section II of this preamble; see also 
90 FR 8444-45. Congress has authorized DHS to apply these penalties 
against aliens who are entering or attempting to enter the United 
States unlawfully and against aliens who have failed to comply with 
removal and departure orders. See 90 FR 27439-41. The enforcement of 
these statutory penalties is a legitimate and integral component of 
ensuring compliance with the Nation's immigration laws and maintaining 
the integrity of the immigration system. See 90 FR 27444-46. Indeed, 
the IFR is achieving this objective, as DHS has issued over 176,000 
civil penalties under the IFR (compared to approximately 12,000 
penalties issued under 8 CFR part 280). These penalties have encouraged 
greater compliance with removal and voluntary departure orders as 
evidenced by the nearly 82,000 aliens with removal orders and voluntary 
departure orders who have self-departed the United States after DHS 
began issuing civil penalties in March 2025, and the nearly 7,200 
aliens who self-departed from the United States after receiving notice 
of a civil penalty issued under the IFR.\27\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \27\ See Office of Homeland Security Statistics analysis of 
Alien Departures by Civil Fine, DHS Enforcement, and EOIR Case 
Outcomes (Oct. 7, 2026).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Similarly, the Departments reject the claim that this rule is 
intended to dehumanize or punish people navigating the immigration 
system. DHS notes that these penalties generally are not imposed until 
after the aliens have completed immigration proceedings and received a 
determination that they are not authorized to remain in the United 
States. The IFR did not create new categories of violative conduct or 
expand the scope of existing penalties. Instead, it updated the 
procedural framework that applies to these statutorily authorized 
penalties to ensure that DHS can assess them efficiently against aliens 
who have failed to comply with the Nation's immigration laws. This 
framework allows DHS to avoid unnecessarily diverting resources from 
ICE's and CBP's missions to apprehend, detain, and remove aliens who 
have illegally entered and are unlawfully present. See 90 FR 27447. DHS 
remains committed to administering these authorities in a manner 
consistent with principles of due process, other statutory and 
regulatory requirements, and the Nation's longstanding values of 
fairness and respect for the rule of law.
    Comment: One commenter claimed that the IFR is discriminatory 
because its streamlined penalty process applies only to aliens, while 
the Departments' regulations continue to provide additional procedural 
protections to companies that violate the immigration laws when they 
are faced with a fine. The commenter characterized the IFR as saying 
that the Departments cannot provide aliens with the same due process 
protections that they can afford companies like airline carriers 
because of the large number of fines that ICE has issued against 
aliens. The commenter claimed that this is a crisis of DHS's own making 
rather than a rational reason for distinguishing between aliens and 
companies when designing civil penalty procedures. The commenter 
further argues that the IFR is discriminatory because other regulations 
require the Departments to consider mitigating circumstances when 
imposing penalties on employers and companies that violate immigration 
laws, but the IFR does not afford aliens the same treatment or allow 
them to seek mitigation.
    Response: The Departments disagree with the commenter's assertion 
that the IFR is discriminatory because it establishes a streamlined 
penalty process for aliens but not for carriers. The IFR is not 
intended to favor carriers over aliens. It addresses an immediate 
enforcement need: deterring large numbers of aliens from entering the 
United States unlawfully and encouraging compliance with removal and 
departure orders.
    As an initial matter, the Departments note that aliens and carriers 
are not similarly situated under the INA. Aliens are the direct 
subjects of removal and departure orders and are personally responsible 
for complying with those



orders, if not removed by ICE. They receive an opportunity for a full 
and fair hearing during section 240 removal proceedings, including an 
opportunity to contest removability and seek relief.\28\ When an alien 
fails to comply with a removal or departure order after such 
proceedings, that violation directly undermines the orderly 
administration of the immigration system and the integrity of the 
immigration laws. By contrast, carriers are regulated third parties 
that frequently transport passengers, including aliens, into the United 
States, but are not directly responsible for an alien's independent 
decision to violate the Nation's immigration laws. Rather, their 
obligations are tailored to their role as carriers, arising from 
statutory and regulatory requirements to verify the travel documents of 
passengers seeking to travel to the United States, such as those in INA 
273(a), 8 U.S.C. 1323(a). Noncompliance by carriers is addressed 
through a separate statutory provision, INA 273, 8 U.S.C. 1323, through 
a long-standing regime of inspections, penalties, and cooperative 
compliance measures with CBP tailored to entities engaged in 
international transportation.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \28\ As noted in the IFR, under the INA, certain aliens can also 
be ordered removed by DHS with limited or no review by EOIR. See 90

felons under INA 238(b), 8 U.S.C. 1228(b)). As the IFR explained, 
however, aliens ordered removed through these processes generally 
must be detained, which reduces the likelihood of the alien's 
failure to depart. Id. Therefore, while applicable to all 
administratively final removal orders, the failure to depart civil 
monetary penalties are most relevant to aliens ordered removed 
through section 240 removal proceedings. Id.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The IFR focused on streamlining the process for collection of 
penalties against aliens because DHS identified an urgent need to 
increase the scale of such penalties and facilitate more timely 
processing, as well as to reduce incentives to unlawfully enter the 
United States and to ignore removal and departure orders. 90 FR 27447-
48; see also Section II of this preamble. The streamlined process is 
intended to allow DHS to issue penalties more quickly and at a volume 
necessary to promote compliance and deterrence. DHS did not identify a 
comparable, immediate need to revise the penalty process for carrier 
violations. 90 FR 27447.
    For years, CBP has assessed civil monetary penalties against 
carriers for violations of their obligations under the immigration laws 
\29\ and has routinely worked with carriers to improve compliance.\30\ 
Carriers that operate regular transportation services into the United 
States already have strong incentives to verify passengers' travel 
documents to avoid substantial and repeated fines, as well as the costs 
of securing and returning inadmissible passengers.\31\ These incentives 
are further reinforced by CBP programs and arrangements with carriers 
designed to strengthen document screening and compliance, including 
CBP's voluntary document validation program and memoranda of 
understanding under which civil penalties may be reduced if carriers 
submit to CBP review of their screening processes and demonstrate 
successful screening procedures, as described in INA section 273, 8 
U.S.C. 1323 violations.\32\

    As explained in the IFR, carrier fines also raise distinct 
considerations, including different grounds for violations and issues 
related to statutorily authorized mitigation procedures, that are not 
present for the alien-focused civil penalties covered by this rule. See 
90 FR 27447-48. These factors can in some cases make carrier penalty 
processes more complex and less suitable for the streamlined procedures 
adopted in the IFR. In addition, the existing regulations in 8 CFR part 
280 were designed initially for carrier fines, not for the alien-
focused civil penalties covered by this rule. See 90 FR 27440-41; see 
also National Fines Office, 54 FR 18648 (May 2, 1989) (describing 8 CFR 
part 280 procedures as applying to ``violations of the [INA] by 
transportation companies''). The Departments concluded that addressing 
these carrier-specific issues in the IFR could have delayed action on 
the more pressing need to streamline penalties for aliens.
    Quite simply, the IFR leaves the existing penalty framework for 
carriers intact while addressing a separate enforcement challenge 
related to aliens who unlawfully enter or remain in the United States 
in violation of the immigration laws. The Departments agree that it 
remains important to ensure that carriers comply with their obligations 
under immigration laws and that CBP can administer carrier penalties 
efficiently and effectively. Focusing this rulemaking on alien 
penalties does not preclude future consideration of whether changes to 
carrier penalty procedures may be warranted. The decision to address 
alien penalties first reflects prioritization based on pressing 
enforcement needs, not discrimination against aliens in favor of 
carriers. See Ctr. for Biological Diversity v. EPA, 722 F.3d 401, 409-
10 (D.C. Cir. 2013) (quoting City of Las Vegas v. Lujan, 891 F.2d 927, 
935 (D.C. Cir. 1989) (agencies may address problems in stages and 
``treat a problem partially'' or regulate ``in a piecemeal fashion.''). 
The Departments therefore reject the claim that it is irrational or 
discriminatory to focus this rule on civil penalties against aliens 
without amending the procedures that apply to carriers.
    For similar reasons, the Departments disagree with the commenter's 
claim that the need for streamlined procedures is a ``problem of DHS's 
own making,'' which, according to the commenter, was created by DHS's 
decision to issue large numbers of penalties against aliens. The 
Departments acknowledge that ICE rarely issued such fines prior to this 
Administration. As explained in the IFR, however, the Departments have 
determined that DHS must now use these penalties more robustly in light 
of the significant number of aliens who



have violated removal and departure orders and have unlawfully entered 
the country in recent years. 90 FR 27446-47. The increased use of 
penalties is intended to deter continued violations of the immigration 
laws and is consistent with this Administration's enforcement policies. 
Simply put, the IFR addresses the widespread failure by certain aliens 
to comply with the immigration laws and with removal or departure 
orders. The streamlined procedures in the IFR reflect a legitimate and 
rational interest in promoting timely and efficient enforcement against 
aliens who violate these laws. Congress provided these penalties and 
related authority in the INA; this rule merely modifies DHS's 
administration of collecting those penalties to implement that existing 
statutory authority more efficiently.
    Finally, the streamlined procedures preserve the essential elements 
of due process for aliens. Aliens subject to these penalties continue 
to receive notice of the proposed penalty and an opportunity to seek 
review. Agencies may design procedures that take account of enforcement 
realities and deterrent effect, provided that the procedures preserve 
the core protections of meaningful notice and opportunity for a 
hearing. This rule maintains those protections while allowing DHS to 
more effectively enforce existing statutory penalties.
    The Departments also disagree with the commenter's claims that the 
IFR discriminates against aliens in favor of companies because the IFR 
does not allow aliens to seek mitigation of civil penalties. The 
commenter's assertion overlooks that Congress established distinct 
statutory frameworks governing civil penalties imposed on employers and 
carriers, on the one hand, and the civil penalties at issue in this 
rule, on the other.
    First, the commenter's reference to certain mitigating 
considerations for employer-related penalties under INA 274A, 8 U.S.C. 
1324a, is misplaced. Congress has explicitly directed EOIR 
Administrative Law Judges (``ALJs'') to consider the ``mitigating'' 
factors cited by the commenter when imposing a civil penalty against an 
employer under INA 274A, 8 U.S.C. 1324a. See INA 274A(e)(5), 8 U.S.C. 
1324a(e)(5). By contrast, the INA civil penalty provisions underlying 
this rule contain no comparable statutory requirement to consider 
mitigating factors. Compare INA 274A(e)(5), 8 U.S.C. 1324a(e)(5), with 
INA 240B(d)(1)(A), 274D(a)(1), and 275(b)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1229c(d)(1)(A), 
1324d(a)(1), 1325(b)(1). The differing procedures therefore reflect 
differences Congress itself intended in these statutory schemes, not 
disparate treatment by the Departments, and the rule properly 
implements the procedures authorized for these distinct violations.
    Second, the Departments disagree with the commenter's statement 
that ``an [alien's] right to seek mitigation'' has been curtailed under 
the IFR. The prior penalty process at 8 CFR part 280 did not provide 
all aliens subject to the civil penalties covered by this rule with a 
right to seek mitigation. Rather, 8 CFR 280.5 clarifies that an 
individual subject to a civil penalty covered by 8 CFR part 280 may 
only seek mitigation if it ``is authorized by the [INA].'' By statute, 
only certain individuals and entities subject to civil penalties 
covered by 8 CFR 280 are eligible to seek mitigation. For example, INA 
273(e), 8 U.S.C. 1323(e), directs DHS to reduce, refund, or waive 
certain carrier penalties upon a showing of circumstances that would 
justify reduction, refund, or waiver. However, for the reasons 
discussed more fully in Section III.D.7 of this preamble, the INA does 
not authorize aliens to seek mitigation of the failure to depart and 
unlawful entry civil penalties. Accordingly, the Departments disagree 
that the aliens had a right to seek mitigation under 8 CFR part 280 and 
that this IFR denies them that right. For this reason, the Departments 
also disagree with the commenter that the IFR is facially 
discriminatory because it does not allow aliens to seek mitigation but 
preserves companies and corporations' ability to do so. Rather, the IFR 
merely implements Congress's choice. It is Congress, not the 
Departments, that has authorized carriers, companies, and employers to 
seek mitigation of certain immigration-related civil penalties, while 
not extending the same opportunity to aliens.

C. Justification and Need for the Rule

1. Nature of the Civil Fines
    Comment: Several commenters took issue with the IFR's claim that 
the straightforward and readily verifiable nature of the failure to 
depart penalties supports the Departments' decision to streamline the 
underlying penalty process. 90 FR 27441-46. Commenters claimed that DHS 
has erroneously issued many civil fines over the past year under the 
prior penalty process, including to aliens with temporary or permanent 
immigration status and with an approved visa petition and related 
waiver request. A commenter also claimed that DHS has issued fines to 
aliens with pending motions seeking to reopen or rescind removal 
orders. One commenter claimed that their client received a NIF that 
incorrectly stated a voluntary departure order had been issued several 
years prior to the date of actual issuance. Another alleged that, based 
on their clients' experiences, DHS frequently does not use or seek out 
the relevant information to determine whether aliens are willfully 
evading a removal order, thus frequently making incorrect assessments 
of such civil monetary penalties. One commenter stated that DHS appears 
to be issuing these fines in bulk through an automated system, often 
based on incomplete or inaccurate records and without considering 
aliens' individual circumstances. Collectively, these commenters argued 
that the number of alleged errors seen in these fines contradict the 
IFR's assertion that these penalties are straightforward and readily 
verifiable and raise concerns that the number of errors will be even 
higher under the IFR's streamlined process.
    Response: Civil penalties are issued based on the facts of an 
alien's case; an alien who chooses to appeal to DHS may present 
evidence relevant to their specific circumstances. Prior to issuing a 
failure to depart civil penalty, immigration officers verify there are 
no applications or actions pending litigation--including appeals, 
motions, and petitions for review (``PFRs'')--that would affect the 
finality of a removal order or allow the alien to lawfully remain in 
the United States. In the jurisdictions in which the filing of a PFR 
results in an automatic stay of removal, ICE generally will not issue 
the civil fine until there are no legal impediments to removal. 
Additionally, when calculating a fine under INA 274D, 8 U.S.C. 1324d, 
immigration officers account for any periods after the removal order 
became administratively final during which the alien was authorized to 
remain in the United States due to, for example, a stay of removal 
issued by EOIR, DHS, or a federal circuit court of appeals.
    DHS rejects the claim that it is issuing these penalties in bulk 
through ``an automated system'' without a human verifying that there is 
a final executable removal order, and there are no legal impediments to 
removal. DHS further notes that aliens assessed a failure to depart 
civil penalty may raise on appeal any issues that purportedly affect 
the finality of the removal order, dates of issuance, or the alien's 
willfulness in failing to depart.
    Finally, ICE acknowledges that, in some limited number of cases, it 
mistakenly issued penalties under the pre-IFR procedures in 8 CFR part 
280.



However, ICE does not agree that the risk of such errors will increase 
under the more streamlined IFR procedures that this rule finalizes. The 
IFR was designed to simplify and speed up the process of issuing and 
finalizing ICE civil penalty decisions. It does not change ICE's 
process for deciding in the first place whether an alien is subject to 
a civil penalty. Moreover, as discussed above in Section II of this 
preamble, aliens have appealed civil penalties under both the pre-IFR 
and post-IFR procedures, albeit to different agencies, and have 
succeeded in having penalties set aside when issued in error at similar 
rates under both procedures. For these reasons, DHS continues to 
believe that the IFR provides aliens with sufficient opportunity to 
challenge a penalty they believe was issued in error and to have those 
penalties rescinded. The commenters' examples of errors in a limited 
number of individual cases under the pre-IFR process do not, on their 
face, call into question the adequacy of the IFR's process for error-
correction. See Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319, 344 (1976) (finding 
that ``procedural due process rules are shaped by the risk of error 
inherent in the truth-finding process as applied to the generality of 
cases.'').
2. Compliance With Removal Orders
    Comment: One commenter disagreed with the IFR's premise that 
increased use of civil penalties will deter immigration violations. 
Another commenter disagreed that the IFR would encourage individuals to 
comply with removal and departure orders through self-departure. The 
commenter stated that the IFR fails to account for the practical 
realities faced by many aliens who are unable to depart the United 
States, including aliens who cannot obtain travel documents because of 
the lack of U.S. consular relations with their home government and 
those who face dangers returning over land. According to the commenter, 
fining aliens who genuinely cannot depart is unjust and inconsistent 
with encouraging compliance with removal orders.
    Response: The Departments disagree with commenters' claims that 
this rule will not encourage compliance with removal and departure 
orders through self-departure. In fact, since March 26, 2025, when DHS 
began issuing civil penalties, over 82,000 aliens with removal orders 
or voluntary departure orders have self-departed. DHS's ability to 
impose statutorily authorized civil penalties swiftly and in proportion 
to the large number of aliens with removal and departure orders is a
