critical part of DHS's efforts to encourage such aliens to depart the 
United States. Indeed, the IFR is achieving this objective, as DHS has 
issued approximately 176,000 fines under the IFR (compared to 
approximately 12,100 fines issued under 8 CFR part 280). These fines 
have encouraged greater compliance with removal and voluntary departure 
orders as evidenced by the over 7,700 illegal aliens who self-departed 
from the United States after receiving notice of a civil fine issued 
under the IFR. Moreover, DHS believes that these civil penalties are 
likely having a broader effect on encouraging compliance with removal 
orders as indicated by the total number of aliens with removal or 
voluntary departure orders who have self-departed the United States 
since DHS began issuing these penalties.
    DHS disagrees that it failed to consider that certain aliens may 
face impediments to departing the United States, including aliens who 
cannot obtain travel documents through U.S. consular relations with 
their country of citizenship or nationality. When an alien remains in 
DHS custody, immigration officers help them obtain and complete the 
necessary paperwork, including assisting where possible with consulate 
interaction.\33\ When an alien has been released on supervision, the 
alien must sign ICE Form 220B, attesting that he or she will assist DHS 
in obtaining necessary travel documents in the event that a final order 
of removal is issued.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \33\ ICE notes that aliens in this situation could be subject to 
a range of options, including further detention, orders of 
supervision, removal to a third country, or in some cases, parole. 
These options do not grant the alien status in the United States and 
aliens remain subject to their final order of removal. 8 CFR 241.13.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    DHS notes that aliens subject to a final order of removal who fail 
to timely depart the United States will be subject to civil penalties. 
Evidence that an alien has made a good faith attempt to obtain travel 
documents needed to timely depart is held by only aliens and DHS is not 
privy to this evidence until an alien presents it to DHS. During the 
appellate process, the alien or counsel may present evidence of the 
alien's inability to obtain travel documents due to no fault of his or 
her own. DHS officers retain the discretion to rescind civil penalties 
depending on the circumstances, such as a good-faith attempt to obtain 
travel documents. In addition, an alien need not depart to their 
country of citizenship or nationality; they need only depart the United 
States.
    Moreover, as directed by the President, DHS has removed many 
impediments to an alien's ability to self-depart the United States. See 
90 FR 8443. For example, DHS in partnership with the State Department 
is offering aliens free flights and providing travel document 
assistance to any non-criminal alien who uses the CBP Home app to 
indicate their intent to depart whether to their home country or a 
third country other than the United States. See DHS Press Release, DHS 
Announces Historic Travel Assistance and Stipend for Voluntary Self-
Deportation (May 5, 2025), https://dhs.gov/news/2025/05/05/dhs-announces-historic-travel-assistance-and-stipend-voluntary-self-deportation [https://perma.cc/8ST2-RHHP]. Indeed, DHS data indicates 
that over 104,000 aliens have voluntarily departed the United States 
through this program since the IFR took effect on June 27, 2025 through 
September 14, 2026.\34\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \34\ See Office of Homeland Security Statistics analysis of 
Alien Departures by Civil Fine, DHS Enforcement, and EOIR Case 
Outcomes (Oct. 7, 2026).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Comment: Another commenter explained that pressuring aliens to 
depart the United States to avoid civil fines undermines their existing 
rights and forecloses eligibility for immigration relief. One commenter 
said that leaving during removal proceedings can result in the loss of 
the statutory right to a fair hearing before an Immigration Judge. 
These commenters argued that departing interrupts the continuous 
presence requirement for cancellation of removal, thereby depriving 
qualifying aliens of this form of relief. Similarly, a commenter stated 
that departing terminates an alien's pending application for adjustment 
of status, impacting eligibility for lawful permanent resident status. 
Commenters also noted that departure can trigger statutory re-entry 
bars, creating barriers to lawful return and future immigration 
benefits. In this regard, one commenter characterized the IFR's goal of 
incentivizing aliens to self-depart as a ``legal trap'' that deprives 
aliens of due process and access to immigration benefits while barring 
their reentry.
    Response: The Departments acknowledge that an illegal alien's 
departure from the United States can trigger various immigration 
consequences. However, the Departments disagree with the claim that 
this rule, which uses civil penalties and the CBP Home application to 
encourage aliens to leave the United States, unfairly denies them 
access to Immigration Court proceedings or immigration relief. Rather, 
the penalties covered by this rule primarily apply to



aliens who have already gone through Immigration Court proceedings, 
which have resulted in an order of removal or grant of voluntary 
departure, and have failed to depart as required after the conclusion 
of such proceedings. Thus, commenter concerns about the implications of 
an alien's departure on the outcome of removal proceedings are 
unfounded. Relatedly, concerns about impacts to continuous physical 
presence are equally unfounded. The alien would stop accruing 
continuous physical presence, at the latest, on the date that they were 
served with the Notice to Appear to implement the removal proceedings 
that resulted in a final order of removal or grant of voluntary 
departure, not the date that they departed after being notified that 
they are subject to civil fines and penalties. INA 240A, 8 U.S.C. 
1229b(d)(1). Departures for reasons other than the imposition of civil 
fines and penalties that may take place prior to the commencement of, 
or during, an alien's removal proceedings are beyond the scope of this 
rulemaking.
    Moreover, aliens who are subject to removal orders or have failed 
to comply with voluntary departure orders are generally not eligible 
for, or face significant barriers to obtaining, the forms of relief 
mentioned by commenters. Under INA 240B(d)(1)(B), 8 U.S.C. 
1229(d)(1)(B), aliens who fail to comply with voluntary departure 
orders are generally ineligible, for a period of 10 years to seek 
cancellation of removal, adjustment of status, and other forms of 
relief. Furthermore, aliens under removal orders generally must reopen 
their removal proceedings to seek such immigration relief. However, the 
BIA has held that reopening is generally not justified for relief based 
on eligibility that arose after the removal order. See Matter of H-Y-Z-
, 28 I&N Dec. 156, 161 (BIA 2020) (``[E]quities that were acquired 
while [an alien] remained illegally in the United States after being 
ordered removed . . . generally do not . . . warrant discretionary 
reopening''); see also Matter of Yauri, 25 I&N Dec. 103, 105 (BIA 2009) 
(``[U]ntimely motions to reopen to pursue . . . adjustment of status . 
. . will ordinarily be denied''). More broadly, aliens subject to final 
executable removal orders do not have a right to remain in the United 
States to apply for motions to reopen or potential immigration benefits 
and, in many instances, they do not even have a right to remain to 
pursue pending applications for immigration benefits or motions to 
reopen.\35\ There may be limited circumstances where penalizable aliens 
can obtain the relief that the commenters mention. The number of cases 
in which an alien could obtain such relief in these circumstances is 
small, and civil penalties do not actually prevent aliens from applying 
for such relief. At most, it has an incidental deterrent impact on the 
alien, which is justified by the policies that the rule promotes. 
Therefore, the Departments disagree with commenters' claims that the 
IFR's goal of encouraging self-departure impermissibly deprives an 
alien of potential eligibility for immigration benefits or relief.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \35\ See, e.g. Dada v. Mukasey, 554 U.S. 1, 21 (2008) 
(explaining that an alien subject to a removal order ``may be 
removed by the DHS . . . even if the motion to reopen has yet to be 
adjudicated''); Dada Achacoso-Sanchez v. INS, 779 F.2d 1260, 1264 
(7th Cir. 1985) (``Congress has not given deportable aliens a right 
to the reopening of deportation proceedings.''); see also Riasati v. 
I.N.S., 738 F.2d 1115, 1118 (10th Cir. 1984) (``[a] pending visa 
application does not entitle an alien to a stay of deportation'') 
(citations and quotations omitted). The Departments acknowledge that 
certain aliens may be entitled to a stay of removal after filing for 
certain immigration benefits or certain motions to reopen. See, 
e.g., 8 CFR 214.205(g) (T-visas with a positive bona fide 
determination); INA 240(c)(7)(C)(iv), 8 U.S.C. 1229a(c)(7)(C)(iv) 
(VAWA self-petitioners); INA 240(b)(5)(C), 8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(5)(C) 
(motions to reopen an in-absentia order based on lack of notice). As 
explained in Section III.E.2 of this preamble, DHS does not issue 
civil fines in these circumstances.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    For similar reasons, the Departments also disagree with the claim 
that the IFR's goal of encouraging self-departure creates a ``legal 
trap'' for aliens who may become subject to reentry bars if they leave 
the United States. The Departments acknowledge that aliens who are 
subject to final removal orders or have accrued unlawful presence may 
be barred from re-admission to the United States for a certain number 
of years after departing. INA 212(a)(9), 8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(9). However, 
Congress did not intend for such consequences to excuse an illegal 
alien's continued presence in the United States. Enactment of these 
reentry bars plainly demonstrates that Congress intended immigration 
violations to carry significant consequences and did not view the 
possibility of future inadmissibility as a reason to excuse compliance 
with departure obligations. Accordingly, it is important for the 
Departments to faithfully carry out Congress's intent in a streamlined 
manner within the bounds of the law.
    Moreover, the Departments note that relief may be available to 
certain aliens who are barred under these inadmissibility grounds if 
they later have a valid basis to re-enter the United States. See INA 
212(a)(9)(A)(iii), 8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(9)(A)(iii) (exception to re-entry 
bar for certain aliens ordered removed who seek permission to re-
enter); see also INA 212(a)(9)(B)(v), 8 U.S.C. 1182(a)(9)(B)(v) (waiver 
to unlawful presence bars for certain aliens).
    Finally, to the extent that commenters are concerned about the 
impact of the unlawful entry civil monetary penalties, the Departments 
believe that concerns about aliens leaving the United States and 
abandoning removal hearings or benefits applications to avoid these 
specific penalties are speculative. The Departments do not believe that 
it is reasonable to assume that such aliens would abandon viable claims 
for relief or ongoing Immigration Court hearings given the more modest 
amount of these penalties.\36\ See DHS, Press Release DHS Announces It 
Will Forgive Failure to Depart Fines for Illegal Aliens who Self-Deport 
Through the CBP Home App (June 9, 2025). Furthermore, Congress has made 
clear that aliens who enter unlawfully are subject to such penalties 
notwithstanding the initiation or pendency of removal proceedings. See 
INA 275(b)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1325(b)(1).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \36\ Indeed, the Departments note that the fees for filing many 
immigration benefits applications, including cancellation of removal 
and adjustment of status, are higher than the civil penalty for 
unlawful entry.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Comment: One commenter questioned DHS's reliance on the CBP Home 
application as an available mechanism for compliance incentives. The 
commenter asserted that the application is not broadly accessible to 
all aliens subject to civil monetary penalties under the IFR but is 
limited to aliens who entered at or between a port of entry, those who 
arrived under a parole program, and those whose Temporary Protected 
Status had been terminated. The commenter stated that the application 
therefore excludes many aliens who could be fined under this rule and 
does not provide meaningful relief from fines or available incentive 
programs.
    Response: All non-criminal aliens who schedule their self-departure 
through the CBP Home App and depart will receive forgiveness of any 
civil penalties issued by DHS for failing to depart the United States. 
DHS has updated its website to reflect the full scope of the DHS 
policy.\37\ Thus, the departure incentives announced by DHS are not 
limited to the category of aliens identified by commenters, and DHS 
encourages all aliens subject to removal



or departure orders to take advantage of this opportunity and receive 
forgiveness for any civil penalty.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \37\ See, DHS Press Release, CBP HOME: Assistance to Voluntarily 
Self-Deport, https://www.dhs.gov/cbphome [https://perma.cc/PWQ2-W6ZJ] (Sept. 1, 2026).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Comment: Several commenters questioned the IFR's empirical basis 
for the assertion that civil monetary penalties will deter immigration 
violations and promote compliance with removal and departure orders. 
One stated that the IFR lacks evidence-based support for this 
justification and pointed to ICE's prior use of fines and subsequent 
recission of that policy as demonstrating that these fines are 
ineffective at achieving these purposes. One commenter stated that 
previous rules understood this and resultingly did not enforce these 
penalties, due to the cost of administering them far outweighing any 
fines collected. Collectively, these commenters viewed the IFR as 
lacking an empirical foundation, unlikely to alter behavior, and 
ineffective in achieving its compliance and enforcement goals.
    One commenter claimed that behavioral research on sanctions and 
procedural justice shows that fines do not deter unlawful behavior or 
encourage compliance with the law if the process for imposing them is 
unfair. The commenter cited to a ``policy briefing'' \38\ discussing 
research suggesting that people are more likely to comply with court 
orders when they believe that the underlying process is respectful, 
neutral, accessible, and provides an opportunity for them to 
participate before a decision is rendered.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \38\ Emily Gold LaGratta, Criminal Justice Alliance, To Be Fair: 
Procedural Fairness in Courts (Oct. 2014), https://justiceinnovation.org/publications/be-fair-procedural-fairness-courts [https://perma.cc/YL4F-UVU9].
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Response: The Departments disagree with the assertion that this 
rule lacks an empirical basis or relies on unsupported assumptions 
regarding deterrence. Congress has expressly authorized civil monetary 
penalties for the violations addressed in this rule and has long 
identified such penalties as a tool that may promote compliance with 
these statutory obligations. See 90 FR 27439-40. The Departments' role 
in this rulemaking is to ensure that DHS can efficiently utilize these 
statutory penalties consistent with Congress's objective in enacting 
them, not to reconsider the policy judgement underlying those statutory 
authorities or to undertake a new empirical assessment of their 
effectiveness. Moreover, as explained in Section I of this preamble, 
the IFR is achieving its intended incentive and deterrence 
objectives.\39\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \39\ See Office of Homeland Security Statistics analysis of 
Alien Departures by Civil Fine, DHS Enforcement, and EOIR Case 
Outcomes (Oct. 7, 2026).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    As explained in the IFR, DHS does not believe that its prior 
limited experience assessing these penalties in 2019 demonstrates that 
these penalties are ineffective. When ICE rescinded the prior penalty 
policy in 2021, there were only 26 active cases,\40\ which DHS 
concluded was an insufficient sample size to judge the effectiveness of 
these civil penalties. DHS explained its belief that these civil 
penalties would be more effective at achieving their deterrence and 
compliance objectives if applied quickly and at scale. In addition, the 
IFR was designed to address many of those administrative challenges 
that ICE faced when issuing civil penalties in 2019, by streamlining 
the procedures for these civil monetary penalties, thereby reducing 
operational burden and costs. Finally, the Departments noted that DHS's 
decision to stop issuing civil penalties under the prior Administration 
was based on that Administration's findings that there is no indication 
that these penalties promoted compliance with the alien's departure 
obligations. On January 20, 2025, President Trump directed DHS to focus 
enforcement resources on carrying out final orders of removal and 
enforcing laws related to illegal entry and unlawful presence. E.O. 
14159 also directed DHS to assess and collect all fines and penalties 
authorized by law. This rule is needed to help DHS meet these 
directives. See 90 FR 27447-48.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \40\ See ICE Memorandum for Tae D. Johnson, Acting Dir., ICE, 
from Corey A. Price, Acting Exec. Assoc. Dir., Enforcement and 
Removal Operations, ICE, Re: Recission of Civil Penalties for 
Failure to Depart (Aug. 6, 2021).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    With respect to comments on sanctions and ``procedural justice,'' 
the Departments note that the rule preserves the core procedural 
protections necessary to ensure fairness and meaningful participation, 
including written notice of the proposed penalty, information about the 
factual basis for it, an opportunity to present a written response with 
supporting evidence, and independent supervisory review by an official 
who was not involved in the initial determination. These protections 
reflect the principles of neutrality, respect, accessibility, and 
meaningful opportunity to be heard that the cited research suggests may 
support voluntary compliance.
    Finally, while commenters questioned whether civil penalties would 
deter unlawful behavior, Congress has already determined that these 
penalties may serve an enforcement and compliance function, and the 
Departments' procedural refinements help ensure these penalties can be 
administered efficiently and fairly in accordance with due process 
principles required by law. In any event, the Departments believe that 
DHS's robust use of these penalties is helping to achieve their 
compliance function as demonstrated by the over 82,000 aliens with 
removal and voluntary departure orders who self-departed after DHS 
began issuing these penalties, and as demonstrated by the fact that 
nearly 7,200 aliens self-departed after receiving a civil fine under 
the IFR.\41\ Accordingly, the Departments conclude that the rule has a 
sufficient basis.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \41\ See Office of Homeland Security Statistics analysis of 
Alien Departures by Civil Fine, DHS Enforcement, and EOIR Case 
Outcomes (Oct. 7, 2026).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

3. Use of Government Resources
    Comment: Commenters said that a large-scale penalty process will 
waste government time and resources. One claimed that issuing fines on 
a large scale would be an inefficient use of DHS resources because few 
aliens will pay them. Commenters discussed several factors that make 
collection improbable and administrative enforcement costly. They noted 
that many aliens have limited financial resources to pay these fines 
and the amounts are so high that aliens will not take them seriously. 
One commenter also said that the IFR will only further confuse many 
aliens as they do not understand the immigration system and many will 
not pay if they will be deported anyway. Another commenter said that 
sending a large number of fines to the Treasury Department for 
collection is wasteful because DHS itself cannot verify that aliens 
subject to these fines are actually in the United States, citing the 
IFR's statement that DHS records do not always reliably indicate which 
aliens actually remain in the United States after a removal or 
departure order. Another commenter also pointed to DHS's prior 
conclusion that the resources needed to impose these penalties 
outweighed the potential collections from a transient alien population 
that generally lacks the means to pay. Accordingly, commenters claimed 
that DHS should not expend substantial time and resources pursuing 
these penalties.
    Response: The Departments do not agree that this rule's goal of 
streamlining the civil penalty process is wasteful or an improper use 
of Government



resources. As an initial matter, the IFR and this rule are a critical 
part of DHS's efforts to use all statutorily available tools to achieve 
the Administration's immigration enforcement and border security 
objectives. This includes issuance of civil monetary penalties to 
encourage aliens to comply with removal and voluntary departure orders 
and to deter unlawful entries. The purpose of the rule is to streamline 
the civil penalty process to ensure that DHS can use these statutorily 
authorized penalties swiftly and at the scale needed to respond to the 
large number of aliens who have entered the United States or remain 
unlawfully. See 90 FR 27442; see also Section I of this preamble. Quite 
simply, this rulemaking is intended to help ensure that DHS has a 
workable process for issuing civil monetary penalties against aliens 
who unlawfully entered or failed to depart the United States as part of 
ICE's and CBP's missions to apprehend, detain, and remove aliens who 
have illegally entered the United States and are unlawfully present.
    More fundamentally, the Departments do not agree that civil 
penalties are an ineffective solution to the problem that many aliens 
remain in the United States in contravention of removal and departure 
orders. To the contrary, Congress has authorized DHS to impose these 
civil penalties on such aliens as a means to encourage them to comply 
with removal and departure orders and to impose consequences on those 
who fail to comply. 90 FR 27446. Indeed, DHS's use of these statutorily 
authorized tools is working to achieve the objective as discussed above 
in Section I of this preamble.
    Similarly, the Departments disagree with one commenter's claims 
that attempting to collect failure to depart penalties is wasteful 
because DHS cannot verify that aliens issued fines remain in the United 
States. As discussed in the IFR, DHS acknowledges that it does not 
maintain comprehensive departure records for all aliens, particularly 
for aliens who cross land borders, and, therefore, DHS may have issued 
a certain number of penalties to aliens who have already departed. 90 
FR 27445. ICE believes however, based on its experience, that it is 
reasonable to assume that a large number of aliens with final removal 
and departure orders remain in the United States.\42\ Id. Therefore, 
consistent with the President's direction in section 8 of E.O. 14159, 
90 FR 8444-45, DHS believes that the IFR's goal of quickly imposing 
penalties to encourage compliance with removal and departure orders 
justifies the resource expenditure, even if some number of penalties 
are not collected because the alien departed.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \42\ According to data in DHS's ENFORCE Alien Removal Module, 
there are 1.9 million aliens with final executable orders of removal 
out of a total of 2.1 million final orders of removal (last visited 
Sep. 10, 2026).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Finally, the IFR fully explains why the Departments believe that 
this rule is needed notwithstanding ICE's prior determination in 2021 
that the resource burdens outweigh the amount that can be collected 
from a transient population of aliens that lacks the means to pay. 90 
FR 27446-47. In the IFR, DHS first noted that its limited experience 
implementing these civil monetary penalties in prior years does not 
demonstrate that these penalties are innately ineffective. 90 FR 27447. 
Moreover, DHS explained that the IFR is intended to reduce potential 
resource burdens that DHS previously experienced when issuing these 
penalties by streamlining the underlying civil penalty process. Id. 
Additionally, DHS noted that the collection of civil penalties was not 
the only or even the primary goal; rather, DHS believes that maximizing 
the use of these civil penalties will encourage illegal aliens who are 
subject to them to voluntarily depart the United States. Id. As 
discussed above, DHS's use of these civil penalties is achieving this 
objective, and the use of the CBP Home app to self-deport is a cost-
effective means of achieving this objective.
    Comment: At least one commenter suggested that pursuing fines on a 
large scale would merely divert limited agency resources away from 
higher priority enforcement objectives, such as apprehending aliens who 
pose threats to public safety or national security. The commenter 
concluded that the IFR's approach would ultimately increase costs for 
the Departments without meaningfully advancing enforcement goals. 
Similarly, one commenter claimed that the IFR would not promote public 
safety but would have the opposite effect by heightening fear and 
discouraging engagement with law enforcement amongst immigrant 
communities. According to the commenter, imposing high civil fines on 
aliens, including those without criminal histories, would lead to fewer 
reports of crime, diminishing public safety for all. Another commenter 
suggested that a more effective and resource-efficient approach would 
be to focus enforcement on employers who hire unauthorized workers, 
suggesting that such entities can be expected to understand and comply 
with employment verification laws and will be better motivated by civil 
penalties, or the threat of civil penalties, to follow those laws.
    Response: The Departments disagree that implementing the civil 
penalty process described in the IFR will divert resources away from 
higher priority enforcement objectives or fail to advance statutory 
enforcement goals. Congress has expressly authorized the imposition and 
collection of civil penalties under INA 240B(d), 8 U.S.C. 1229c; INA 
274D, 8 U.S.C. 1324d; and INA 275(b), 8 U.S.C. 1325. The Departments 
therefore have a responsibility to maintain procedures that enable the 
effective administration of these statutory authorities. Implementing a 
clear, streamlined penalty process does not diminish the Departments' 
ability to prioritize cases involving threats to public safety or 
national security, including cases where the alien fails to depart or 
illegally enters the United States. Rather, the IFR promotes 
administrative efficiency by updating and consolidating procedural 
steps.
    Additionally, the concerns about the imposition of civil penalties 
heightening fear and discouraging engagement with law enforcement by 
the immigrant community is speculative. The commenter failed to provide 
information or evidence to support the concern that civil penalties 
will discourage aliens from reporting crime or engaging with law 
enforcement. Even if there is a disincentive to report crime or engage 
with law enforcement, the commenter failed to provide a basis to 
conclude that these disincentives stem from making the process of 
imposing civil penalties more efficient, rather than from the existence 
of civil penalties or immigration enforcement more generally.
    The Departments also disagree that the penalty process undermines 
public safety by discouraging aliens from reporting crime or engaging 
with law enforcement. The penalties addressed in the IFR apply only in 
limited circumstances specified by statute and do not alter DHS's 
longstanding policies and efforts aimed at encouraging victims, 
witnesses, and other individuals to cooperate with law enforcement 
regardless of immigration status. Nothing in the IFR changes 
protections for victims of crime, humanitarian programs, or DHS's 
ability to exercise discretion on a case-by-case basis. The 
Departments, therefore, do not expect the procedural updates in the IFR 
to meaningfully affect crime reporting or relationships between 
immigrant communities and law enforcement.



    The Departments further disagree that focusing enforcement 
resources on employers who hire unauthorized workers would be a more 
effective or statutorily appropriate approach. Employer sanctions and 
worker-related civil penalties are governed by distinct provisions of 
the INA, and the IFR did not amend or affect those frameworks. While 
the Departments enforce employer compliance laws through separate 
authorities, those efforts do not displace the need to implement civil 
monetary penalties against aliens where Congress has authorized their 
use and vested DHS with authority to enforce them. The IFR ensures 
streamlined procedures for carrying out the statutory provisions for 
civil monetary penalties applicable to aliens for failure to depart, 
failure to voluntarily depart, and improper entry, while employer-
related enforcement continues under its own statutory framework.
    For these reasons, the Departments conclude that the IFR's civil 
penalty procedures are an appropriate use of agency resources. The 
procedures promote efficient administration of existing statutory 
penalty authorities to meet immigration enforcement priorities and 
challenges.

D. Comments on Specific Provisions

    1. Removal of Notice of Intent To Fine
    Comment: Several commenters asserted that eliminating the notice of 
intent to fine (NIF) erodes procedural protections by transforming what 
was once a preliminary document signaling DHS's intent to issue a fine 
into a final agency decision. Commenters stated that this change 
reduces the time that aliens have to understand and respond to fines, 
seek legal advice, and submit an appeal. Additionally, one commenter 
suggested that eliminating the NIF process--which the commenter 
characterizes as being designed to notify aliens of potential penalties 
and allowing them to rectify the violation--is inconsistent with the 
goal of incentivizing aliens to comply with removal and departure 
orders.
    Response: The Departments disagree with commenters' 
characterization of the rule. Although the IFR eliminated the NIF 
process for these penalties, it continues to require written notice of 
penalties that identify the factual and legal basis for liability, see 
8 CFR 281.1(c), and provides aliens with an opportunity to submit a 
written response with supporting evidence before a final determination 
is made, see 8 CFR 281.1(e). Indeed, the differences between the NIF 
process prior to the IFR under 8 CFR part 280 and the process 
established by the IFR under 8 CFR part 281 are less substantial than 
commenters suggest. Under both regulations, if an alien fails to 
respond to the NIF or the penalty decision, as applicable, the alien 
will be liable for the penalty. See generally 90 FR 27449-54 (comparing 
8 CFR 280 and 8 CFR 281). The only difference is that, under the part 
280 process, a supervisory officer must convert a NIF into a final 
unappealable decision; under the IFR, the penalty decision 
automatically becomes final if the alien does not appeal. Compare 8 CFR 
280.13(a)(2), with 8 CFR 281.1(f)(3). Under both regulations, an alien 
who timely appeals a penalty decision is entitled to additional process 
before a final decision is issued. Compare 8 CFR 280.13(b), with 8 CFR 
281.1(e). Therefore, the IFR merely converts the prior two-stage NIF 
process under 8 CFR part 280 into a single process that eliminates 
duplicate administrative steps and paperwork if an alien does not 
appeal, but the fundamental safeguards of notice and an opportunity to 
be heard remain unchanged. Id.
    The Departments acknowledge that the IFR reduces the amount of time 
that an alien has to contest a penalty and to submit supporting 
evidence compared to the NIF process. Prior to the IFR an alien 
generally was required to answer a NIF within 30 calendar days and 
could submit supporting evidence at an in-person hearing, if requested. 
8 CFR 280.12. Under the IFR, an alien must file an appeal postmarked 
within 15 business days of the date of service of the civil penalty 
decision and the alien is generally required to submit all evidence in 
support of the appeal at the time of filing. 8 CFR 281.1(e)(1). 
However, as explained in the IFR and in response to related comments in 
this preamble, the Departments believe that shortening the timeline for 
appeals and evidentiary submissions is appropriate for the failure to 
depart and unlawful entry penalties due to the straightforward and 
readily determinable nature of these penalties.
    Moreover, the Departments note that in some respects the IFR 
simplified the process for aliens to contest civil penalties compared 
to the procedures under 8 CFR part 280. An alien may trigger an appeal 
under the 8 CFR 281.1 process by simply filing a notice of written 
appeal indicating that the alien is contesting the penalty. Indeed, DHS 
uses the Form 281, Notice of Violation and Order, which includes a 
field for aliens to use to appeal a penalty. The alien may, but is not 
required to, submit written argument or documentary evidence contesting 
the penalty. Id. In contrast, under the NIF process, the alien must 
provide a written defense, in duplicate, under oath setting forth the 
reasons why a fine should not be imposed. See 8 CFR 280.12.
    In addition, this final rule amends 8 CFR 281.1(e) to permit aliens 
to file an appeal that is postmarked after the 15-business-day deadline 
where the alien asserts, and ICE determines after considering on a 
case-by-case basis all the evidence presented with the appeal, that 
there was a mail delay in receiving the immigration officer's decision 
and order issued under 8 CFR 281.1(c)(1). Additionally, to help ensure 
timely processing and avoid administrative delays by postal carriers on 
the backend, DHS encourages aliens to obtain contemporaneous, time-
stamped evidence of deposit of their mailed appeal directly from the 
U.S. Postal Service (``USPS'') or their chosen commercial carrier 
because merely depositing an appeal in a standard mail collection box 
does not guarantee an immediate postmark or proof of the date of 
dispatch. This amendment, which provides an exception to the 15-
business-day deadline to appeal, addresses commenters' concerns 
relating to the reduced time for aliens to submit an appeal under 8 CFR 
part 281. Even assuming that the IFR's streamlined process makes it 
more challenging for aliens to appeal and submit supporting evidence in 
some cases, the Departments believe that this risk is outweighed by 
DHS's strong interest in the revised civil penalty process as discussed 
further in the IFR and this preamble.
    Finally, regarding one commenter's claim that eliminating the NIF 
is inconsistent with the IFR's goal of incentivizing compliance with 
removal and departure orders, the Departments note that the IFR was 
designed to achieve several goals. As explained in the IFR preamble, 
one goal of this rule was to ensure that DHS has a workable process for 
issuing civil penalties against aliens without diverting resources away 
from ICE's and CBP's missions to apprehend, detain, and remove illegal 
aliens. 90 FR 27447; see also Section I of this preamble. Eliminating 
the NIF serves this goal by removing a duplicative step (i.e., the 
requirement to issue a separate final decision) in cases where an alien 
does not appeal the civil penalty decision. The Departments note that 
aliens continue to have an avenue to rectify any fines resulting from 
these immigration violations. As the IFR explains, DHS will rescind 
outstanding civil penalties in cases where a qualifying alien uses the 
CBP Home app



to depart the United States. See 90 FR 27444.
    Comment: One commenter claimed that eliminating the preliminary NIF 
makes notice and the opportunity to be heard occur only after DHS 
imposes a civil monetary penalty, violating due process. Citing Mathews 
v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. 319 (1976), the commenter argues that similar to 
how the government must give a disability benefits recipient notice and 
an opportunity to submit information prior to terminating benefits, DHS 
must give aliens notice of the fine and an opportunity to challenge the 
accuracy of DHS's information and its conclusions before DHS imposes 
the fine. The commenter contends that the IFR violates due process 
because aliens are given no opportunity to submit information or 
contest the penalty prior to the final decision.
    Response: The Departments disagree with the commenter's 
characterization of the IFR. The IFR provides aliens with notice and an 
opportunity to contest civil penalties before they become final. As 
explained in the IFR, a decision imposing a civil monetary penalty 
becomes final only if the alien does not timely file an appeal, not at 
the time of issuance of the civil penalty.\43\ See 8 CFR 281.1(f)(3); 
see also 90 FR 27450. If the alien timely appeals, the initial penalty 
decision will remain inoperative during the pendency of the appeal. 8 
CFR 281.1(e)(1), (f)(3). At the end of the appeal process, and after 
considering any arguments and evidence submitted by the alien, a 
supervisory immigration officer who did not issue the initial penalty 
decision issues a final decision in writing affirming the initial 
penalty decision or withdrawing the decision and serves it on the 
alien. See 8 CFR 281.1(e). Therefore, contrary to the commenter's 
claim, the IFR provides an alien with both notice and an opportunity to 
challenge the penalty decision prior to the alien becoming liable for 
the penalty, in accordance with the pre-deprivation process upheld in 
Mathews v. Eldridge. 424 U.S. at 319.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \43\ As a practical matter, the same is true of the NIF process; 
if an alien does not timely answer the NIF, DHS may issue a final 
decision imposing the penalty which the alien cannot appeal. See 8 
CFR 280.13(a)(2).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Comment: Citing 5 U.S.C. 554(b), a commenter claimed that 
``eliminating the NIF also violates the [Administrative Procedure Act] 
because there is no notice of the matters of fact and law asserted, 
including what constitutes willfulness under these circumstances, and 
what factors are relevant to defenses or challenges to the penalty.'' 
More broadly, the commenter claims that the removal of the NIF violates 
``a foundational principle of administrative law: meaningful notice 
must precede the imposition of civil penalties to satisfy due process 
requirements.'' The commenter notes that federal statutes, including 
immigration statutes, consistently underscore the importance of notice 
in administrative proceedings, and discusses 8 U.S.C. 1182(n)(2)(C), 
which governs the civil penalty process for employers who violate 
certain labor conditions under the H1-B visa program as an example.
    Response: As an initial matter, the Departments note that, although 
the IFR eliminates the NIF process for these penalties, it continues to 
require DHS to issue a written notice that sufficiently identifies the 
basis for liability and provides aliens with an opportunity to contest 
such penalties before they become final. Under 8 CFR 281.1(c)(1), the 
initial penalty decision must include the statutory basis for the 
penalty, the amount and type of the penalty being imposed, and a brief 
statement of the reasons for the decision. DHS implements this 
requirement through Form 281, Notice of Violation and Order, which 
provides aliens with all of the required information, including 
information about the date that the alien became subject to a final 
removal or departure order or when the alien was apprehended entering 
the United States unlawfully. For the failure to depart penalties under 
section 274D(a)(1) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1324d(a)(1), the Form 281 also 
identifies the particular violation--e.g., willful failure or refusal 
to depart pursuant to a removal order; willful failure or refusal to 
make timely application in good faith for travel documents; willful 
failure or refusal to present for removal as required by DHS.
    This information ensures that aliens understand the basis for the 
penalty and have the requisite information in the event they seek to 
challenge it. See 90 FR 27449. Indeed, DHS notes that the NIF process 
does not require DHS to provide the alien with any additional 
information about the basis for a civil penalty beyond what the IFR and 
this rule require. See 8 CFR 280.1, 280.11. Moreover, as discussed in 
response to the comment immediately above, under the IFR an alien 
retains an opportunity to challenge a civil penalty decision issued 
pursuant to the IFR before it becomes final. Therefore, the Departments 
disagree that by eliminating the NIF this rule violates any 
``principles of administrative law'' related to notice in the civil 
penalty context.
    The Departments also note that the IFR's procedures are not subject 
to the requirements in 5 U.S.C. 554(a) because they are not 
adjudications ``required by statute to be determined on the record 
after opportunity for an agency hearing.'' Moreover, unlike the H1-B 
civil penalty statute cited by the commenter, the civil penalty 
statutes relevant to this rule do not specify the procedures that DHS 
must follow to impose these penalties. 90 FR 27448. As discussed in the 
IFR, Congress has set forth detailed procedures that the Government 
must follow when imposing certain immigration-related civil penalties, 
but Congress's omission of similar procedures for the penalties covered 
by this rule indicates that Congress intended to give DHS discretion to 
employ procedures that DHS reasonably believes are appropriate for such 
penalties. See id.; see also Vt. Yankee Nuclear Power Corp., 435 U.S. 
at 543 (concluding that ``[a]bsent constitutional constraints or 
extremely compelling circumstances the administrative agencies should 
be free to fashion their own rules of procedure and to pursue methods 
of inquiry capable of permitting them to discharge their multitudinous 
duties'') (cleaned up). For the reasons discussed further in the IFR 
and throughout this preamble, the Departments believe that the IFR's 
streamlined process, including the removal of the NIF, is reasonable 
and appropriate for these penalties given their typically 
straightforward nature and DHS's need to ensure that it has an 
efficient process for issuing these penalties more quickly and at scale 
to deter unlawful entries and to encourage compliance with removal and 
departure orders, while also providing aliens with sufficient notice of 
the basis for the penalty decision and opportunity to contest it before 
it becomes final.
2. Notice of Grounds for the Penalty
    Comment: Commenters objected to adequacy of the notice of the 
grounds for issuing the civil monetary penalties. One commenter said 
that the IFR's requirement that DHS must include a ``brief statement of 
the reasons'' for imposing a penalty is inconsistent with DHS's burden 
of proving by ``clear and convincing, and unequivocal evidence'' that 
an alien is liable. Commenters suggested that aliens cannot defend 
against fines without additional information or explanation in the 
penalty decision. One commenter said that the IFR violates the 
Administrative Procedure Act (``APA''), citing 5 U.S.C. 556, and due 
process principles requiring notice to reasonably apprise parties of 
the action and provide an



opportunity to present objections, because DHS is not required to 
provide a complete record supporting the penalty.
    Response: The Departments disagree that the penalty decision 
contains insufficient information for an alien to understand the basis 
for the penalty or to challenge it or that the IFR deprives aliens of 
their due process notice and hearing rights through lack of a record. 
There is no such requirement in statute for a hearing to be on the 
record in the civil penalties context or any indication that Congress 
intended the APA's procedures governing adjudications to apply. 
Therefore, DHS was not required to adopt the adjudication procedures in 
5 U.S.C. 554 and the follow-on procedures in 5 U.S.C. 556 that apply to 
adjudications governed by 5 U.S.C. 554. Regardless, new section 8 CFR 
281.1(e)(3) provides the materials that compose the record supporting a 
particular civil penalty.
    As an initial matter, DHS reiterates that the legal and factual 
predicates for these penalties are relatively straightforward and 
readily determinable based on information within DHS's and the alien's 
possession. 90 FR 27442; see also Section II of this preamble. For 
example, the INA authorizes DHS to impose a civil monetary penalty for 
failure to depart if two conditions are met: (1) the alien was granted 
voluntary departure or is subject to a final executable order of 
removal; and (2) the alien voluntarily failed to depart in the allotted 
time set forth in the voluntary departure order or willfully failed to 
depart under a final removal order. See INA 240B(d)(1), 274D(a)(1)(A), 
8 U.S.C. 1229c(d)(1), 1324d(a)(1)(A).\44\ The penalty decision provides 
aliens with sufficient information as to each of these elements.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \44\ The Departments focus on the failure to depart penalties 
consistent with the scope of commenters' concerns. To the extent 
that commenters are raising similar concerns about the unlawful 
entry penalties, commenters' concerns are addressed in Section 
III.E.2 of this preamble.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    With respect to the first element (the removal or departure order), 
the civil penalty decision, i.e., DHS Form 281, Notice of Violation and 
Order, explicitly lists whether the alien is being fined on the basis 
of a voluntary departure order or a removal order, and it provides the 
date that such an order was issued. DHS does not agree with commenters 
that DHS can only prove the existence of a removal or voluntary 
departure order by attaching the order to the penalty decision. The 
information contained in the penalty decision reflects that the 
immigration officer issuing the penalty has reviewed relevant DHS 
records and the alien's immigration files as required by ICE guidance 
and has determined based on those records that the alien is subject to 
a final executable removal order or voluntary departure order. See 90 
FR 27442-43; see also Section I of this preamble. To the extent that an 
alien believes that DHS records are mistaken, the alien can appeal the 
penalty decision and provide documentary evidence needed to dispute the 
decision. DHS assumes that aliens retain important documents, including 
legal documents demonstrating, for example, that the alien has been 
granted a stay of removal or has a pending appeal, or other documents 
reflecting that the alien is not subject to a final executable removal 
or departure order. Commenters have provided only speculative reasons 
to believe otherwise. Moreover, under the IFR's process, if an alien 
requests a copy of the relevant documents in connection with an appeal, 
the IFR requires DHS to provide such documents. 8 CFR 281.1(e)(3). 
Commenters have not provided any concrete evidence demonstrating that 
requiring DHS to provide a copy of the alien's removal or voluntary 
departure order would allow aliens to more effectively challenge a 
penalty decision. Indeed, ICE notes that the prior process under 8 CFR 
part 280 did not require DHS to provide a copy of an alien's removal or 
voluntary departure order when issuing a NIF and the DHS sees no reason 
for requiring it now. See 8 CFR 280.11.
    With respect to the second (willfulness or voluntariness) element, 
the penalty decision lists whether the alien is being issued a civil 
penalty for willfully failing or refusing to depart the United States, 
or for instead, voluntarily failing to comply with a voluntary 
departure order. DHS does not believe that any additional information 
is required. As the Departments explained in the IFR and in Section II 
of this preamble, statutory and regulatory requirements impose a duty 
on Immigration Judges to inform aliens of their obligation to depart 
and of the consequences of failing to do so, including that they could 
be liable for civil penalties. See 90 FR 27440-41. Absent contrary 
evidence, the presumption of regularity satisfies DHS's burden to 
demonstrate that an Immigration Judge provided notice of these 
obligations and consequences, see U.S. Postal Serv. v. Gregory, 534 
U.S. 1, 10 (2001), and an alien's failure to comply with the order 
after receiving notice of the consequences satisfies DHS's burden to 
demonstrate that the alien is liable for the penalty. See Section I of 
this preamble. To the extent that an alien contests the voluntary or 
willful nature of his or her failure to depart due to circumstances 
beyond the alien's control (e.g., hospitalization, incarceration, 
inability to obtain travel documents, lack of notice of a removal or 
voluntary departure order), the Departments note that the alien, not 
DHS, is in the best position to produce such evidence and may do so 
during the available appeals process before DHS. See Zenith Elec. Corp. 
v. United States, 988 F.2d 1573, 1583 (Fed. Cir. 1993) (``The burden of 
production should belong to the party in possession of the necessary 
information.'').
    For these reasons, the Departments conclude that the information 
provided in the penalty decision is facially consistent with DHS's 
burden of proof to demonstrate an alien's liability for a civil penalty 
covered by this rule. Commenters argue that DHS must meet the ``clear 
and convincing evidence standard'' described in Woodby v. INS, 385 U.S. 
276, 277 (1964). However, this standard applies to the burden of proof 
for deportable aliens in removal proceedings, not in the civil 
penalties' context. See 8 CFR 1240.8(a). Even assuming that DHS must 
meet the same ``clear and convincing evidence standard'' here, any 
challenge that DHS did not meet its burden of proof must be raised by 
an alien during the appeal process and based on the facts in his or her 
individual case.
    Finally, with respect to commenters' claim that the IFR violates 5 
U.S.C. 556 because it does not require DHS to provide a complete record 
supporting the penalty, DHS notes that 5 U.S.C. 556 applies only to 
hearings required by 5 U.S.C. 553 or 554. To the extent that the 
commenter is suggesting that civil penalty ``adjudications'' fall 
within the ambit of 5 U.S.C. 554(a) and therefore require DHS to follow 
the procedures in both 5 U.S.C. 554 and 556, DHS disagrees. There is no 
requirement in statute for a hearing to be on the record in the civil 
penalties context, let alone to comply with the procedures in 5 U.S.C. 
554 and the follow-on procedures under 5 U.S.C. 556 that also apply to 
adjudications governed by 5 U.S.C. 554. See Marathon Oil Co. v. E.P.A., 
564 F.2d 1253, 1263 (9th Cir. 1977) (stating that ``[t]he failure of 
Congress to provide for any hearing whatsoever within an administrative 
process may well be a valid indication that Congress either did not 
feel that it was providing for an ` ``adjudication'' ' in the 
traditional sense of the word or did not intend the APA procedures to 
apply''); see also City of West Chicago, Ill. v. NCR, 701 F.2d 632,



641 (7th Cir. 1983) (``Congress must clearly indicate its intent to 
trigger the formal on-the-record hearing provisions of the APA.''). 
Regardless, 8 CFR 281.1(e)(3) provides the materials that compose the 
record supporting a particular civil penalty and as explained in 
response to other comments in this preamble, the IFR's other procedures 
satisfy due process.
    Comment: One commenter claimed that the IFR should require DHS to 
attach a copy of the underlying voluntary departure order when imposing 
a fine for failure to depart under INA 240B(d), 8 U.S.C. 1229b(d). The 
commenter also states that many voluntary departure orders do not 
comply with INA 240B(d)(3), 8 U.S.C. 1229c(d)(3), which, according to 
the commenter, requires orders to include written warnings about 
potential fines for failure to depart. Accordingly, the commenter 
suggests that DHS can only meet its burden of proof to impose a fine if 
DHS provides a copy of the order containing the required warning.
    Response: As an initial matter, the Departments disagree that 
Immigration Judges and the BIA regularly do not provide statutorily 
required civil monetary penalty warnings when granting voluntary 
departure. Absent information to the contrary, the presumption of 
regularity applies as both Immigration Judges and the BIA are legally 
required to provide these warnings. See Gregory, 534 U.S. at 10; 8 CFR 
1240.26(k)(3). The commenter's general assertion--in ``many'' cases 
Immigration Judges and the BIA do not comply with this obligation--
without any factual basis is speculative and insufficient to overcome 
the presumption of regularity. To the extent an alien's voluntary 
departure order does not contain the required warning, the alien can 
file a timely appeal of the penalty decision and submit a copy of the 
allegedly deficient order. Moreover, for the reasons discussed in the 
IFR and in the comment response above, the Departments believe that, 
given the straightforward nature of these penalties, the penalty 
decision provides sufficient notice to the alien of the basis for the 
penalty and how to contest it. See also 90 FR 27443-44, 27452.
3. Service by First Class Mail
    Comment: Several commenters claimed that the change in service of 
process raises due process concerns. One commenter observed that the 
rule permits DHS to unilaterally send fines by ordinary mail despite 
previously issuing NIFs by personal service or certified mail. Another 
commenter states that previous rules required that communications be 
sent by certified mail or served in person, guaranteeing receipt, and 
that the IFR removing this provision to instead allow service by 
ordinary mail will dramatically increase the likelihood that intended 
recipients will not receive information about their fine, miss their 
appeal window, and unknowingly accrue large amounts in civil monetary 
penalties. Another commenter suggests that these risks are amplified in 
this context given the highly transient nature of the population 
subject to these fines. One commenter explained that service by regular 
mail will not reasonably apprise aliens of the fine because regular 
mail makes it significantly less likely that the alien will receive the 
decision in a timely manner if at all. This commenter also points out 
that in the removal proceedings context in which DHS uses service by 
regular mail a significant amount of the information provided in 
mailings is also available online unlike in this civil penalty context. 
They state that here, in this context, aliens have no other way to 
access the information or be on notice that they have penalties brought 
against them. They also note that this is particularly an issue for 
those who have been fined incorrectly and explain that since the 
beginning of 2025 they have heard from permanent residents who have 
been in the United States for decades and would have no reason to 
believe there are pending proceedings against them who received NIFs. 
Other commenters also raised that authorizing service by regular mail 
increases the likelihood of delay or non-receipt, one noting that 
regular mail cannot be tracked.
    Another commenter claimed that the IFR fails to explain how 
ordinary mail saves money and staff time compared to personal service 
or certified mail. The commenter also noted that the IFR does not 
explain why ICE cannot use personal service for aliens with removal 
orders because, as the IFR notes, these aliens are required to attend 
in-person check-ins with ICE.
    Response: The Departments disagree that permitting service of civil 
monetary penalty determinations by regular mail raises due process 
concerns or fails to provide constitutionally adequate notice. Due 
process does not require use of any particular method of service or 
guarantee of actual receipt. Rather, it requires that the chosen method 
be ``reasonably calculated, under all the circumstances,'' to inform 
interested parties of the action and to permit them an opportunity to 
respond. Mullane, 339 U.S. at 314 (stating that notice under due 
process must be of a sufficient nature as to reasonably convey the 
required information). Service by regular mail has long been recognized 
as a constitutionally sufficient method of notice in civil, 
administrative, and immigration contexts, including in removal 
proceedings, and other DHS communications. See e.g., Gardner v. City of 
Columbus, Ohio, 841 F.2d 1272, 1279 (6th Cir. 1988) (recognizing that 
service by regular mail satisfied due process notice requirements, 
while among other factors, noting government's observation that service 
by certified mail would be more costly); Urbina-Osejo v. INS, 124 F.3d 
1314, 1317 (9th Cir.1997) (stating that ``notice of a deportation 
hearing sent by regular mail to the last address provided by the alien 
to the INS satisfies the requirements of constitutional due process''); 
Matter of Grijalva, 21 I&N Dec. 27 (BIA 1995) (holding that notice sent 
by regular mail is presumed sufficient if it is properly addressed and 
mailed according to established procedures and that the presumption of 
delivery may be rebutted with evidence of non-receipt). The IFR adopted 
this established practice.
    Penalty determinations are sent to the address the alien has 
provided to DHS or that otherwise appears on file. As the IFR explains, 
DHS has a reasonable expectation that aliens will take these 
requirements seriously because failure to do so can result in a range 
of consequences including criminal penalties. INA 266, 8 U.S.C. 1306. 
In general, aliens in the United States are under specific statutory 
and regulatory obligations to register their presence, see INA 261-264, 
8 U.S.C. 1301-1304; 8 CFR part 264, and to keep the U.S. Government 
apprised of their current address while in the country, see INA 265, 8 
U.S.C. 1305; 8 CFR 265.1. Most aliens subject to the monetary penalties 
covered by this rule are warned of their address obligations upon 
initiation of section 240 removal proceedings, and DHS is taking steps 
to ensure that all aliens are aware of, and comply with, registration 
and address requirements consistent with this Administration's 
policies. Additionally, DHS provides convenient and reliable ways for 
aliens to update their addresses including through online portals, and 
immigration officers have access to current address data maintained in 
DHS and EOIR databases.
    Although some commenters expressed concern that personal service or 
certified mail had previously been used for NIFs, the governing 
statutory provisions do not require the use of those methods for civil 
monetary penalty notices, and neither do due process principles impose 
such a



requirement. INA 240B(d)(1)(A), 8 U.S.C. 1229c(d)(1)(A); INA 
274D(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1324d(a)(1); & INA 275(b)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1325(b)(1). 
See also Mullane, 339 U.S. at 314 (``Personal service has not in all 
circumstances been regarded as indispensable to the process due to 
residents, and it has more often been held unnecessary as to 
nonresidents. We disturb none of the established rules on these 
subjects.''); Dusenbery v. United States, 534 U.S. 161, 161-62 (2002) 
(upholding notice sent by certified mail to a prison, even though 
inmate claimed he never received it, demonstrating that due process 
does not require proof of actual receipt, and explaining that Mennonite 
Board of Missions v. Adams, 462 U.S. 791, 797 n.3 (1983) did ``not say 
that the State must provide actual notice, but that it must attempt to 
provide actual notice'') (emphasis in original).\45\ Furthermore, even 
a Notice to Appear (NTA), which initiates section 240 removal 
proceedings and thus carries greater legal consequences, may be served 
by regular mail. INA 239(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1229(a)(1). Although the 
statute previously required certified mail, Congress removed that 
requirement in IIRIRA, expressly permitting service by other forms of 
mail. See INA 239(a)(1)-(2), as amended by IIRIRA, Public Law 104-208, 
div. C, tit. III, 304(a)(3), 308(b)(6), 110 Stat. 3009-546, 3009-587-
88, 3009-615. The INA now provides that service by mail ``shall be 
sufficient if there is proof of attempted delivery to the last address 
provided by the alien.'' INA 239(c), 8 U.S.C. 1229(c). By contrast, the 
INA is silent as to the method of service for civil monetary penalties 
under INA 240B(d), 274D(a), 275(b), 8 U.S.C. 1229c(d), 1324d(a), 
1325(b). Accordingly, this final rule will allow DHS to use routine 
service, including regular mail which in turn will lessen DHS's 
administrative burdens, such as the time and resources needed for 
personal service and the additional costs and increased processing 
times associated with certified mail. Routine service also provides an 
alien appropriate notice of the imposition of a civil monetary penalty.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \45\ The agency acknowledges that in Jones v. Flowers, 547 U.S. 
220 at 232 (2006), the Supreme Court held that a person's failure to 
comply with a statutory address update requirement does not forfeit 
the right to constitutionally sufficient notice, and that additional 
reasonable steps may be required before the government takes certain 
actions. The Court emphasized, however, that due process adequacy 
requires balancing the government's interests against the individual 
interests at stake. Id. at 229. For the reasons discussed in the 
IFR, the Departments believe that the Supreme Court's decision is 
distinguishable. See 90 FR 27452 n.44.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The Departments also disagree that service by regular mail 
increases the likelihood that aliens will unknowingly accrue penalties 
or be deprived of an opportunity to appeal. First, the rule's 
procedures are reasonably designed to prevent aliens from unknowingly 
accruing civil monetary penalties. Under INA 262, 8 U.S.C. 1302, most 
aliens present in the United States for 30 days or more are required to 
apply for registration and fingerprinting. As a result, most aliens are 
subject to the address update requirement in INA 265, 8 U.S.C. 1305. 
Moreover, most aliens subject to the penalties addressed in this rule 
are specifically advised of these obligations upon initiation of 
section 240 removal proceedings. INA 239(a)(1)(F), 8 U.S.C. 
1229(a)(1)(F). DHS provides convenient and reliable ways for aliens to 
update their addresses, including use of online portals, and 
immigration officers have access to current address data maintained in 
DHS and EOIR databases. 90 FR 27452.
    Against that backdrop and as noted in the IFR, the Supreme Court 
has recognized that service by regular mail may, in some circumstances, 
provide better notice than certified mail or other methods. Jones, 547 
U.S. at 234-35. This rule adopts that approach. 90 FR 27453. Based on 
ICE's experience, service by ordinary mail is often more likely to 
reach aliens, including those who may be attempting to evade detection 
or who have moved without updating their address. Id. Such aliens, or 
members of their household, may be less likely to answer the door for 
personal service or to accept certified mail, whereas regular mail is 
delivered directly to their mailbox. Id. Even when an alien has moved, 
regular mail may still result in the current occupant forwarding 
address information or otherwise alerting the intended recipient. Id. 
(citing Jones, 547 U.S. at 235). Moreover, the rule does not mandate 
use of regular mail in all cases. DHS retains discretion to use other 
methods of service where appropriate. 90 FR 27453 (citing 8 CFR 
281.1(d)). Accordingly, DHS reasonably believes that notices sent to 
the most recent address provided by the alien satisfy due process 
requirements.
    Secondly, the rule includes sufficient procedural protections that 
mitigate the effects of any variation in mail delivery times and afford 
a meaningful opportunity for appeal. Consistent with 8 CFR 281.1(e), an 
alien shall file a written notice of appeal with the Department 
postmarked within 15 business days of the date of service of the 
decision. Although service of the immigration officer's decision is 
complete upon mailing, the rule mitigates the effects of variability in 
mail delivery times at the appeal stage by defining timeliness based on 
the postmark date of the appeal rather than the date of receipt. As 
explained in the IFR, ``DHS will calculate the timeliness of an appeal 
based on the date that the alien's appeal is postmarked.'' 90 FR 27450 
(citing 8 CFR 281.1(e)). Under this framework, an alien who mails an 
appeal within the 15-business-day period is not penalized for postal 
delays occurring after the appeal is sent. This approach allocates the 
risk of mail delay at the filing stage to the Government and helps 
ensure that ordinary variations in mail delivery do not result in 
forfeiture of appeal rights.
    Along with the notice of appeal, an alien may, but is not required 
to, provide a written defense or documentary evidence, or both, setting 
forth the reasons why a penalty should not be imposed. Id. After the 
appeal is filed, a supervisory immigration officer who did not review 
the initial decision and order must conduct a de novo review and may 
request supplemental evidence or information, in which case aliens 
receive an additional 15 days to provide supporting material. 90 FR 
27450 (citing 8 CFR 281.1(e)(2)). The officer may, in their discretion, 
call for additional briefing or written filings from the alien, and the 
alien will have 15 days from the receipt of that request to provide the 
information. Id. The officer will also provide the alien with copies of 
pertinent documents and records relevant to the penalty, if the alien 
requests, unless they are law enforcement sensitive, or disclosure is 
prohibited by law. 90 FR 27450 (citing 8 CFR 281.1(e)(3)). Moreover, if 
the alien files a notice of appeal, the initial civil penalty decision 
will remain inoperative during the appeal. 90 FR 27450 (citing 8 CFR 
281.1(e)(1)).
    In addition, the Departments recognize that aliens may, in limited 
circumstances, experience delayed or untimely delivery of notices 
served by mail that is outside aliens' control. To address this concern 
while preserving the integrity and administrability of the appeals 
process, this rule provides a narrow, case-by-case mechanism for 
accepting appeals filed after the 15-day filing period when the alien 
demonstrates that the delay resulted from mail delivery issues. Under 
the rule, an alien who files an appeal after the applicable deadline 
and asserts that the delay was caused by untimely or delayed mail 
delivery must submit a written explanation and any available



documentary evidence supporting that assertion. If, based on the 
information submitted, ICE determines that the appeal was filed late 
due to mail delay beyond the alien's control, ICE will accept the 
appeal as timely filed and consider it on the merits. By requiring 
aliens to affirmatively raise mail delay and provide supporting 
evidence, the rule ensures that aliens are not prejudiced by mail 
delivery delays beyond their control, while maintaining finality and 
administrative efficiency.
    The Departments acknowledge commenters' concerns that certain 
populations may be more mobile or may have limited access to online 
resources. However, DHS's service method here is identical to the 
method used for numerous other immigration-related notices, including 
those in removal proceedings where similar concerns may exist. Even if 
mobile, aliens have a statutory duty to register their presence and 
keep the U.S. Government apprised of their current address, and DHS has 
a reasonable expectation that aliens will comply with such 
requirements. INA 266, 8 U.S.C. 1306. While the information in penalty 
notices is not available online like it is for removal proceedings 
notices, the constitutionally relevant question is whether the method 
of service is reasonably calculated to inform, not whether parallel 
avenues for accessing the same information exist. See Mullane, 339 U.S. 
at 315 (``The reasonableness and hence the constitutional validity of 
any chosen method may be defended on the ground that it is in itself 
reasonably certain to inform those affected.''). The penalty notice 
itself contains the relevant information: the statutory basis for the 
penalty, the factual allegations, the amount sought, and clear 
instructions on how to appeal. See 8 CFR 281.1(c)(1); 90 FR 27449. Due 
process does not require DHS to maintain a public online portal for 
civil monetary penalty notices, nor does the lack of such a portal make 
regular mail constitutionally insufficient. See Mullane, 339 U.S. at 
315.
    The Departments also disagree with commenters' suggestion that ICE 
must use personal service for individuals who attend in-person check-
ins. Not all aliens subject to civil penalties are enrolled in programs 
involving in-person reporting, and requiring personal service in every 
case would impose significant operational burdens without materially 
improving notice. Regular mail ensures efficient and consistent 
delivery of notices for geographically dispersed aliens.
    Finally, while one commenter questioned whether ordinary mail saves 
time or resources, the IFR explains that allowing service by regular 
mail promotes efficiency. As discussed in the IFR, personal delivery 
often may require burdensome manual efforts to locate the alien. It may 
further require the use of multiple DHS agents or officers to appear on 
location to ensure officer safety, and multiple attempts at personal 
service if not effectuated on the first attempt, thereby diverting 
officers from their other duties. 90 FR 27444-45. Service by certified 
mail involves preparation of individual mailings in each case, 
including handwriting envelopes, which has proven to be costly and 
resource intensive and would become even more so as DHS expands its use 
of these civil penalties. Indeed, ICE estimates that the certified mail 
requirement costs the agency $23.53 for each civil monetary penalty, 
which includes certified mail fees, materials, and labor. 90 FR 27444. 
Consequently, personal service or certified mail imposes higher costs 
and increases processing times and is unnecessary to satisfy 
constitutional or statutory notice requirements. See Mullane, 339 U.S. 
at 306. The Departments also recognize commenters' concerns that some 
individuals, including lawful permanent residents, may have reported 
receiving penalty-related notices in error. The IFR's service 
provisions do not increase the likelihood of incorrect notices. 
Instead, the procedural framework contains safeguards and corrective 
mechanisms, including written notice and a mandatory de novo 
supervisory review over any appeal. The initial civil penalty decision 
remains inoperative while a timely administrative appeal is pending. 
This provides structured mechanisms to correct any errors promptly. Any 
alien who believes a notice was issued in error may file a simple 
written appeal explaining as much, triggering the supervisory review 
process. These procedures ensure that aliens have meaningful 
opportunities to contest errors.
    Accordingly, the Departments conclude that service by regular mail, 
coupled with the exception to the 15-business-day deadline to appeal 
when ICE determines that there was a mail delay under 8 CFR 
281.1(e)(2), is a reasonable, appropriate, and constitutionally 
sufficient method of providing notice of civil monetary penalty 
determinations under the INA, particularly given the IFR's procedural 
safeguards that ensure aliens retain meaningful opportunity to contest 
penalties. See Mathews v. Eldridge, 424 U.S. at 335.
4. 15-Day Appeal Deadline and Process
    Comment: Commenters argued that a 15-business-day appeal deadline 
will prevent aliens from being able to contest these civil fines. 
Commenters listed several barriers they claim will prevent aliens from 
meeting the appeal deadline. One commenter asserted that a significant 
number of aliens that receive these fines speak a language other than 
English, but the IFR lacks any language accommodation, creating a 
barrier to responding within 15 days. Another commenter also noted that 
some may struggle to understand fine-related communications not 
delivered in their primary language. They noted that they expect this 
to be a common occurrence given that DOJ's July 14, 2025, memorandum 
regarding implementation of Executive Order 14224, Designating English 
as the Official Language of the United States, 90 FR 11363 (Mar. 6, 
2025), directed a reduction in multilingual services at federal 
agencies. This commenter also asserted that a 15-day appeal period is 
unrealistic and unfair because aliens will lack sufficient time to 
understand the fines and their applicability and legal nuances and the 
related processes and will be unfamiliar with the IFR's new provisions. 
Another commenter stated that the 15-business-day period would make 
obtaining legal representation difficult and expensive and asserted 
that the IFR minimized the complexity of proving and imposing civil 
penalties. Another commenter stated that the 15-business-day period 
does not account for the time needed to access the necessary 
information required to contest a penalty decision. They note that some 
medical records are accessible online but that many health networks 
cite a 7-to-14-business-day turn around to provide medical records and 
that federal law requires medical records to be processed in 30 days. 
They also explained that state and local incarceration, court records, 
and travel documents are difficult to access and involve waiting times 
in excess of 15 business days. The commenter also claimed that 
obtaining travel documents takes significant time because many 
countries' embassies are located in Washington, DC and require aliens 
to appear in person. The commenter also noted that aliens whose 
citizenship is not recognized by a country may have difficulty securing 
an appointment.
    Response: The Departments disagree that the 15-day deadline for 
submitting an administrative appeal will prevent aliens from contesting 
civil penalties. The revised process continues to provide aliens with 
written notice of the



proposed penalty that identifies the factual and legal basis for the 
determination and explains the steps to request the review. The 
Departments also disagree that the lack of language accommodation in 
the IFR, such as a requirement to translate penalty determinations and 
appeal instructions into each respondent's native language, prevents 
aliens from meeting the 15-day appeal deadline. As with other 
immigration notices and charging documents, including NTAs, removal 
orders, voluntary departure orders, and USCIS decision notices, civil 
monetary determinations are issued in English, and neither the INA nor 
the Constitution obligates DHS to translate such documents into every 
alien's native language. See Ojeda-Calderon v. Holder, 726 F.3d 669, 
675 (5th Cir. 2013) (citing Nazarova v. INS, 171 F.3d 478, 483 (7th 
Cir. 1999) (explaining that due process does not require immigration 
notices to be in a language the alien can understand). Civil penalty 
decisions issued under this final rule will continue to include written 
instructions explaining how to file an appeal. Aliens may also seek 
assistance from legal representatives, community organizations, or 
interpreters. Aliens may provide additional documentation if the 
supervisory officer requests supplemental briefing during de novo 
review. Accordingly, the Departments conclude that the English language 
format of penalty notices is consistent with longstanding immigration 
practice and constitutional requirements as well as DOJ's memorandum 
implementing Executive Order 14224 by minimizing non-essential 
multilingual services, redirecting resources toward English-language 
education and assimilation, and ensuring compliance with legal 
obligations through targeted measures where necessary. Memorandum for 
all Federal Agencies, from Pamela Bondi, Attorney General, Re: 
Implementation of Executive Order No. 14,224: Designating English as 
the Official Language of the United States of America at 2, 7 (July 14, 
2025) https://www.justice.gov/ag/media/1407776/dl.
    Aliens also remain free to seek legal representation at any point 
in the process, including after filing the initial written appeal 
request. Nothing in the IFR limits a respondent's ability to obtain 
counsel or work with legal service providers. The IFR merely 
standardizes the timeframe for the initial appeal filing while 
preserving a meaningful opportunity, through mandatory de novo review 
and a potential supplemental briefing period, to submit evidence or 
legal argument. Considering these procedural safeguards, the 
Departments conclude that the 15-day appeal period is a reasonable and
