appropriate procedural requirement.
    In addition, the IFR also only requires that the alien submit a 
written appeal explaining the basis for contesting the civil penalty, 
as the grounds on which an alien may contest a civil penalty are 
limited and generally involve facts uniquely within the alien's 
knowledge. As the IFR noted, aliens will ordinarily possess the 
necessary information to contest these fines. 90 FR 27450. If an alien 
submits an appeal with assertions that are unsupported by documentary 
evidence because there was no time for the alien to obtain these 
documents, then the supervisory immigration officer reviewing the 
appeal can request the documents during the course of the appeal to 
verify the validity of the alien's assertions. See 8 CFR 281.1(e)(3). 
Additionally, the fact that it takes an alien longer than 15 days to 
obtain travel documents is irrelevant because the fines are issued 
after the time period aliens have been given to obtain travel documents 
and depart has elapsed. The streamlined procedures are designed to 
ensure timely resolution of cases and maintain the integrity of 
enforcement actions. DHS believes the 15-day appeal period, coupled 
with ICE's discretion to equitably toll the appeal deadline when ICE 
determines that there was a mail delay under 8 CFR 281.1(e)(2), strikes 
an appropriate balance between efficiency and fairness, providing 
adequate opportunity for aliens to contest violations and demonstrate 
lawful status or other circumstances that may preclude liability.
    Comment: Commenters also expressed concern with the interaction 
between the 15-day appeal deadline and the IFR's provisions allowing 
DHS to serve fines by regular mail. One commenter pointed out that, 
according to the U.S. Postal Service, ordinary mail takes 1-5 business 
days to reach its destination. The commenter noted that this leaves an 
alien with only 10 days to appeal a fine once received and, if sent in 
advance of a weekend, an alien only has 8 days. Another commenter 
reiterated that this 15-day appeal period is not enough time to 
meaningfully respond and noted that other federal regulations governing 
civil penalties include a 5-day mail presumption. They also stated they 
``were aware of many people who have received notices that were dated 
several days before they were mailed out.''
    Response: The Departments disagree that the interaction between the 
15-business-day appeal deadline and the IFR's service provisions 
prevents aliens from having a meaningful opportunity to appeal. The 
Departments recognize that aliens may, in limited circumstances, 
experience delayed or untimely delivery of notices served by mail that 
is outside the alien's control. To address this concern while 
preserving the integrity and administrability of the appeals process, 
this final rule amends 8 CFR 281.1(e) to provide a case-by-case 
mechanism for accepting appeals filed after the 15-day filing period 
when the alien demonstrates that the delay resulted from mail delivery 
issues. Under the rule, an alien who files an appeal after the 
applicable deadline and asserts that the delay was caused by untimely 
or delayed mail delivery must submit a written explanation and any 
available documentary evidence supporting that assertion. If, based on 
the information submitted, ICE determines that the appeal was filed 
late due to mail delay beyond the alien's control, ICE will accept the 
appeal as timely filed and consider it on the merits. By requiring 
aliens to affirmatively raise mail delay and provide supporting 
evidence, the rule ensures that aliens are not prejudiced by mail 
delivery delays beyond their control, while maintaining finality and 
administrative efficiency. In addition, although one commenter merely 
referenced anecdotal reports to assert some notices may have been 
mailed after the date listed on the document, this new exception to the 
15-day filing period will provide aliens more time file their appeal 
for mail delays that occur while the notice is in transit and for 
processing delays from the time date the notice is signed until it is 
placed in the mail.
    Moreover, due process principles require that notice be reasonably 
calculated to inform the respondent of the action and provide a 
meaningful opportunity to respond. See Mullane, 339 U.S. at 314. The 
combination of written notice, the exception to the 15-business day 
deadline to appeal when ICE determines that there was a mail delay 
under 8 CFR 281.1(e)(2), mandatory de novo review, and a potential 15-
day period for supplemental briefing satisfies these constitutional 
requirements and provides aliens with a realistic and fair opportunity 
to contest civil fines. DHS believes that the nature of the failure to 
depart and unlawful entry penalties typically turn on routine and 
straightforward determinations of fact, meaning that an appeal period 
greater than 15-days is unnecessary. In fact, there has been a higher 
appeal rate of



civil penalties for failure to depart issued under 8 CFR part 281, as 
compared to 8 CFR part 280, which suggests that aliens are able to 
meaningfully file appeals within the shortened timeline. DHS believes 
this is because of the straightforward factual issues associated with 
these penalties. Additionally, the appeal process under 8 CFR part 281 
discourages frivolous or non-meritorious appeals, focusing resources on 
cases with substantive claims.
    Comment: Commenters raised general due process and fairness 
concerns with the 15-day appeal deadline and process. One commenter 
asserted that shortening the appeal deadline from 30- to 15-days 
eliminates a key due process safeguard. Commenters also claimed that 
DHS's interest in reducing the appeal period to avoid a backlog of 
penalties is outweighed by the alien's interest in having enough time 
to meaningfully respond to these penalties, especially given the 
amounts. One commenter stated that shortening the appeal period 
increases the chance that an alien could face serious penalties without 
even realizing what they are accused of. As an example, one commenter 
claimed that many aliens, including those who were brought to the 
United States as children, may not even be aware that they are subject 
to a removal order. A commenter claimed that, in light of the many 
barriers that aliens face responding to these penalties, the appeal 
period is ``clearly designed'' to prevent as many aliens from 
contesting these civil penalties as possible.
    Response: The Departments disagree that the 15-day appeal deadline 
or the revised procedures deprive aliens of due process or create 
unfair barriers to contesting civil penalties. Due process requires 
that individuals receive notice reasonably calculated to inform them of 
the proposed action and a meaningful opportunity to be heard before a 
determination becomes final. The IFR preserves these core protections. 
Aliens continue to receive written notice setting out the factual and 
statutory basis for the penalty and providing clear instructions on how 
to appeal as explained in more detail in responses to comments about 
the appeal deadline in this Section, III.D., of the preamble.
    Comment: Commenters also took issue with the lack of extensions for 
good cause. One commenter alleged that the lack of extensions for good 
cause further contributes to the erosion of procedural protections. 
Another commenter suggested that DHS should account for demonstrations 
of good faith compliance efforts.
    Response: The Departments decline to modify the IFR to permit good 
cause extensions for late-filed appeals because the Departments do not 
believe that creating exceptions to the appeal deadline will 
meaningfully reduce the risk of error. See Bowen v. City of New York, 
476 U.S. 467 (1986) (recognizing that agencies may impose deadlines for 
appeals, and that equitable tolling (exceptions) is only appropriate in 
exceptional circumstances and that routine or general exceptions are 
not required for due process). The Departments believe the risk of 
error is minimized through the robust procedures already in place, 
which ensure that aliens are provided with notice of the fine, an 
opportunity to appeal, and clear instructions on how to contest the 
penalty. The appeal process focuses on factual determinations, and 
aliens are best positioned to produce the necessary information to 
contest a fine within the established timeframe.
    On the other hand, the Departments note that permitting good-cause 
extensions or excusing late filed appeals impedes DHS's ability to 
efficiently administer the penalty process as DHS expands its use of 
these penalties. DHS has a strong interest in ensuring that it can 
finalize penalty decisions quickly in response to the large number of 
aliens who have entered the United States unlawfully in recent years 
and the significant numbers of aliens who have failed to comply with 
removal and voluntary departure obligations. See 90 FR 27422-23; see 
also Section II of this preamble. It would be inconsistent with DHS's 
finality interests to allow late filed appeals. Such appeals would 
delay or impede DHS's ability to move forward with the collection 
process or would require DHS to re-open or pull back any final penalty 
decisions already transmitted for collection. Therefore, a strict 
appeal deadline allows DHS to have greater certainty in the finality of 
its penalty decisions and it allows DHS to more effectively achieve the 
IFR's objectives of incentivizing compliance with the immigration laws 
and imposing consequences on those who do not comply.
    DHS acknowledges these finality concerns could, to some extent, be 
mitigated by imposing an outer deadline on late-filed appeals or by 
restricting the length of ``good cause'' extensions. The Departments 
decline to adopt this approach for several reasons. First, DHS believes 
that such an approach would undermine the Departments' goals regarding 
the 15-day appeal deadline. See 90 FR 27442-43. Allowing an alien to 
have a certain amount of time to file an untimely appeal would, as a 
practical matter, merely extend the appeal 15-day appeal deadline. As 
discussed in the IFR and in response to the other similar comments in 
this preamble, the Departments believe that a 15-day appeal period 
supports DHS's need to have an efficient and administrable process 
while also affording the alien meaningful appellate rights especially 
given the straightforward nature of these penalties. See 90 FR 27444-
45. For similar reasons, granting extensions would also unnecessarily 
delay the appeal process. The Departments believe that, in the vast 
majority of cases, aliens should have ready access to any information 
needed to contest these penalties and therefore do not need additional 
time to file an appeal. In these circumstances, allowing extensions 
would unnecessarily hinder DHS's ability to effectively administer the 
appeal process and impose civil penalties more swiftly and at scale to 
achieve the IFR's intended purposes.
    Second, although adopting a ``good cause'' or ``good faith'' 
standard may reduce the number of aliens eligible to receive an 
extension or file an untimely appeal, these amorphous standards are 
likely to invite inconsistent practices among immigration officers and 
inconsistent results among similarly situated aliens. Although these 
standards are ubiquitous in law, they are hard to define, context 
specific, and often require a balancing of various legal issues. See 
Matter of L-A-B-R-, 27 I & N Dec. 405, 412 (A.G. 2018) (stating that 
``definitions of good cause tend to be nebulous and elusive'' and 
noting that courts have ``elaborated context-specific multifactor 
balancing tests, rather than bright-line rules''). The Departments 
believe that imposing an additional time-intensive burden on 
immigration officers to make such determinations would be inconsistent 
with the IFR's purpose of streamlining appeals for these 
straightforward penalties.
    Comment: One commenter noted that a 15-day appeal period is much 
shorter than the timeframe that other agencies afford for other civil 
monetary penalties. The commenter cited several regulations that 
provide a 60-day appeal period governing civil monetary penalties for 
fraud, misrepresentations, and false claims in social security and 
health care benefits programs. The commenter claimed ``[t]hese 
timelines reflect a broader regulatory recognition that individuals 
must be afforded adequate time to receive, review, and respond to 
significant legal determinations'' which, according to the commenter, 
the IFR does not provide.
    Response: The Departments disagree that the 15-day appeal period is



inadequate merely because other federal agencies afford longer 
timelines for contesting civil monetary penalties in unrelated 
statutory schemes. Appeal periods vary widely across federal 
programs,\46\ and the timelines cited by the commenter arise under 
distinct statutes with different penalty structures, evidentiary 
frameworks, and administrative adjudication procedures. The INA 
provisions for the straightforward civil penalties at issue here, INA 
240B(d), 274D, and 275(b), 8 U.S.C. 1229c(d), 1324d, and 1325(b), do 
not prescribe any particular appeal period, and nothing in due process 
jurisprudence requires the Departments to align procedures with 
unrelated programs such as those governing Social Security, healthcare 
fraud, or false claims penalties. See Clev. Board of Educ. v. 
Loudermill, 470 U.S. 532 (1985) (reaffirming that the formality and 
procedural requisites for due process vary depending on the importance 
of the interests involved and the circumstances); see also Mathews, 242 
U.S. at 319. The relevant question is whether the procedures 
established by this rule provide sufficient notice and a meaningful 
opportunity to be heard before the determination becomes final. The 
rule satisfies this standard. The appeal requires only a brief written 
request for review and allows for the submission of written supporting 
evidence or documentation. Additionally, as explained above, upon 
appeal, the supervisory immigration officer must conduct a de novo 
review of the record within 10 days and may request additional evidence 
or information, affording the respondent another 15 days to provide it.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \46\ For example, in February 2026, EOIR issued an IFR 
establishing a generally applicable 10-day deadline for filing an 
appeal from a decision of an Immigration Judge. Appellate Procedures 
for the Board of Immigration Appeals, 91 FR 5267 (Feb. 6, 2026) 
(partially vacated on procedural grounds by Amici Ctr. for Immigr. 
Rts. v. EOIR, 822 F. Supp. 3d 119, 168 (D.D.C. Mar. 8, 2026)). These 
processes were implemented within the context of the robust 
procedures afforded to the aliens before the Immigration Court prior 
to any administrative appeal, the availability of electronic filing, 
and the need for immediate efficiency reforms in light of the BIA's 
historic pending caseload. See 91 FR 5272. Moreover, those processes 
do not involve the imposition of monetary fines, or any other 
penalties, but rather involve legal determinations regarding an 
alien's removability from the United States. Further, even in other 
situations which do involve civil monetary penalties in an 
immigration context--i.e. those imposed under INA 274A and 274C, 8 
U.S.C. 1324a and 1324c--the administrative appellate deadline is 
only 10 days. See 28 CFR 68.54(a).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Moreover, these penalties differ from the examples cited by the 
commenter. The penalties addressed in this IFR implement longstanding 
statutory requirements tied to an individual's immigration history and 
do not involve the complex evidentiary or program-eligibility 
determinations characteristic of Social Security or health-care fraud 
adjudications. These penalties are straightforward in nature and turn 
on routine and straightforward determinations of fact that can be 
decided quickly on a written record. The narrow factual bases for these 
penalties support the reasonableness of the 15-day appeal window, in 
which aliens can submit written evidence or documentation for de novo 
review.
    Comment: Commenters also raised concerns with the appeal process 
itself. One commenter argued that the IFR allows the appellate reviewer 
to conduct factfinding in the first instance. The commenter argued that 
fact finding should be reserved for the initial decisionmaker. Another 
commenter stated that permitting supervisory immigration officers to 
call for additional evidence on a 15-day schedule but mandating a 
decision no later than 45 days after the alien appeals will force 
officers to choose between gathering critical information and meeting 
the 45-day deadline.
    Response: The Departments disagree that the IFR impermissibly 
allows supervisory immigration officers to conduct fact finding in the 
first instance. The initial penalty determination is made by the 
enforcement officer based on the available evidence. The supervisory 
review stage is an internal appellate review designed to ensure 
accuracy and procedural fairness. Allowing the reviewing officer to 
request supplemental evidence and information does not convert the 
supervisory officer into a primary factfinder. Rather, it enables the 
reviewer to ensure that the existing record is complete, and that the 
respondent has had a full opportunity to present information relevant 
to the determination. Nothing in the IFR authorizes the supervisory 
immigration officer to engage in unrestricted factfinding. The 
officer's role is limited to reviewing the record and evaluating any 
supplemental evidence or information.
    The Departments also disagree that the 45-day timeline for issuing 
a final decision places the supervisory immigration officer in an 
untenable position. The IFR provides a structured sequential process 
that ensures adequate time for both review and supplemental filing as 
needed. The officer conducts a de novo review of the record within 10 
days of the appeal filing. If additional information is necessary for a 
fair and complete adjudication, the officer may request supplemental 
evidence or information, and the respondent then has 15 days from 
receipt of that request to submit materials. The supervisory officer 
then retains the remaining portion of the 45-day period to complete the 
review and issue a decision. This framework provides sufficient time 
for both the respondent's submission and the officer's analysis, while 
promoting timely resolution, an important consideration in 
administering statutory civil monetary penalty schemes.
    The Departments note that the 45-day timeframe balances the 
government's interest in prompt resolution and administrative 
efficiency with the respondent's interest in a meaningful opportunity 
to supplement the record when necessary. The structured process ensures 
that respondents are heard, that determinations are made based on a 
complete record, and that decisions are issued in a timely manner.
    Accordingly, the Departments conclude that the supervisory review 
process, including the ability to request supplemental evidence or 
information and the 45-day timeline for issuing a final decision, is 
appropriate and reasonable.
5. Removal of In-Person Hearings
    Comment: Several commenters claimed that eliminating in person 
hearings will deprive aliens of due process protections that ensure 
their appeal is thoroughly presented and fully considered. Citing 
Mathews v. Eldridge, one commenter said in-person hearings are critical 
because they allow aliens to present oral evidence and clarify 
misunderstandings. Another commenter stated that eliminating in-person 
hearings means that DHS will only review written filings, briefs, and 
any documentary evidence submitted which, according to the commenter, 
deprives aliens from a meaningful opportunity to be heard. Another 
commenter alleged that the limited due process rights under the new 
process will contribute to an ``extremely high'' possibility for error.
    Response: The Departments disagree that eliminating in-person 
hearings deprives respondents of due process protections or prevents 
their appeals from being fully and fairly considered. As an initial 
matter, as discussed above in Section I of this preamble, the 
Departments note that only four aliens requested an in-person interview 
of the 450 appeals and over 12,000 civil penalties under the pre-IFR 
process, indicating that aliens do not place much value on the need for 
in-person hearings to contest civil penalties. Moreover, under the 
Mathews balancing test, the



question is whether the procedures established by the IFR provide 
notice reasonably calculated to inform the alien of the action and a 
meaningful opportunity to be heard before a final decision is issued. 
The IFR satisfies both requirements. Aliens receive written notice 
detailing the factual basis and statutory grounds for the penalty and 
are afforded the opportunity to file an appeal with the option of 
including a written defense or documentary evidence. The initial appeal 
requires only a brief written request for review, and aliens may 
provide additional documentation if the supervisory immigration officer 
requests supplemental evidence or information. The supervisory officer 
must conduct a de novo review, ensuring that the respondent's written 
submissions and any relevant evidence are fully considered.
    The Departments also disagree with commenters' assertions that in-
person hearings are necessary to present oral evidence or clarify 
misunderstandings. Civil monetary penalties under INA 240B(d), 274D, 
and 275(b), 8 U.S.C. 1229c(d), 1324d, and 1325(b), turn on objective 
factual bases such as a prior removal order or a failure to comply with 
terms of voluntary departure that are typically documented in DHS 
records. Written submissions allow respondents to contest factual 
inaccuracies, provide additional documentation, or explain 
circumstances that negate the willfulness of the alien's failure to 
depart. As explained in the IFR, an in-person interview would not 
enhance the fairness or accuracy of the civil monetary penalty process 
because of the straightforward issues and types of evidence involved in 
these cases, which do not turn on credibility determinations or require 
the cross-examination of witnesses. If an alien, through no fault of 
his or her own, did not receive notice of the removal or voluntary 
departure order or was prevented from complying due to circumstances 
beyond his or her control, the alien can provide a written explanation 
and simple documentary evidence to support the claim. Accordingly, a 
requirement for in-person hearings would not meaningfully improve the 
accuracy or fairness of determinations, given the narrow factual issues 
typically involved in these penalties. See Mathews, 424 U.S. at 343-44 
(considering for due process purposes both the nature of the issues to 
be decided and the nature of the evidence to be presented, such as 
whether it consists mainly of documents or whether the resolution of 
the issue hinges on the need for in person testimony).
    The risk of error is also mitigated by the IFR's multi-layered 
procedural safeguards. Aliens may file supplemental evidence if invited 
by the supervisory officer, and the officer must independently evaluate 
the record before issuing a final decision. These safeguards ensure 
that errors can be identified and corrected without necessitating 
formal, trial-type hearings. The Departments note that many 
administrative penalty and adjudication schemes, including certain 
USCIS benefit adjudications, and numerous civil penalty processes 
across the federal government operate without in-person hearings, and 
courts have recognized such frameworks as consistent with due process 
requirements.
    For these reasons, the Departments conclude that an in-person 
hearing is not required and that the written, supervisory review 
process established by the IFR provides respondents with a fair and 
meaningful opportunity to present their claims.
    Comment: One commenter also said that eliminating in-person 
hearings will put vulnerable populations at risk, such as aliens with 
low-income, a lack of representation, and a limited understanding of 
English. Citing Goldberg v. Kelly, the commenter alleged that because 
the respondents in this context are often low income, non-English 
speaking, and unrepresented by legal counsel, review of the paper file 
only is an insufficient means to afford due process. Another commenter 
also cites Goldberg v. Kelly, alleging that where DHS imposes such a 
toll on families and target ``very means by which to live,'' the 
private interests cannot be described as ``modest.''
    Response: The Departments disagree that eliminating in-person 
hearings fails to protect vulnerable populations or violates due 
process principles, including those discussed in Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 
U.S. 254 (1970). The Supreme Court has long recognized that procedural 
due process generally requires notice and an opportunity to be heard 
before the Government deprives an individual of a protected property 
interest, while also emphasizing that due process ``has never been a 
term of fixed and invariable content,'' FCC v. WJR, U.S. 265, 275 
(1949), as its ``exact boundaries are undefinable, and its content 
varies according to specific factual contexts,'' Hannah v. Larche, 363 
U.S. 420, 442 (1960). The circumstances presented here differ 
materially from those at issue in Goldberg. In Goldberg, the Court 
considered the termination of ongoing public assistance benefits that 
were essential to recipients' subsistence and daily living expenses. 
The Court considered the deprivation at issue to be immediate and 
uniquely harmful, distinguishing it from ``virtually anyone else whose 
governmental entitlements are ended.'' Goldberg, 397 U.S. at 263-64. 
The Court therefore concluded that a pre-termination evidentiary 
hearing was required to minimize risk of an erroneous deprivation. Id.
    By contrast, the IFR concerns not the deprivation of a 
constitutional property interest but the imposition of civil monetary 
penalties authorized by statute for violations of INA 274D(a)(1), 8 
U.S.C. 1324d(a)(1); INA 240B(d)(1)(A)-(B), 8 U.S.C. 1229c(d)(1)(A)-(B); 
and INA 275(b)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1325(b)(1). These penalties do not involve 
the termination of subsistence benefits or other government benefits. 
Nor do such determinations typically turn on complex credibility 
assessments; rather, they generally involve documentary evidence and 
objective statutory criteria. Therefore, the risk of government error 
is minimal, and the appeal process provides an adequate opportunity for 
error correction. Accordingly, the procedural concerns present in 
Goldberg are not implicated to the same degree here. Generally, civil 
fines are issued after aliens have received sufficient due process to 
challenge the findings against them and after the aliens have been 
adequately warned, by ICE and the immigration judge, of the 
consequences of failing to abide by the terms of the final order.
    Under the Mathews framework, due process requires procedures that 
are reasonably designed to ensure fairness in light of the private 
interest affected, the risk of erroneous deprivation, and the 
Government's interest. Applying those factors here confirms that an in-
person hearing is not required. The private interests at stake, while 
important, are financial in nature, not subsistence-level. The risk of 
error is mitigated by the IFR's multi-layered procedural safeguards, 
including written notice, an initial appeal requiring only a brief 
written request and explanation, mandatory de novo review by a 
supervisory immigration officer, and the ability of that officer to 
request supplemental evidence, giving aliens an additional 15 days to 
provide evidence or explanation. These safeguards provide aliens, 
including those that are recent arrivals, low-income, or limited-
English proficient,



with meaningful opportunities to be heard.
    The Departments also disagree that vulnerable populations require 
an in-person hearing to ensure adequate participation. Aliens may seek 
assistance from legal service providers or community organizations. 
Because the initial appeal filing is minimal and does not require 
complex filing, aliens are not required to navigate technical 
evidentiary matters within the initial 15-day period. The ability to 
supplement the record during supervisory review further ensures that 
aliens can clarify misunderstandings, correct errors, or provide 
additional information without the need for a formal oral hearing.
6. Removal of BIA Review
    Comment: Several commenters took issue with the IFR's justification 
for moving appellate review from the BIA to DHS, suggesting that it was 
insufficient. These commenters broadly suggested that the Departments 
erroneously discounted the legal complexity of these penalties, 
asserting that DHS immigration officers do not have the legal training 
and experience necessary to adjudicate complex legal challenges. One 
commenter also challenged the IFR's statement that the BIA lacks 
experience adjudicating these civil penalties, noting that the IFR 
itself relied on a BIA precedent decision to explain the scope of the 
voluntary departure penalty. Additionally, commenters also said that 
the BIA's backlog of cases is not a valid reason to eliminate BIA 
review. One commenter said that the backlog is a self-created problem 
attributable to the Attorney General's recent decision to reduce the 
size of the BIA. Another commenter argued that the BIA's backlog is a 
result of Congressional funding decisions, and the Departments should 
not try to solve this funding problem by eliminating the BIA's 
jurisdiction over certain categories of cases.
    Response: As an initial matter, the Departments disagree with the 
commenters' suggestion that the Departments' explanations for removing 
the BIA's jurisdiction over these penalties are insufficient. The IFR 
fully explains the Departments' reasons for eliminating BIA review. 
These reasons include: (1) the straightforward nature of these 
penalties and the lack of an operational need, such as an established 
subject-matter expertise, for the BIA to adjudicate such appeals; (2) 
the fact that the BIA has a large backlog of cases and appeals take a 
long time to resolve; (3) the need to prevent these cases from 
exacerbating the BIA's backlog; and (4) the need to focus EOIR's 
resources on its statutorily prescribed functions under the INA, which 
do not include civil penalty appeals. See 90 FR 27441, 27444-47. The 
Departments believe that these reasons are sound and refer readers to 
the IFR for further discussion.
    The Departments disagree that these penalties involve complicated 
legal issues that warrant BIA review. The Departments are not persuaded 
by commenter arguments related to the constitutionality of the IFR's 
streamlined procedures, civil penalty amounts, statute of limitations 
issues, and the scope of the unlawful entry penalty, which have been 
addressed below at Parts III.D.8, and E. Therefore, the commenters' 
examples are inconsequential to the Departments' conclusions that BIA 
review is (1) unnecessary because these civil penalties typically turn 
on straightforward issues of fact that supervisory immigration officers 
are prepared to adequately review and (2) inadvisable because the BIA's 
limited, specialized resources are better used to address its 
unprecedented pending caseload rather than to review decisions that can 
be adequately reviewed by supervisory immigration officers. See 90 FR 
27453. Further, the Departments note that if an alien believes that a 
supervisory immigration officer's penalty decision was legally 
erroneous, the alien may, after exhausting administrative remedies, 
seek judicial review under the APA or may challenge the decision in 
connection with any enforcement action brought to collect the penalty.
    Regarding one commenter's claim that the value of BIA review is 
demonstrated by the fact that the IFR's preamble relied on a BIA 
precedent decision to explain the scope of the voluntary departure 
penalty, the Departments note that the IFR cited that decision only to 
show that aliens generally will have limited defenses to these 
penalties. See 90 FR 27443. As a preliminary matter, the cited 
decision, Matter of Zmijewska, did not involve a civil penalty issue 
but instead addressed an alien's ineligibility for immigration relief 
because of the alien's failure to comply with a voluntary departure 
order. 24 I&N Dec. 87, 93-95 (BIA 2007).
    Even still, Matter of Zmijewska clarifies that the sole exception 
to an alien being penalized for failure to depart after being granted 
voluntary departure is narrowly ``limited to situations in which an 
alien, through no fault of his or her own, is unaware of the voluntary 
departure order or is physically unable to depart''--which turns not on 
complicated issues of law but on issues of fact that can easily be 
demonstrated by the alien and adjudicated by a supervisory immigration 
officer. Id. at 945. Therefore, this BIA decision does not undermine 
the Departments' decision to remove BIA review but instead actively 
supports it.
    Further, while the BIA is certainly qualified to adjudicate cases 
as straightforward as these civil penalties cases, it has not developed 
specialized expertise through historical practice, as it has only ever 
reviewed civil penalties cases, not adjudicated the factual findings 
they involve in the first instance. Moreover, as the IFR correctly 
points out, the BIA has little specialized expertise even in reviewing 
appeals of these civil penalties. See 90 FR 27450 (noting that only a 
handful of appeals resulted from civil penalties issued under President 
Trump's first term); see also Section I of this preamble (discussing 
the small number of BIA appeals in proportion to the number of civil 
penalties issued in the months leading up to the IFR). Because of this, 
there is effectively no operational necessity to this review being 
performed by the BIA instead of by a supervisory immigration officer 
within DHS, the administrative body that has the historical practical 
experience of adjudicating these penalties and providing internal DHS 
review over such determinations, even under a framework where the BIA 
had appellate authority. Thus, the Departments reaffirm that the BIA's 
lack of experience adjudicating these penalties in the first instance 
and lack of meaningful expertise even in reviewing them are valid bases 
(but not the sole bases) for removing BIA appellate review.
    Finally, the Departments disagree that the BIA's backlog is not a 
valid reason to remove BIA review of these penalty decisions. As 
discussed above, the BIA's backlog has prompted a need for 
reconsideration of the BIA's role as an appellate tribunal and renewed 
focus on implementing streamlining case processing measures. As such, 
in February 2026, the BIA issued an IFR establishing, among other 
efficiency measures, that the BIA will generally summarily dismiss 
appeals unless it votes en banc to consider the appeal on the merits. 
91 FR 5267, 5270.\47\ Divesting the BIA responsibility over DHS 
imposition and enforcement of civil fines and penalties, an area where 
there is no statutory requirement for



EOIR review and where the BIA has no unique adjudicatory expertise, 
creates operational efficiencies, as the BIA need not devote resources 
to adjudicate such appeals, which may fluctuate over time and with the 
IFR's streamlined processes aimed at issuing such penalties at scale.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \47\ See Amica Ctr. for Immigrant Rts. v. EOIR, No. CV 26-696 
(RDM), 2026 WL 662494, at *34 (D.D.C. Mar. 8, 2026) (partially 
vacating the rule).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Additionally, the Attorney General's recent decision to reduce the 
number of permanent Appellate Immigration Judges who sit on the BIA 
does not undermine the Departments' concerns that preserving BIA review 
could unnecessarily delay the penalty process and exacerbate the BIA's 
backlog. Rather, as EOIR explained in a recent rule, ``increasing the 
size of the BIA has not necessarily equated to a corresponding increase 
in the number of cases adjudicated or a reduction in the pending 
caseload.'' \48\ Reducing the Size of the Board of Immigration Appeals, 
90 FR 15525, 15526 (Apr. 14, 2025). EOIR also noted that the size of 
the BIA has had ``significant institutional costs, including effects on 
the cohesiveness of the Board's decision-making process and the 
collegiality among Board members, a loss of uniformity in its non-
precedent decisions, increased difficulty providing effective 
leadership, as well as an administrative and supervisory strain on the 
Board's limited legal staff.'' Id. None of these reasons for reducing 
the size of the BIA contradict the Departments' stated justification 
for removing the BIA's jurisdiction over these penalties, including 
concerns about BIA adjudication timelines and its backlog. For similar 
reasons, the Departments do not agree that they must wait for Congress 
to provide additional funding for the BIA, rather than removing BIA 
jurisdiction over certain categories of cases. As discussed in the IFR, 
Congress has not required EOIR or the BIA to review these civil penalty 
decisions, and nothing in the INA precludes the Attorney General from 
exercising his authority to remove the BIA's regulatory appellate 
authority over these penalties. 90 FR 27448.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \48\ As EOIR noted in another recent rule, between fiscal year 
2015 and the end of fiscal year 2025, as the number of permanent 
Appellate Immigration Judges increased, the BIA's pending case load 
increased more than five-fold--from 37,285 pending appeals to 
202,946 pending appeals. Appellate Procedures for the Board of 
Immigration Appeals, 91 FR 5267, 5270 (Feb. 6, 2026) (citing EOIR, 
Adjudication Statistics: All Appeals Filed, Completed, and Pending 
(Nov. 18, 2025), https://www.justice.gov/eoir/media/1344986/dl?inline [https://perma.cc/88C5-MU4N]).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Comment: Several commenters argued that replacing BIA appellate 
review with DHS appellate review impermissibly consolidates enforcement 
and adjudication powers within one agency. They further argued that the 
IFR's appeal structure creates an inherent conflict of interest because 
DHS cannot be impartial when reviewing its own actions. One commenter 
argued that this consolidation of enforcement and adjudication 
functions violates due process. The commenter explained that the 
Supreme Court has long recognized that due process requires 
impartiality from adjudicators, and that any arrangement that gives 
rise to even a ``possible temptation'' to act in a biased way that 
benefits the decisionmaker violates due process. See Ward v. Village of 
Monroeville, 409 U.S. 57, 60 (1972). The commenter asserted that DHS 
assessing these penalties and reviewing appeals raises at least a 
possibility of temptation to impermissibly affirm the determinations, 
noting that the IFR itself was issued to allow DHS to impose these 
penalties more swiftly and at scale. Another commenter noted that these 
civil penalties are deposited into a DHS account that directly funds 
immigration detention, removal operations, and border wall 
construction. They suggested that this creates a powerful institutional 
incentive for DHS to maximize fine revenue, and, therefore, BIA review 
is needed to mitigate this potential conflict of interest. To address 
these concerns, this commenter urged the Departments to restore BIA 
review or to create an independent review board, separate from ICE and 
CBP, to review civil penalty appeals. They also suggested that if the 
IFR's structure is preserved, the rule should, at minimum, sever the 
financial interest DHS has in imposing these fines by redirecting civil 
penalty revenue to the Department of the Treasury's general fund rather 
than retaining it in DHS's enforcement accounts.
    Response: DHS strongly rejects commenters' speculative suggestion 
that DHS immigration officers cannot be impartial and neutral when 
adjudicating civil penalty appeals. DHS has designed the appeal process 
to ensure that an alien's appeal is fairly and fully considered on the 
merits alone. Indeed, the IFR makes clear that any appeal of a penalty 
decision must be reviewed by a separate supervisory immigration officer 
who was not involved in the initial civil monetary penalty decision. 
Additionally, the IFR instructs the supervisory officer to review the 
appeal record de novo, which ensures that officers decide each appeal 
solely on the law and facts presented without providing any weight in 
favor of the initial decision. There is a presumption of regularity 
that attaches to the actions of government agencies, see U.S. Postal 
Serv., 534 U.S. at 10, and commenters have offered no support for their 
claim that immigration officers will deny otherwise meritorious 
challenges to civil penalties simply because they are employed by the 
same agency that issues and enforces these penalties.
    Moreover, the Supreme Court has long held that it does not violate 
due process to combine enforcement and adjudication functions within a 
single agency. See Withrow v. Larkin, 421 U.S. 35, 56-58 (1975) 
(holding that the fact that the initial charge in an administrative 
proceeding is brought by the same agency that later adjudicates the 
matter is not, in and of itself, violative of due process); see also 
Marcello v. Bonds, 349 U.S. 302 (1955) (rejecting the argument that the 
former INS's comingled prosecutorial and adjudicative functions, under 
a prior version of the INA, deprived aliens of due process in 
deportation proceedings). Thus, the Departments disagree with 
commenters' suggestion that the consolidation of enforcement and 
adjudication functions within the same agency violates due process or 
inherently increases the risk of biased decision-making.
    The caselaw cited by one commenter does not undermine the 
Departments' conclusion that the IFR's appeal procedures comport with 
due process. At most, the cited cases stand for the principle that an 
agency's adjudicatory procedures could violate due process if the 
adjudicator has a direct financial or pecuniary interest in the outcome 
of the case, has prejudged the case, or has some other concrete 
conflict of interest. These cases, however, do not support the 
commenter's broad argument that DHS immigration officers cannot be 
neutral and unbiased merely because they are part of DHS. Rather the 
caselaw is clear: there is a presumption of honesty and integrity in 
administrative officials exercising adjudicative functions, even where 
there is a combination of investigative and adjudicative functions, and 
some evidence of actual bias must be presented to overcome this 
presumption. See Marcello, 349 U.S. at 311; Withrow, 421 U.S. at 47; 
see also Baran v. Port of Beaumont Navigation District, 57 F.3d 436, 
446 (5th Cir. 1995). The commenter has not offered any actual and non-
speculative reason to think that DHS officers cannot be neutral but 
will instead be ``tempted'' to impermissibly affirm penalty decisions 
issued by other DHS officers.
    The other concerns cited by commenters do not support their



contention that civil penalty appeals must be adjudicated by the BIA or 
an agency outside of DHS. The Departments acknowledge that INA 280(b), 
8 U.S.C. 1330(b), provides that any civil monetary penalties collected 
from aliens shall be deposited into a DHS account that funds 
immigration detention, removal operations, and border wall 
construction. DHS disagrees, however, with one commenter's view that 
DHS officers adjudicating civil penalty appeals will be encouraged to 
maximize fine revenue for this DHS fund. DHS officers adjudicating 
civil penalty appeals are bound by strict legal and procedural 
standards to ensure impartiality and fairness in their decision-making 
processes.\49\ These officers are tasked with applying the law and 
evaluating the facts of each case independently, without regard to the 
financial implications of their decisions.\50\ DHS has robust 
supervisory review mechanisms in place to ensure that adjudications are 
conducted in compliance with applicable laws, regulations, and ethical 
standards. The fine amounts are governed by statute and regulations 
and, once an immigration officer determines that a civil penalty should 
be issued, the officer's discretion in choosing the fine amount is 
bound by those statutory and regulatory limits, and this rule does not 
alter the penalty amounts themselves authorized by statute. 
Furthermore, the primary purpose of civil monetary penalties under the 
INA is to enforce compliance with immigration laws, not to generate 
revenue. DHS remains committed to upholding the integrity of the 
adjudication process and ensuring that decisions are made based solely 
on the merits of each case, rather than any external considerations 
related to funding.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \49\ E.g., Goldberg v. Kelly, 397 U.S. 254, 271 (1970) 
(recognizing that government decisionmakers adjudicating matters 
involving property must be impartial).
    \50\ Id.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Similarly, DHS disagrees that officers will have an incentive to 
affirm penalty decisions on appeal because the IFR's preamble 
emphasizes DHS's desire to maximize the use of these penalties. The 
Departments agree that the IFR was designed to maximize DHS's ability 
to impose civil penalties in proportion to the scale of illegal aliens 
in the United States--not the total amount of the penalties. The IFR 
achieves this purpose by streamlining the penalty process, but it does 
not dictate the outcome of any penalty appeal or otherwise pressure 
immigration officers to affirm initial penalty decisions. Rather, as 
discussed above, the IFR makes clear that a supervisory officer must 
review appeals de novo based solely on DHS records and any evidence or 
argument submitted by the alien. Moreover, the IFR provides officers 
with a 45-day period to adjudicate appeals, which will ensure that they 
have ample time to consider all of the evidence and arguments provided 
by the alien. Accordingly, DHS believes that statements in the IFR's 
preamble will not cause immigration officers to prejudge appeals or 
impermissibly affirm penalty decisions. DHS clarifies that it expects 
each supervisory immigration officer to decide individual appeals based 
solely on the law and the facts presented.
    Finally, the Departments note that BIA review is not needed to 
ensure that immigration officers comply with these regulatory 
requirements and decide each appeal on the basis of its own facts and 
circumstances. If an alien believes that an immigration officer's 
decision was erroneous and not based on the applicable law and the 
facts of the case, then after exhausting administrative remedies, the 
alien may seek judicial review under the APA or may challenge the 
decision in connection with any enforcement action brought by DOJ to 
collect the penalty.
    For all of these reasons, individually and collectively, the 
Departments decline to modify the IFR to restore BIA review. Similarly, 
DHS declines to create an independent body, separate from ICE and CBP, 
to adjudicate civil penalty appeals because DHS believes that ICE and 
CBP supervisory officers are fully capable of deciding each appeal on 
the basis of its individual facts and circumstances without bias or 
prejudgment. Additionally, creating an independent board or body would 
conflict with the purpose of the IFR to streamline the civil penalty 
process, including the appeal process, because it could take additional 
time to create and to put in place processes that would ensure that the 
board receives filings and records in a timely manner. Finally, with 
respect to one commenter's claim that, in order to remove any conflict 
of interest, DHS should redirect penalty revenue to a general Treasury 
fund rather than retaining it in DHS accounts, DHS notes that it cannot 
redirect funds in contravention of INA 280(b), 8 U.S.C. 1330(b).
    Comment: Several commenters characterized the IFR's appeal process 
as lacking transparency and accountability. They noted that the BIA 
makes its decisions publicly available and has a well-established 
process for publishing decisions on emerging legal issues. In contrast, 
commenters noted that the IFR does not require DHS to make its civil 
fine decisions public or treat them as precedential in cases raising 
similar issues. Commenters argued that this will contribute to 
arbitrary and inconsistent decisions and a lack of accountability.
    Response: As discussed in the IFR and above, the civil penalties 
covered by this rule typically turn on straightforward issues of fact, 
rather than complicated questions of law. See 90 FR 27453. Accordingly, 
the Departments disagree with commenters that there is a need for DHS 
to establish a process for publishing decisions on emerging legal 
issues involving these penalties. DHS also notes that ICE and CBP have 
issued guidance to immigration officers regarding these penalties, 
including guidance on the various legal issues that commenters have 
identified and that are discussed throughout this preamble. Finally, 
nothing in this rule prevents an alien from bringing a federal court 
challenge to a penalty decision or from raising any legal defense that 
may be available to the alien in connection with a DOJ enforcement 
action to collect the penalty. DHS will comply with any adverse court 
ruling and will apply any legal precedent applicable to these penalties 
that results from such a challenge.
    To the extent that commenters are suggesting that DHS must publish 
civil penalty decisions to provide transparency, accountability, and 
consistency in the penalty amounts being assessed, ICE and CBP are 
applying a uniform practice of assessing the maximum statutorily 
authorized penalty amount in each case, consistent with the statute of 
limitations. DHS has an interest in issuing these penalties quickly and 
at the maximum authorized amount to encourage aliens to comply with 
removal and voluntary departure orders. To achieve these dual 
objectives, DHS has determined that ICE and CBP should assess the 
maximum penalties authorized by law.
7. Mitigation Factors; Motions To Reopen
    Comment: Commenters argued that the rule should allow aliens to 
seek mitigation, and it should clarify that DHS should consider 
mitigating factors when assessing penalties. One commenter recommended 
a tiered penalty system based on severity and good faith compliance 
efforts. Another commenter recommended that the agencies adopt a means-
tested fine structure that considers the recipient's



financial capacity. Another commenter points out that the government 
considers mitigating factors for employers subject to penalties. They 
state that in assessing fines against employers of aliens under the 
Immigration Reform and Control Act, the government considers factors 
such as the size of their business, their good faith, the seriousness 
of the violations, whether the employee is an alien, and the employer's 
history of previous violations. Finally, one commenter argues that the 
rule undermines procedural fairness by eliminating any right for aliens 
to request reopening while preserving reopening authority for DHS.
    Response: The Departments disagree that the IFR should authorize 
aliens to seek mitigation of penalty amounts, create a tiered penalty 
structure, or adopt a means-tested framework for assessing penalties. 
The civil monetary penalties addressed in this rule arise under INA 
240B(d), 274D, and 275(b), 8 U.S.C. 1229c(d), 1324d, and 1325(b). These 
statutory provisions do not require DHS or DOJ to adjust penalty 
amounts based on mitigating circumstances, financial capacity, or 
subjective good-faith factors, nor do they provide a means for aliens 
to request discretionary mitigation. In contrast, several of the 
statutes cited by commenters, including those governing certain 
employer sanctions under the IRCA, explicitly establish mitigating 
factors that DHS or DOJ must consider when assessing penalties. 
Congress included no such language in the statutory provisions at issue 
here. Additionally, President Trump's Executive orders direct DHS to 
``ensure the assessment and collection of all fines and penalties [DHS] 
is authorized by law to assess and collect from aliens unlawfully 
present in the United States'' \51\ and to ``take all appropriate 
action to secure the borders of our Nation . . . [including by] 
deterring and preventing the entry of illegal aliens into the United 
States.'' \52\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \51\ E.O. 14159, Protecting the American People Against 
Invasion. E.O. 14159, 90 FR 8443 (Jan. 20, 2025).
    \52\ E.O. 14165, Securing Our Borders, 90 FR 8467 (Jan. 20, 
2025).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    At the same time, the IFR does not foreclose DHS from rescinding or 
reopening decisions on its own initiative, where doing so is necessary 
to ensure administrative accuracy, correct an error, or address other 
considerations relevant to sound enforcement. This internal authority 
is procedural in nature and serves the agency's interest in 
consistency, fairness, and error correction. Allowing aliens to file 
motions to reopen before DHS for the purpose of seeking mitigation, 
particularly after the supervisory review process, would undermine the 
Department's legitimate interests in finality, administrative 
efficiency, and the timely initiation of the collection process, which 
are essential to administering a nationwide penalty scheme. The civil 
monetary penalties addressed in this rule arising under INA 240B(d), 
274(D), and 275(b), 8 U.S.C. 1229c(d), 1324d, and 1325(b), do not 
confer a statutory right on aliens to request reopening of a final 
civil monetary penalty determination. The Departments therefore decline 
to create a new regulatory mechanism that would effectively grant 
aliens a right to reopen final decisions or seek mitigation after 
supervisory review has concluded.
    The Departments also disagree with commenters who argued that 
fairness requires adopting mitigation factors analogous to those 
applicable to employers sanctioned under the IRCA. That comparison is 
misplaced. IRCA explicitly directs the government to consider certain 
mitigating factors when assessing employer penalties. By contrast, the 
penalties at issue here are based on statutory conditions, such as 
failure to comply with voluntary departure or the presence of a prior 
removal order, that turn on objective, records-based facts. These 
provisions do not require a discretionary, multi-factor penalty 
assessment. The Departments are not required to import into these 
statutes mitigation frameworks that Congress has chosen to include 
elsewhere but omitted here.
    For these reasons, the Departments conclude that the IFR 
appropriately reflects the statutory framework governing civil 
penalties under INA 240B(d), 274D, and 275(b), 8 U.S.C. 1229c(d), 
1324d, and 1325(b), and that adopting a mitigation regime, a tiered 
fine system, a means-tested structure, or respondent-initiated motions 
to reopen is not required by the governing statutes, and is 
administratively impractical and beyond the scope of this rulemaking.
8. Civil Penalty Amounts; 8 CFR 281.1(g)
    Comment: Some commenters argued that the fines imposed by the IFR 
implicate the Eighth Amendment's Excessive Fines Clause. They contend 
that, under U.S. Supreme Court precedent, even if a penalty is deemed 
``civil,'' it constitutes punishment for purposes of the Excessive 
Fines Clause if it serves retributive or deterrent purposes, rather 
than remedial ones. They broadly claimed that the IFR authorizes DHS to 
issue fines that serve no remedial purpose, and the IFR's self-
expressed intent--to deter future unlawful entries and encourage 
greater compliance with removal and voluntary departure orders--
reflects a punitive purpose. Commenters broadly stated that these 
penalties are excessive under the Eighth Amendment because they can 
result in sums ``disproportionate'' to the underlying immigration 
violations.
    One commenter noted that there is a wide range of circumstances 
surrounding an alien's decision to come to the United States or remain 
in the country after a removal order or voluntary departure order and 
suggested that the Departments' failure to consider these circumstances 
violates the Excessive Fines Clause. The commenter listed examples, 
including aliens fleeing persecution or seeking a better life for their 
children, aliens who were unable to depart due to illness, financial 
problems, aliens with pending challenges to a removal order, and aliens 
who were removed in absentia and were unaware of the order. One 
commenter suggested that DHS should cap fines at levels that reflect 
the nature of the violation and an alien's ability to pay.
    Response: As an initial matter, the Departments note that the IFR 
did not change the scope or amount of the civil monetary penalties that 
Congress has established. It only changed the procedures for issuing 
and adjudicating these civil monetary penalties and for allowing an 
alien to contest them. See 90 FR 27454. DHS has imposed the maximum 
statutory penalties under both the IFR's streamlined penalty process 
and the prior penalty process in 8 CFR part 280. This indicates that 
commenters' Eighth Amendment concerns are directed primarily at the 
penalty amounts authorized by Congress, not at the IFR's procedures, 
and are therefore outside of the scope of this rule. Nevertheless, in 
so far as commenters are suggesting the IFR is unlawful because it does 
not require DHS immigration officers to assess proportionality or 
consider mitigating factors before imposing the maximum penalty amount, 
the Departments respond as follows: (1) these civil monetary penalties 
do not fall within the Eighth Amendments Excessive Fines Clause, and 
(2) even if treated as ``fines,'' they are not excessive under the 
factors in United States v. Bajakajian, 524 U.S. 321 (1998).
    The Supreme Court has never held that civil monetary penalties for 
immigration violations are ``fines'' for purposes of the Excessive 
Fines Clause.



The Court's cases in this area have either involved sanctions ordered 
as penalties for criminal conduct, or civil forfeiture actions imposed 
after a criminal conviction, where the property was used in the 
commission of the crime. See Alexander v. United States, 509 U.S. 544, 
558 (1993) (criminal forfeiture of property); Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at 
328 (criminal forfeiture of currency); Austin v. United States, 509 
U.S. 602, 619-22 (1993) (civil forfeiture of property used to commit 
drug crimes). By contrast, the penalties covered by this rule are not 
imposed in connection with criminal offenses. They are civil measures 
designed to promote compliance with the immigration laws and support 
DHS's enforcement efforts. The Supreme Court has long recognized that 
Congress may impose civil monetary penalties for violations of the 
Nation's immigration laws, and that such penalties are not criminal in 
nature. See, e.g., Oceanic Steam Nav. Co. v. Stranahan, 214 U.S. 320, 
337 (1909). Moreover, the fact that these penalties are intended to 
serve a deterrence purpose does not render them subject to the 
Excessive Fines Clause because ``deterrence may serve civil as well as 
criminal goals.'' Hudson v. United States, 522 U.S. 93 105, (1997) 
(internal quotation marks omitted); see also Garner v. U.S. Dep't of 
Labor, 221 F.3d 822, 827 (5th Cir. 2000) (``That a statute serves to 
deter future conduct does not automatically render it punitive.''). In 
addition, Congress clearly intended these penalties to serve a remedial 
purpose. As explained in Section II of this preamble, apprehending, 
detaining, and removing removable aliens, and conducting section 240 
removal proceedings imposes significant costs on the Departments, and a 
large number of unlawful entries strain resources at the border. 
Congress recognized these harms and authorized civil penalties to both 
encourage compliance with the immigration laws and to help fund DHS's 
border security and removal efforts. See INA 280(b)(3), 8 U.S.C. 
1330(b)(3) (providing that the Immigration Enforcement Account is 
available for removal of criminal aliens and structures along certain 
portions of the United States border); see also H. Rep. No. 104-469 pt. 
1 at 155 (1996).
    Even if these penalties were considered fines under the Excessive 
Fines Clause, DHS's decision to impose the maximum amount authorized by 
Congress without considering each alien's individual reasons for 
unlawful entry or failure to depart after a removal or departure order 
is neither excessive nor unconstitutional. Courts of appeals generally 
apply the following factors from Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at 337-40, to 
determine whether a fine is ``grossly disproportional'' to the gravity 
of an offense: (1) the amount of the penalty authorized by Congress and 
the nature of the harm that results from a violation; (2) the class of 
persons to whom the statute principally applies; and (3) a comparison 
with potential criminal penalties. Taken together, these factors 
support the conclusion that the IFR need not be amended to limit DHS's 
authority to impose the maximum statutory penalties or to require a 
proportionality analysis before issuing a civil penalty or otherwise 
consider mitigating factors.
    With respect to the first factor, judgments about the appropriate 
penalty amount for a violation ``belong in the first instance to the 
legislature.'' Bajakajian, 524 U.S. at 322. The civil monetary 
penalties covered by this rule reflect Congress's considered judgment 
that the conduct involved--an alien's unlawful entry or failure to 
depart after a removal or departure order--is particularly serious and 
warrants substantial fines to promote compliance with immigration laws. 
See 90 FR 27454. Consistent with Congress's judgment and current 
enforcement priorities, DHS has determined that imposing the maximum 
authorized penalties is an appropriate response to the large number of 
aliens who have unlawfully entered the United States or have violated 
removal and departure orders in recent years. See Section II of this 
preamble. Courts have held that an agency's civil penalty decision is 
not excessive under the Eighth Amendment when it does not exceed the 
statutory maximum. See Newell Recycling Co. v. EPA, 231 F.3d 204, 210 
(5th Cir. 2000) (``No matter how excessive (in lay terms) an 
administrative fine may appear, if the fine does not exceed the limits 
prescribed by the statute authorizing it, the fine does not violate the 
Eighth Amendment''); see also Pharaon v. Bd. of Governors of the Fed. 
Res. Sys, 135 F.3d 148, 155-57 (D.C. Cir. 1998).
    The specific statutorily authorized penalty amounts are also 
proportionate to the underlying immigration law violations. For the 
unlawful entry penalty, the maximum penalty (adjusted for inflation) is 
$500 for each entry. See 8 CFR 280.53(b)(15). That amount is not 
disproportionate to unlawful entries, including repeated unlawful 
entries, in violation of the immigration laws in light of Congress's 
concerns when enacting this penalty. See H. Rep. No. 104-469 at 155 
(1996) (noting that unlawful entry ``with no consequences undermines 
the credibility of our efforts to secure the border'').
    For voluntary departure civil penalties, Congress has authorized 
Immigration Judges to set penalties between $1,992 and $9,970 (as 
adjusted for inflation). See 8 CFR 280.53(b)(3). Under longstanding 
regulations, Immigration Judges or the BIA must select an amount within 
that range that reflects the likelihood that the alien will comply with 
voluntary departure or may apply a presumptive amount of $3,000. See 8 
CFR 1240.26(l); 73 FR 76927, 76936 (Dec. 18, 2008). DHS adheres to the 
amount set by EOIR. That amount is not excessive because it reflects 
both the adjudicator's assessment of the incentive needed to secure 
compliance and Congress's desire to ensure consequences for violating 
departure orders. See H. Rep. No. 104-469, at 122 (noting how aliens 
with voluntary departure and had ``very little incentive'' to actually 
depart the United States prior to IIRIRA).
    For failure to depart after a removal order, Congress has 
authorized DHS to impose a penalty of $998 per day (as adjusted for 
inflation) for each day an alien willfully fails to depart. Commenters 
argue that these penalties are excessive because the cumulative total 
may, in some cases, exceed $1,000,000. The Departments disagree. 
Congress designed this provision so that each day of willful failure to 
depart constitutes a separate, repeating violation. See Section III.E. 
of this preamble. In this context, proportionality is assessed by 
looking at each per day penalty, not the cumulative amount. See e.g. 
United States v. Schwarzbaum, 127 F.4th 259, 276 (11th Cir. 2025). A 
$998 per diem penalty is not excessive compared to other immigration-
related civil penalties. It reflects Congress's judgment as to the 
seriousness of the harm that flows from each day an alien remains in 
the United States in willful violation of a removal order and how these 
willful violations undermine the credibility of the immigration laws 
and warrant a separate penalty.
    Even when viewed cumulatively, the per diem failure to depart 
penalty is not excessive. Congress added this authority in IIRIRA to 
strengthen immigration enforcement and to increase the consequences for 
ignoring removal orders, in response to the problem of aliens remaining 
in the United States--sometimes for years--after final deportation 
orders. See H.R. Rep. No. 104-469, pt. 1, at 160 (1996) (explaining 
when enacting IIRIRA that ``aliens who have final orders of deportation 
[often]



remain in the United States indefinitely'' and noting that ``[a]s a 
result, the resources expended to identify, apprehend, and provide a 
hearing to a deportable alien are all too often wasted''). Against this 
backdrop, Congress expressly authorized DHS to impose per-day penalties 
that may reach substantial sums when an alien willfully remains in the 
United States for extended periods in violation of a removal order. In 
these circumstances, imposing the maximum daily amount, even where it 
results in a large total, is not excessive because the total directly 
reflects a long-running, repeated violation. See Schwarzbaum, 127 F.4th 
at 284 (``when a cumulative fine is made up of constitutionally 
proportionate penalties, the cumulative fine ``is, literally, directly 
proportionate to the offense'') (citation and internal quotations 
omitted).
    Taken together, the three penalties covered by this rule reflect 
Congress's calibrated assessment of the harm associated with each type 
of violation. Lower penalties for unlawful entry generally apply to 
aliens apprehended while entering and who are often subject to prompt 
return or expedited removal, thereby conserving resources associated 
with section 240 removal proceedings. Higher penalties for failure to 
depart reflect Congress's judgment that remaining in the United States 
after a departure or removal order both seriously undermines the 
integrity of the immigration system and results in wasted enforcement 
and adjudicative resources. See H. Rep. No. 104 469, pt. 1, at 160. 
Accordingly, the Departments believe that imposing the maximum 
statutorily authorized amount of these penalties is both consistent 
with Congress's purpose in enacting these penalties and not excessive 
given those amounts reflect the value of the harm Congress placed on 
such violations. See United States v. Chaplin's, Inc., 646 F.3d 846, 
852 (11th Cir. 2011) (``Congress, as a representative body, can distill 
the monetary value society places on harmful conduct'').
    The second Bajakajian factor--whether the penalties apply to the 
class of persons for whom the statute was principally designed--also 
supports the Departments' position. Aliens subject to these penalties 
fall squarely within the class Congress targeted. For unlawful entry 
penalties, an alien's apprehension while attempting to enter the United 
States unlawfully is sufficient to support the penalty. For failure to 
depart penalties, ICE guidance instructs officers to confirm that the 
alien is subject to a final removal or voluntary departure order, that 
there is no DHS record of the alien's departure, and that, based on 
available records, there are no legal impediments or other 
circumstances that would negate a willful or voluntary failure to 
depart. For per diem penalties, ICE guidance further requires officers 
to exclude periods when the alien was lawfully permitted to remain in 
the United States, such as during the pendency of a stay of removal. 
This is all Congress has required. Congress has clearly provided that 
any alien who engages in the proscribed conduct--unlawfully entering 
the United States or willfully or voluntarily failing to depart after a 
removal or departure order--is subject to a civil penalty up to the 
statutory maximum. By contrast to other immigration-related civil 
penalties \53\ and contrary to commenters' suggestion, Congress has not 
required DHS to adjust the penalty based on proportionality or to 
consider specific mitigating circumstances. To the extent that 
commenters are suggesting that DHS must consider factors such as an 
alien's inability to obtain travel documents, hospitalization, or other 
circumstances beyond the alien's control, such factors could negate the 
``willfulness'' or ``voluntariness'' of an alien's conduct and, if the 
alien demonstrates them on appeal, the alien may not be subject to the 
penalty at all. However, the alien is best positioned to raise these 
considerations on appeal because DHS would generally not have knowledge 
of such circumstances. The second Bajakajian factor therefore supports 
DHS's decision to assess these penalties up to the maximum statutorily 
authorized amount without first conducting a proportionality analysis 
or considering mitigating circumstances.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \53\ See e.g., INA 274A(e)(5), 8 U.S.C. 1324a(e)(5) (listing 
various factors that must be considered when determining the 
appropriate amount of the penalty for certain employment-related 
immigration violations); INA 273(e), 8 U.S.C. 1323(e) (directing DHS 
to prescribe regulations for reducing carrier penalties for 
transporting undocumented aliens in appropriate circumstances).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The third Bajakajian factor--comparison to potential criminal 
sanctions--likewise weighs against a finding of excessiveness. In 
IIRIRA, Congress not only created the civil failure to depart penalty 
but also amended INA 243, 8 U.S.C. 1253, to make it a criminal offense 
for an alien to willfully fail or refuse to depart within 90 days of a 
final removal order. Congress authorized imprisonment of up to four 
years, a fine, or both, with enhanced penalties for certain criminal 
aliens. See INA 243(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1253(a)(1). Congress has also 
authorized criminal penalties for unlawful entry, including up to six 
months' imprisonment, a fine, or both, with increased penalties for 
repeat offenses. See INA 275(a), 8 U.S.C. 1325(a). These criminal 
penalties are significantly more severe than the civil penalties at 
issue, and Congress specifically provided that the maximum civil 
penalties may be imposed in addition to any criminal sanctions. See INA 
274D(b), 275(b), 8 U.S.C. 1324d(b), 1325(b). In light of this statutory 
framework, all three Bajakajian factors weigh strongly against 
commenters' arguments that imposing the maximum statutory civil 
penalties violates the Excessive Fines Clause.
    For these reasons, the Departments decline to amend the rule to 
limit the discretion of DHS immigration officers to impose the maximum 
statutory penalty amounts or require that they apply proportionality 
factors before doing so. Finally, regarding one commenter's concern 
about ``ability to pay,'' the Departments note that Congress has not 
required DHS to consider an alien's ability to pay in assessing these 
penalties, and the Supreme Court has not held this factor must be 
analyzed under the Excessive Fines Clause. Absent a legal requirement 
for DHS to consider an alien's ability to pay, DHS believes that 
adjusting a fine amount lower based on an alien's ability to pay would 
diminish the rule's deterrent effect.
    Comment: One commenter alleged that 8 CFR 281.1(g) is inconsistent 
with 8 CFR 1240.26(l) mandating that the Immigration Judge or BIA 
advise the alien of the civil penalty amount at the time of granting 
voluntary departure or a presumptive amount of $3,000 will be set. 
Another commenter noted that DHS has increased the penalty amounts in 8 
CFR 280.53 for failure to depart violations incrementally over time 
from $500 per diem penalty in 2011, to a $998 per diem penalty in 2025, 
with DHS making incremental adjustments each year in between. The 
commenter claims that ``the amount of fines that allegedly accrued on 
any given day should have been limited to the amount authorized by the 
regulation in effect on that day.'' The commenter acknowledges that the 
Federal Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustment Improvements Act of 2015 
allows DHS to adjust civil penalty amounts for inflation each year and 
to apply adjustments retroactively, but the commenter argues that 
``charging a lump sum without itemizing the exact amounts that DHS 
alleges to have accrued on any specific dates nor any explanation for 
why DHS believes fines accrued during this particular timeframe



deprives respondents of critical information necessary to contest such 
charges.'' The commenter argues the IFR is defective because it does 
not require DHS to itemize penalties that ``DHS alleges to have accrued 
on any specific dates nor [provides] any explanation for why DHS 
believes fines accrued during this particular timeframe.''
    Response: First, DHS notes that the IFR does not direct immigration 
officers to apply the penalty amounts listed in 8 CFR 280.53. Rather, 8 
CFR 281.1(g) merely refers them to that provision so that they have 
access to information concerning the current inflation adjusted amount 
for each penalty. Immigration officers must determine how to apply 
those inflation adjusted rates in the context of each individual case, 
or whether to apply those rates at all, consistent with ICE and CBP 
guidance. Indeed, contrary to one commenter's claim, ICE guidance 
directs immigration officers to apply the penalty amount set by an 
Immigration Judge or the BIA or a $3,000 amount if no penalty amount is 
included in the voluntary departure order when assessing voluntary 
departure civil penalties. Accordingly, DHS is assessing voluntary 
departure penalties consistent with 8 CFR 1240.26(l).
    Further, the Departments do not agree that DHS should itemize 
penalty amounts in penalty decisions imposing fines for willful failure 
to depart under INA 274D(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1324d(a)(1). The commenter's 
suggestion that ``the amount of fines that allegedly accrued on any 
given day should [be] limited to the amount authorized by the 
regulation in effect on that day'' is inconsistent with the Federal 
Civil Penalties Inflation Adjustment Improvements Act of 2015, Public 
Law 114-74 (Nov. 2, 2015), 28 U.S.C. 2461 note. The 2015 Amendments 
amended section 6 of the Inflation Adjustment Act to provide that 
``[a]ny increase under this Act in a civil monetary penalty shall apply 
only to civil monetary penalties, including those whose associated 
violation predated such increase, which are assessed after the date the 
increase takes effect.'' Congress's specific reference to applying the 
adjustments to civil monetary penalties ``whose associated violation 
predated'' the effective date of the adjustment clearly contemplates 
that inflation adjustments after 2015 can be applied to violations 
occurring prior to the effective date of the increased civil penalty 
amounts--but only if the civil penalties are ``assessed after the date 
the increase takes effect.'' That is precisely how DHS applies the 
failure to depart penalties under INA 274D(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1324d(a)(1). 
Specifically, DHS applies the inflation adjusted amount that is in 
effect on the day that the penalty is ``assessed''--i.e., when DHS 
issues the penalty decision--regardless of the date of the removal 
order or the amount that was authorized on any one day in the period 
for which the penalty applies--i.e., any day that the alien willfully 
failed to depart the United States after the final removal order.
    To the extent that the commenter is concerned about DHS applying 
the current inflation adjusted rate to violations that occurred prior 
to the Inflation Adjustment Improvements Act of 2015, DHS notes that 
the commenter's concern is misplaced. As discussed above in this 
preamble, an alien is liable for a per diem penalty for each day he 
willfully remains in the United States after a final removal order 
regardless of when the removal order first became final. However, DHS 
is applying the failure to depart penalty for only five years back from 
the date of the penalty decision. Therefore, DHS would only assess the 
per diem penalty at the adjusted rate in place at the time of the 
penalty decision for a total of five years back from the date of the 
decision, even if the alien's removal order became final prior to 2015.
    Regarding commenters' suggestion that DHS needs to itemize penalty 
decisions because the alien may not be liable for a per diem penalty 
for some portion of the period that the alien remained in the United 
States, ICE guidance directs immigration officers account for any 
periods after the removal order became administratively final during 
which the alien was authorized to remain in the United States (e.g., a 
stay of removal, a later approved immigration benefit). See Section 
III.E.2 of this preamble. To the extent that an alien's individual 
circumstances excused an alien's willful or voluntary failure to depart
