for some period of time (e.g., the alien was hospitalized or 
incarcerated or otherwise was unable to depart due to circumstances 
beyond the alien's control), the alien is best positioned to raise 
these issues on appeal. DHS cannot be expected to know about an alien's 
individual circumstances that prevented the alien from departing.

E. Other Matters Related to the IFR

1. Statute of Limitations
    Comment: Several commenters asserted that the rule does not explain 
how the federal statute of limitations applies to the civil penalties 
imposed under the IFR. One commenter suggested that the IFR's 
streamlined penalty procedures make it difficult for aliens to raise 
statute of limitations defenses, and the complexity of these defenses 
undermines the IFR's assumption about the readily verifiable and 
straightforward nature of these penalties. One commenter argued that 
the IFR does not require DHS to include information in the penalty 
decision about when the violation occurred which makes it difficult for 
aliens and their counsel to determine if DHS is correctly applying the 
statute of limitations. The commenter suggested that the 15-day appeal 
period, combined with the use of ordinary mail to serve decisions, 
could prevent aliens and their attorneys from investigating statute of 
limitations issues and raising the statute of limitations as a defense 
to these penalties. The commenter argued that eliminating BIA review is 
particularly problematic because DHS immigration officers do not have 
the legal expertise to resolve complex statute of limitations issues, 
and DHS does not have a mechanism to issue binding decisions on legal 
issues including those involving statutes of limitation.
    Commenters offered their views regarding how the federal statute of 
limitations, 28 U.S.C. 2462, applies to the penalties covered by this 
rule. For the failure to depart penalties, commenters claimed that the 
five-year statute of limitations begins to run the moment the voluntary 
departure period ends or when a removal order becomes final. They 
stated that DHS cannot impose fines for conduct that happened more than 
five years ago, such as remaining in the United States after a 
voluntary departure order period expired or after a removal order 
became final, particularly when there is no caselaw or statute 
recognizing a ``continuing violation'' theory for these penalties. For 
the unlawful entry penalties, commenters said that the limitations 
period begins to run once an alien is apprehended while in the process 
of entering or attempting to enter the United States.
    Response: The Departments disagree that the rule should be 
rescinded because it fails to include a statute of limitations 
provision. As an initial matter, the Departments emphasize the IFR's 
limited scope. The IFR changed only the procedures by which DHS issues 
and adjudicates certain civil monetary penalties and the manner in 
which aliens may contest them. The IFR did not change or alter the 
criteria for issuing these penalties, including how DHS interprets or 
applies the general federal statute of limitations for these penalties. 
Indeed, the Departments note that none of the Departments' other civil



monetary penalty regulations contain a statute of limitations 
provision, including 8 CFR 280, which, prior to the IFR, governed the 
process for assessing the penalties covered by this rule. Accordingly, 
the Departments believe that it was reasonable and appropriate to limit 
the scope of the IFR consistent with the scope of the Departments' 
other civil penalty regulations, especially because of the IFR's narrow 
purpose of streamlining the process for the failure to depart and 
unlawful entry penalties. Therefore, the Departments decline to amend 
the rule to add a statute of limitations provision. For the same 
reasons, the Departments do not agree with commenters' suggestion that 
failure to include a statute of limitations provisions renders the rule 
arbitrary or capricious.\54\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \54\ To the extent that any civil penalties issued under the IFR 
were determined to be inconsistent with the statute of limitations, 
addressing such fines would be outside of the scope of this final 
rulemaking. The preamble to a final rule exists to satisfy the APA's 
requirement of ``a concise general statement of [the rule's] basis 
and purpose,'' 5 U.S.C. 553(c), and addressing fines already issued 
under the IFR--to the extent that is even necessary--plainly falls 
outside of that.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The Departments also disagree that the IFR's streamlined 
proceedings make it too difficult for aliens to assert a statute of 
limitations defense. Consistent with 8 CFR 281.1(c)(1), each penalty 
decision lists the date when the alien became subject to a final 
removal or a voluntary departure order, or when the alien was 
apprehended entering or attempting to enter the United States 
unlawfully. See DHS Form 281, Notice of Violation and Order. Therefore, 
to the extent that an alien believes that the violation occurred 
outside of the statute of limitations, the penalty decision itself 
contains the relevant information to dispute the penalty. Further, 
aliens should already possess any documents needed to dispute the 
information contained in the penalty decision. For example, an alien 
who disputes the date of a final removal or voluntary departure order 
can simply provide a copy of his removal or departure order or any 
documents showing that the alien's removal order or voluntary departure 
period was delayed because of an appeal or a stay of removal. The same 
is true for aliens subject to civil penalties for unlawful entry: the 
relevant charging document will list the date that DHS apprehended the 
alien entering or attempting to enter the United States. Commenters do 
not explain why aliens cannot retain these important documents, and the 
Departments will not assume otherwise. Accordingly, the Departments 
believe that the penalty decision contains sufficient information to 
allow an alien to raise a statute of limitations defense, and the IFR's 
15-day appeal period provides ample time for aliens and their 
attorneys, if any, to gather evidence to compliment or prepare such a 
defense.
    Similarly, the Departments do not agree with commenters' position 
that BIA review is needed because legal questions regarding the statute 
of limitations cannot adequately be resolved by DHS immigration 
officers on appeal.
    ICE and CBP both apply the statute of limitations for these 
penalties in a straightforward way that refutes commenters' arguments 
that additional procedures, including BIA review, are needed due to the 
complexity of statute of limitations issues. First, ICE only assesses 
penalties under INA 240B(d), 8 U.S.C. 1229c(d), if an alien's voluntary 
departure period expired within five years of the order imposing the 
penalty.\55\ CBP only assesses penalties under INA 275(b), 8 U.S.C. 
1325(b), against aliens apprehended in the last five years while 
entering (or attempting to enter) the United States. The Departments 
note these approaches are consistent with commenters' interpretation of 
the general statute of limitations, 28 U.S.C. 2462, applicable to these 
penalties. This application ensures consistency in the assessment of 
these penalties and provides clear direction to immigration officers on 
how far back to assess these penalties. Therefore, aliens do not need 
to prepare, and immigration officers do not need to decide, complicated 
statute of limitations defenses for these penalties in light of this 
approach. If an alien believes a penalty is contrary to this approach, 
the alien can appeal the civil penalty decision and provide a copy of 
the voluntary departure order indicating the date of the violation or, 
in the case of an unlawful entry penalty, the charging document listing 
the date and location of apprehension.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \55\ DHS acknowledges that some fines have been issued based on 
violations that occurred more than five years after the voluntary 
departure period and is taking action to ensure fines issued in the 
future are consistent with the statute of limitations.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    With respect to penalties under INA 274D(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 
1324d(a)(1), for willful failure to comply with a removal order, 
immigration officers can impose these penalties regardless of the date 
of the post-IIRIRA final removal order, but the per diem penalty amount 
should be assessed only for the five-year period preceding the date 
that the penalty is issued. Contrary to commenters' arguments, this is 
consistent with the plain language of the statute and caselaw 
interpreting similar penalty statutes for the purposes of determining 
the application of the general five-year statute of limitations under 
28 U.S.C. 2462. Section INA 274D(a)(1) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 
1324d(a)(1), provides that ``any alien subject to a final removal order 
who--willfully fails or refuses to depart from the United States . . . 
shall pay a civil penalty of not more than $500 to [DHS] for each day 
the alien is in violation of this section.'' (emphasis added). When a 
civil penalty statute imposes a per diem penalty, the ``continuing 
violation'' doctrine applies, and the Government may assess the penalty 
even if the first violation occurred more than five years back. See 
Interamericas Invs., Ltd. v. Bd. of Governors of the Fed. Rsrv. Sys., 
111 F.3d 376, 382 (5th Cir. 1997) (explaining that ``[w]here the civil 
penalty provision at hand contemplates per diem penalties for 
violations, then continuing violations are cognizable under the general 
statute of limitations.''). Similarly, when a statute contemplates 
``repeated violations,'' each new violation restarts the statute of 
limitations, but penalties can be assessed only for the violations 
occurring within that limitations period. See Hamer v. City of 
Trinidad, 924 F.3d 1093, 1100 (10th Cir. 2019) (explaining the repeated 
violation doctrine). Under either doctrine, INA 274D(a)(1), 8 U.S.C. 
1324d(a)(1), plainly indicates that Congress intended for an alien to 
be subject to a continuing or new penalty each day he remains in the 
United States in violation of a removal order regardless of when the 
final removal order was issued. And, as a matter of policy, ICE is 
applying the per diem penalty amount only for the five-year period 
preceding the date that the penalty is issued, consistent with the 
``repeated violations'' doctrine.
    Additionally, the Departments note that aliens can seek judicial 
review of final penalty decisions, after exhausting administrative 
remedies. See 5 U.S.C. 704. Aliens can also raise any available 
defense, including statute of limitations defenses, in connection with 
any enforcement action that DOJ brings to collect these fines.
    For these reasons, individually and collectively, the Departments 
disagree with commenters' view that the IFR should be rescinded or 
revised because it does not address how the statute of limitations 
applies to these penalties. For the same reasons, commenters' views 
about the complexity of statute of limitations issues do not undermine 
the Departments' determination that the process for these penalties can 
be



streamlined because of their straightforward nature.
2. Implementation Matters and Alternatives
    Comment: Implementation concerns and alternatives were also raised. 
One commenter expressed concern that the rule lacks adequate safeguards 
to prevent civil monetary penalties from being applied to aliens who 
currently hold, or are eligible for, lawful or protected status. The 
commenter stated that the rule provides no clear guidance on how DHS 
will avoid imposing fines on individuals who have been granted TPS, 
asylum, or relief under the VAWA or the T and U visa programs. These 
groups, the commenter explained, often have pending or approved 
immigration benefits that authorize their continued presence in the 
U.S. or excuse prior periods of unlawful presence. The commenter also 
noted that the IFR does not address how DHS will handle cases where 
aliens are beneficiaries of prosecutorial discretion, deferred action, 
or stays of removal. According to the commenter, the absence of 
explicit instructions combined with the IFR's streamlined process, 
risks imposing fines on aliens who are lawfully present under DHS 
policy or court order. The commenter stated it was critical to 
recognize that individuals with lawful or protected status are not 
obligated to depart.
    Another commenter suggested that DHS should implement this rule as 
a limited pilot program before implementing it nationwide. The 
commenter said that a pilot-and-evaluate model would allow DHS to 
collect empirical evidence to assess the impact of civil fines on 
compliance, family stability, and financial impact of these penalties 
on aliens and their families. Using this empirical evidence to guide 
adjustments would ensure that civil fine enforcement evolves in 
response to real-world outcomes rather than theoretical assumptions.
    Response: As an initial matter, the Departments reiterate that the 
IFR did not change the categories of aliens subject to civil penalties 
or ICE's process for deciding whether an alien is subject to a civil 
penalty. Rather, the IFR was issued as a procedural rule and governs 
only the procedures that apply to these penalties. Therefore, DHS 
declines to modify the IFR in this final rule to clarify the category 
of aliens who are or are not subject to these penalties. Immigration 
officers confirm an alien's current status based on available records 
before assessing a civil fine by referencing multiple platforms and 
immigration databases. ICE's guidance to immigration officers provides 
that aliens with approved applications for lawful or protected status--
such as TPS, Form I-730 Refugee/Asylee Relative benefits, VAWA 
protections, DACA, and T-visas and U-visas--should not be issued a 
civil fine. ICE also accounts for any deferrals of removal triggered by 
the filing of certain applications before USCIS, consistent with 
applicable statutes and regulations. When calculating a fine under INA 
274D, immigration officers account for any periods after the removal 
order became administratively final during which the alien was 
authorized to remain in the United States due to, e.g., a stay or 
deferral of removal. As part of the individual case review process, 
immigration officers review documents and supporting information across 
multiple immigration systems, including systems and platforms of 
entities such as USCIS, CBP, and DOJ/EOIR. DHS clarifies that lawful 
status cannot be conferred through an immigration officer's exercise of 
discretion and that the immigration officer cannot excuse an alien's 
obligation to depart pursuant to a final removal order. Rather, this 
measure reflects a determination not to pursue enforcement action at 
the time such discretion is exercised. As such, individuals who are 
beneficiaries of this measure remain subject to the underlying 
immigration laws and obligations, including potential civil penalties 
for violations.
    Comment: One commenter asserted that the rule misinterprets and 
overextends the scope of the civil monetary penalty authorized by INA 
275(b), 8 U.S.C. 1325(b). The commenter stated that, by statute, these 
penalties apply only to aliens who are ``apprehended while entering (or 
attempting to enter)'' the United States, and not to those later 
encountered within the interior after an unlawful entry. The commenter 
objected to language in the IFR suggesting that DHS may rely on Form I-
213 or other records of interior apprehension to establish liability 
under INA 275(b), 8 U.S.C. 1325(b). The commenter argued that such an 
interpretation is inconsistent with the plain language of the statute 
and could lead to the improper assessment of fines against aliens who 
were not apprehended at the time of entry. The commenter urged DHS to 
revise the rule to clarify that INA 275(b), 8 U.S.C. 1325(b) penalties 
cannot be imposed on aliens apprehended after entry or encountered away 
from the border. The commenter also stated that the rule should require 
DHS to include specific evidentiary information in any order imposing 
this penalty such as the date of the attempted entry and the date and 
location of the arrest, to ensure that the penalty is applied only in 
circumstances consistent with statutory authority.
    Response: The Departments disagree with the commenter's 
characterization that the rule overextends the scope of penalties under 
INA 275(b)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1325(b)(1). The rule does not expand the 
statutory application of 275(b), 8 U.S.C. 1325(b)(1) but rather 
provides procedural clarity for the assessment and collection of civil 
monetary penalties. The Departments interpret INA 275(b), 8 U.S.C. 
1325(b)(1) to apply to aliens who are apprehended while entering or 
attempting to enter the United States. In practice, CBP will assess an 
INA 275(b), 8 U.S.C. 1325(b)(1), penalty only when it apprehends an 
alien who has entered (or attempted to enter) the United States without 
inspection in the past seven days and who has not yet reached their 
destination, consistent with the statutory language and legislative 
intent of INA 275(b)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1325(b)(1). As indicated above, the 
applicable statute of limitations runs five years from the date of 
apprehension.
    Comment: Commenters expressed concern that the rule does not 
address how civil monetary penalties would apply to aliens whose prior 
removal orders are later reopened, vacated, or otherwise resolved in a 
manner that permits adjustment of status or other immigration relief. 
They noted that DHS often agrees to join motions to reopen removal 
proceedings to allow individuals to pursue lawful status or relief. 
They stated that it was ``critical to recognize that those with lawful 
status in the U.S. are under no obligation to depart,'' and that 
``[t]heir continued presence in the U.S. is not a willful failure to 
depart, but a lawful consequence of the status conferred upon them. 
Another commenter urged DHS to clarify that civil penalties assessed 
must be rescinded when a removal order is reopened and will not be used 
as a basis to deny the alien's future attempts to regularize their 
immigration status. The commenter suggested, without much elaboration, 
that the IFR should clarify that DHS should not apply fines against 
aliens with in absentia removal orders.
    Response: ICE's guidance to immigration officers provides that 
aliens whose removal order is stayed should not be issued an INA 274D, 
8 U.S.C. 1324d, failure to depart penalty. ICE confers with DHS's 
Office of the Principal Legal Advisor before issuing a



failure to depart penalty in any case in which a Motion to Reopen 
(``MTR'') has been adjudicated for review of the reasons for reopening 
asserted by the alien and any circuit-specific case law that may affect 
the viability of the penalty. ICE confirms an alien's current case 
status before assessing or collecting any fine by referencing its 
internal systems. DHS disagrees that fines should not apply to any 
alien with an in absentia removal order but notes that, where an alien 
files an MTR and claims that the alien did not receive notice, their 
removal order is stayed. INA 240(b)(5)(C), 8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(5)(C). DHS 
emphasizes that the assessment of civil penalties is tied to the 
existence of a valid removal order and the alien's willful failure or 
refusal to depart as required by law. If a removal order is reopened, 
vacated, or dismissed, DHS will review the circumstances to determine 
whether the assessed civil penalties remain appropriate.

F. Statutory and Regulatory Requirements

1. Administrative Procedure Act
i. Procedural Rule Exception
    Comment: Several commenters generally asserted that Departments 
lacked authority to issue the IFR without first publishing a notice of 
proposed rulemaking and providing a pre-promulgation comment period in 
accordance with the APA, 5 U.S.C. 553. First, commenters argued that 
the Departments cannot properly characterize the IFR as a procedural 
rule under 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A). Commenters identified changes such as 
eliminating the NIF before issuing a final penalty, reducing the time 
to respond from 30 days to 15 days, allowing service by regular mail 
instead of certified or personal service, and moving appeals from the 
BIA to DHS. They asserted that these changes remove or weaken existing 
protections, implicate due process, change rights and obligations of 
affected individuals, and therefore render the rule substantive, which 
would require compliance with the APA's notice and comment 
requirements.
    Response: The Departments disagree. This rule was properly issued 
without prior notice and comment under 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A), which 
exempts from those requirements ``rules of agency organization, 
procedure, or practice.'' Under the APA, notice and comment is required 
for substantive rules. By contrast, agency rules that prescribe agency 
organization, procedure, or practice are exempt from the notice-and-
comment requirement. See 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A). The ``critical feature of 
the procedural rule exception is that it covers agency actions that do 
not themselves alter the rights or interests of parties, although it 
may alter the manner in which the parties present themselves or their 
viewpoints to the agency.'' JEM Broadcasting Co., Inc. v. FCC, 22 F.3d 
320, 328 (D.C. Cir. 1994) (cleaned up). In JEM Broadcasting, the D.C. 
Circuit upheld a rule that changed the timing and processing of 
applications, not the substantive criteria for deciding them, and 
treated the rule as procedural and exempt from notice and comment. Id.
    As explained in the IFR, this rule fits within that procedural rule 
exemption. See 90 27454. This rule merely prescribes how the 
Departments conduct internal penalty proceedings and administrative 
reviews. The IFR does not alter the statutory obligations under INA 
240B(d), 274D(a)(1), and 275(b); 8 U.S.C. 1229c(d), 1324d(a), and 
1325(b), that authorize civil monetary penalties against aliens who 
fail to depart voluntarily, who willfully refuse to depart after a 
final order of removal, or who are apprehended while unlawfully 
entering or attempting to enter. It does not change the amount of these 
penalties or create new categories of violators or new statutory 
rights. The substantive legal liability remains as defined by statute.
    Rather, the IFR merely revised the process by which the Departments 
impose these civil monetary penalties. For example, allowing DHS to 
serve penalty notices by regular mail (and no longer only by certified 
mail or personal service); shortening the period within which a 
respondent must contest the fine or exercise appeal rights from 30 to 
15 days, moving the appeals process from the BIA to DHS, and other 
procedural streamlining merely alters the manner in which parties 
present themselves or their viewpoints to the Departments. Under the 
IFR, aliens continue to receive written notice of the penalty by 
regular mail and a meaningful opportunity to present a written response 
with supporting evidence before any final determination is made. 
Likewise, replacing BIA review with review by a DHS supervisory 
official who was not involved in the initial decision preserves 
neutral, independent oversight while streamlining the adjudication 
process. Accordingly, this rule is properly classified as a procedural 
rule and exempt from prior notice and comment procedures under the APA.
    Moreover, though not required to do so, the Departments nonetheless 
solicited post-promulgation comments following publication of the IFR 
on June 27, 2025, and accepted comments through July 28, 2025. The 
Departments have carefully reviewed and considered all comment 
submissions received at the docket in developing this final rule.
ii. Foreign Affairs Exemption
    Comment: Commenters also asserted that the Departments' reliance on 
the foreign affairs exemption under 5 U.S.C. 553(a)(1) is legally 
unsupported. They argued that the rule's subject matter--imposing fines 
on aliens--is purely domestic enforcement activity that neither 
regulates nor directly impacts foreign affairs. Additionally, these 
commenters challenged the Departments' assertion that the rule supports 
U.S. foreign policy negotiations as vague, too attenuated, and 
overbroad. One commenter said that under the Departments' reasoning, 
nearly any domestic policy that ``comes up in negotiations with a 
foreign country'' could be exempt from notice and comment. The other 
commenter claimed that the Departments invoked the exception in bad 
faith, arguing that traditional examples of rules meeting the foreign 
affairs exemption involve rules relating to international trade and 
visa issuance.
    One commenter suggested that the Departments did not demonstrate an 
immediate foreign affairs need to bypass the APA's notice and comment 
and delayed-effective-date requirements, noting that the fines covered 
by the IFR have been codified in law for years but only rarely used by 
DHS. The commenter also took issue with the Departments' assertion that 
immediate action is needed to address the shared problem of irregular 
migration to the southern border. The commenter asserted that the IFR 
will not have an appreciable impact on border operations because the 
Administration has already ``shutdown asylum process at the Southern 
border'' and the IFR is primarily targeted at aliens who are already 
illegally present within the United States.
    Response: The IFR is excepted from the APA's notice-and-comment and 
delayed-effective-date requirements because it involves a ``foreign 
affairs function of the United States.'' 5 U.S.C. 553(a)(1). As an 
initial matter, contrary to one commenter's claim, the foreign affairs 
exception is not limited to rules relating to international trade and 
visa issuance. The Supreme Court has never determined what constitutes 
a ``foreign affairs function of the United States.'' Lower federal 
courts have held that this exception applies when the rule in question 
is ``clearly and directly



involve[d]'' in ``a foreign affairs function.'' E.B. v. U.S. Dep't of 
State, 583 F. Supp. 3d 58, 63 (D.D.C. 2022) (cleaned up). In addition, 
although the text of the APA does not require an agency invoking this 
exception to show that such procedures may result in ``definitely 
undesirable international consequences,'' some courts have required 
such a showing. See, e.g., Rajah v. Mukasey, 544 F.3d 427, 437 (2d Cir. 
2008) (quotation marks omitted). The IFR satisfies both standards. Even 
though the Departments issued an IFR, an opportunity for public comment 
after issuing the IFR was provided and this final rule responds to 
those comments. See Little Sisters of the Poor Saints Peter and Paul 
Home, 591 U.S. 657, 683-84 (2020).
    The Departments disagree with commenters' assertions that the IFR 
involves only domestic immigration enforcement and thus does not 
directly impact foreign affairs. First, as discussed in the IFR, the 
rule is directly and clearly connected to a foreign affairs function of 
the United States because it supports this Administration's efforts to 
address the shared international challenge of border security and 
illegal migration. The Secretary of State has made clear that 
``securing America's borders and protecting its citizens from external 
threats is the first priority foreign affairs function of the United 
States,'' In this regard, the United States continues to work closely 
with foreign partner countries to address migration in the Western 
Hemisphere region to secure America's borders and protect its citizens, 
and this rule is clearly and directly related to, and responsive to, 
the United States efforts in this regard. Specifically, the IFR and 
this rule are intended to allow DHS to streamline and maximize its use 
of civil penalties against aliens who are apprehended entering or enter 
unlawfully at the southern border. DHS believes that this additional 
tool will allow it to discourage, prepare for, and respond to unlawful 
migration by increasing the consequences on aliens who make the 
dangerous journey to the United States and enter unlawfully. Therefore, 
measures like the IFR advance the United States' foreign policy 
objectives by demonstrating to partner countries that the United States 
is serious about the shared problem of irregular migration and border 
security and that the Administration is doing its part to address these 
challenges by using all available tools even if they originate from 
U.S. law. Further, the Departments disagree with one commenter's 
suggestion that the Departments invoked the exemption in ``bad faith.'' 
To the contrary, the Departments have relied on the foreign affairs 
exception, under several Administrations, when issuing rules designed 
to help address the shared international challenge of migration to the 
United States southern border.\56\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \56\ See e.g., Securing the Border, 89 FR 48710, 48759-62 (June 
7, 2024); see also Asylum Eligibility and Procedural Modifications, 
84 FR 33829, 33842 (June 16, 2019).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The Departments acknowledge that this rule also applies to aliens 
in the interior of the United States who have violated the immigration 
laws by failing to depart after a removal or voluntary departure. The 
Departments disagree, however, that the problem that the IFR seeks to 
address is purely a domestic one. Rather, as explained in the IFR, the 
United States' ability to address the challenge of aliens remaining in 
the country unlawfully after removal and departure orders depends in 
part on the willingness of other nations to accept the return and 
repatriation of their citizens from the United States. Contrary to 
commenters' claims, the Departments have provided concrete examples of 
the United States' foreign negotiations and efforts aimed at 
encouraging other countries to support the return of their citizens, 
including those with outstanding removal and voluntary departure 
orders. See 90 FR 27455. These efforts include encouraging other 
countries to promptly issue travels documents that allow their 
residents to return home, and more broadly to cooperate with DHS's 
efforts to successfully implement Presidential Proclamation 10935, 
Establishing Project Homecoming, 90 FR 20357 (May 9, 2025), which 
provides aliens with a process to voluntarily depart the United States 
and return to their home countries. See 90 FR 27455-56. All of these 
efforts indicate that the removal and voluntary return of aliens with 
no legal right to remain in the United States is a critical foreign 
policy objective of the United States. For these foreign policy efforts 
to continue to succeed, DHS must continue to demonstrate its own 
commitment to this foreign policy objective, including by encouraging 
aliens to take advantage of these expanded opportunities that the 
United States Government has secured through international efforts. The 
IFR directly and clearly serves this purpose by incentivizing aliens to 
comply with departure obligations, including through these expanded 
departure options, and by imposing consequences on those who fail to 
depart.
    In addition to the IFR's clear and direct involvement in foreign 
affairs, the Departments believed that issuing the rule after notice 
and comment, and with a delayed effective date, could have led to 
definitely undesirable international consequences. As discussed in the 
IFR, these consequences include negative impacts to border security, 
which is a shared regional problem, and DHS's inability to capitalize 
on the momentum that the United States Government had achieved in 
encouraging countries to support the return of their citizens, 
including those with outstanding removal and departure orders. In this 
regard, the Departments disagree with commenters that claimed that the 
Departments did not demonstrate an immediate need for the IFR because 
this Administration's asylum policies at the southern border had 
already reduced irregular border encounters. The IFR acknowledged that 
encounters between POEs at the southern border had decreased 
significantly from their historic highs under the prior Administration. 
See 90 FR 27455. The Departments explained, however, that the IFR would 
help DHS to continue to build on the then-recent progress that DHS had 
achieved at the southern border. See 90 FR 27446, 27455-56. The 
Departments note that DHS was encountering nearly 1,000 aliens per day 
at the southern border only six months prior to the IFR's publication 
and nearly 2,000 aliens per day between June and December 2024.\57\ 
Therefore, although encounter numbers had declined when the IFR was 
issued in large part due to the Administration's border policies, DHS 
reasonably believed at the time that there was a substantial risk that, 
without additional tools in place at the southern border encounters, 
like this IFR, encounters could once again increase.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \57\ See Nationwide Encounters, U.S. Customs and Border 
Protection (Sept. 16, 2026), https://www.cbp.gov/newsroom/stats/nationwide-encounters (select Region: ``US SW Land Border'' and 
Component: U.S. Border Patrol).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Further, the Departments also disagree with the claim that the 
Departments did not demonstrate an immediate need to implement the rule 
under the foreign affairs exception because these civil monetary 
penalties have been authorized for many years but rarely used, and DHS 
has mainly applied them to aliens in the interior. As an initial 
matter, regardless of the past administrations' policies, this 
Administration has made clear that that the rapid return of illegal 
aliens to their home countries is a critical foreign policy objective 
of the United States and



it has conducted its recent foreign policy efforts consistent with this 
objective. In the months prior to issuing this IFR, the Administration 
had been engaged in discussions with several countries aimed at 
ensuring that those countries promptly issue travels documents to 
facilitate the return of their nationals. Moreover, in the weeks prior 
to issuing the IFR, the President directed the Secretary of State and 
the Secretary of Homeland to take all appropriate ``actions to enable 
the rapid departure of illegal aliens from the United States'' \58\ 
including assisting aliens with obtaining travel documents or 
relocating to another country and providing financial incentives and 
support to such aliens. The President also directed the Secretaries to 
notify aliens that should they choose not to take advantage of these 
incentives they will face consequences, including civil fines covered 
by this rule.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \58\ Proclamation 10935, 90 FR 20357, 20357 (May 9, 2025).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    In light of these efforts, the Departments explained that by 
issuing the IFR immediately DHS would be able to capitalize on these 
recent foreign policy efforts by encouraging aliens, through the use of 
civil penalties, to take advantage of these expanded opportunities 
achieved through international discussions and cooperation, to depart 
the United States. The Departments also explained that the IFR would 
allow the U.S. Government to build on this foreign policy momentum by 
demonstrating to other countries that it is committed to using all 
necessary tools to facilitate the rapid departure of illegal aliens and 
that other nations should support the Administration's continued 
efforts to achieve this objective. Quite simply, if the United States 
is unable to demonstrate, through measures like the IFR, that it is 
committed to taking quick and robust action to remove aliens and 
encourage them to depart the United States voluntarily, which depends 
in large part on international cooperation, countries may be less 
inclined to engage with the United States on these ongoing efforts in 
the future. Accordingly, the Departments believe that, contrary to 
commenters' claim, immediate issuance of this rule was appropriate and 
necessary to avoid undesirable international consequences.
iii. Good Cause
    Commenters also argued that the Departments lacked good cause to 
make the IFR effective immediately upon publication, and one commenter 
asserted that the Departments improperly invoked the good cause 
exception under 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B) to issue and immediately implement 
the IFR without prior notice and comment. Commenters argued that the 
IFR does not respond to sudden or unforeseeable emergency, and any need 
for the IFR was an emergency of DHS's own making--i.e., DHS's own 
decision to restart issuing civil penalty program despite previously 
ending that program in 2021 after determining that civil penalties were 
ineffective and legally vulnerable. Commenters also argued that the 
public burden imposed by immediate implementation, particularly on 
immigrant communities and service providers far outweighs any 
government benefit from accelerating enforcement.
    Response: As an initial matter, the Departments note that the IFR 
did not invoke good cause under 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B) to dispense with 
notice and comment. Rather, the Departments issued the IFR under the 
procedural rule exception under 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(A) and the foreign 
affairs exception under 5 U.S.C. 553(a)(1) and invoked good cause under 
5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3) solely to make the rule effective upon publication. 
Section 553(d)(3) permits an agency to waive the standard 30-day 
delayed-effective-date requirement when it finds good cause for the 
rule to take immediate effect, balancing the agency's need for 
immediate implementation against affected persons' need for a 
reasonable amount of time to prepare for the effective date of its 
ruling. As explained in the IFR and reaffirmed here, the Departments 
determined that the ordinary reason for delay in a rule's effective 
date, to give members of the regulated community time to prepare and 
adjust their behavior, does not apply here because the IFR does not 
affect any person's substantive rights. Rather, it merely modifies the 
manner in which DHS issues and adjudicates civil monetary penalties and 
how an alien may contest such penalties. Moreover, the Departments 
found that the benefits of immediate implementation, ensuring 
uniformity, and administrative efficiency in the imposition and 
collection of civil monetary penalties, outweighed any need for 
affected parties to prepare for the effective date and adjust their 
behavior accordingly as this rule does not affect substantive right. 
Thus, the Departments conclude that invocation of the good cause under 
553(d)(3) was lawful and appropriate.
iv. Comment Period Duration
    Comment: Commenters argued that the 30-day post-promulgation 
comment window was inadequate given the breadth and complexity of the 
rule, which alters established practices related to assessing and 
collecting civil penalties under the three INA provisions. Commenters 
also cited Executive Order 12866, Regulatory Planning and Review, 58 FR 
51735, 51740, directing agencies to ``afford the public a meaningful 
opportunity to comment on any proposed regulation, which in most cases 
should include a comment period of not less than 60 days'' and argued 
that the abbreviated timeframe prevented comprehensive analysis of the 
rule's many substantive changes.
    Response: As an initial matter, commenters did not suggest or 
indicate what additional issues the comment period precluded them from 
addressing; to the contrary, the comments received reflect both a 
breadth and a level of detail which suggests that the period was more 
than sufficient. Cf. City of Waukesha v. EPA, 320 F.3d 228, 246 (D.C. 
Cir. 2003) (``In [showing prejudice] in the context of a violation of 
notice-and-comment requirements, petitioners may be required to 
demonstrate that, had proper notice been provided, they would have 
submitted additional, different comments that could have invalidated 
the rationale for the revised rule.'').
    The APA does not prescribe any specific minimum duration for public 
comment periods. While agencies often provide a 30-day period for 
proposed rules, and sometimes longer for complex or economically 
significant rulemakings, the statute simply requires that agencies 
generally afford interested parties an opportunity to participate 
through submission of written data, views, or arguments.
    Although not required to do so, the Departments nonetheless 
provided a 30-day comment period following publication of the IFR on 
June 27, 2025, accepting comments through July 28, 2025. That period 
afforded the public a meaningful opportunity to review the IFR and 
provide input. Indeed, federal courts have presumed 30 days to be a 
reasonable comment period length. See Nat'l Lifeline Ass'n v. Fed. 
Commc'ns Comm'n, 921 F.3d 1102, 1117 (D.C. Cir. 2019). Here, the 
detailed public comments the Departments received are evidence that the 
30-day period was sufficient for the public to meaningfully review and 
provide informed comments. See, e.g., Little Sisters of the Poor Saints 
Peter and Paul Home, 140 S. Ct. at 2385 (``The object [of notice and 
comment], in short, is one of fair notice.'') (citation omitted).
    The Departments received and carefully considered all timely 
submissions. Providing a 30-day



window for comments on a rule of limited procedural scope is consistent 
with longstanding administrative practice and the guidance reflected in 
Executive Orders 12866 and 13563, which encourage agencies to provide 
meaningful participation. The Departments' post-promulgation comment 
process thus satisfied the APA's requirements and furthered its 
purposes of transparency and public involvement, even though prior 
notice and comment were not legally required under 5 U.S.C. 553(a)(1) 
and (b)(A).
2. E.O. 12866 Analysis
    Comment: One commenter asserted that the IFR would impose 
substantial new economic burdens on affected aliens and their 
households, with potentially significant aggregate impacts. They 
contended that the IFR's increased and accelerated civil monetary 
penalties, particularly daily fines approaching $1,000 for failure to 
depart following a final order of removal, could result in liabilities 
large enough to cause long-term financial hardship, including wage 
garnishment, asset seizure, and bankruptcy. They further stated that 
these costs would likely fall disproportionately on low-income 
individuals and mixed-status families, potentially creating spillover 
effects for U.S. citizen spouses and children and exacerbating economic 
insecurity in immigrant communities. The commenter also argued that the 
IFR may generate billions of dollars in annual penalties, and that 
DHS's retention of penalty revenues could create institutional 
incentives to maximize fine issuance. They maintained that the IFR was 
implemented without sufficient economic analysis or public input and 
recommend alternatives such as means-based penalties, hardship waivers, 
or installment plans, independent review mechanisms, and pilot 
implementation to evaluate real world economic effects before 
nationwide implementation.
    Response: The Departments do not agree that this rule needs 
additional economic analysis or that it was adopted without considering 
financial impacts. As previously discussed, the rule does not create 
any new fines, change who can be fined, or increase the dollar amounts 
Congress has already set; it only changes the internal process DHS uses 
to issue and review those fines. Any financial hardship, including 
possible collection actions, comes from the underlying law and from an 
alien's choice to remain in the United States after being ordered to 
leave, not from these procedural updates. DHS's goal is to encourage 
people to follow removal and departure orders and to deter unlawful 
entry, not to generate revenue, and DHS will cancel most failure to 
depart fines when eligible aliens use the CBP Home app to leave the 
country. OMB has reviewed the rule as significant under Executive Order 
12866. DHS has weighed the limited added economic effects of these 
process changes against their enforcement benefits, and the Departments 
provided a 30-day comment period and considered economic and other 
feedback before finalizing the rule.

IV. Severability

    The changes made by the IFR, as amended by this final rule, impact 
provisions that are not necessarily interrelated and can function 
independent of one another. As such, the Departments believe that most 
of the provisions of this final rule can function sensibly and 
independently of other provisions. Therefore, in the event that any 
provisions in this rule are invalidated by a reviewing court, the 
Departments intend the remaining provisions to remain in effect to the 
fullest extent possible.

V. Statutory and Regulatory Requirements

A. Administrative Procedure Act

    The Departments have determined that this rule can take immediate 
effect notwithstanding the 30-day delayed effective date requirement in 
5 U.S.C. 553(d).
    Generally, there is good cause for this rule to take immediate 
effect. See 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3). This rule generally adopts the 
provisions of the IFR, with one change to help mitigate the potential 
effect of mail delays that could impact the amount of time an alien has 
to contest a civil penalty. See 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(1) (excepting from the 
delayed effective date requirements substantive rules that grant or 
recognize an exemption or relieve a restriction). The purpose of the 
30-day waiting period is ``to give affected parties time to adjust 
their behavior before the final rule takes effect.'' Riverbend Farms, 
Inc. v. Madigan, 958 F.2d 1479, 1485 (9th Cir. 1992). Here, however, 
that purpose would not be served by delaying the effective date of this 
final rule or the rule's amendment to account for mail delays because 
the public does not need advanced notice in order to conform their 
behavior to the rule.
    This final rule largely adopts the provisions of the IFR, which 
took effect on June 27, 2025. Consequently, aliens and legal service 
providers who may represent such aliens have long been on notice of 
those procedures and processes this rule adopts. See United States v. 
Gavrilovic, 551 F.2d 1099, 1104 (8th Cir. 1977) (noting that the 
``legislative history of the APA'' indicates that the waiting period 
``was not intended to unduly hamper agencies from making a rule 
effective immediately,'' but intended ``to `afford persons affected a 
reasonable time to prepare for the effective date of a rule . . . or to 
take other action which the issuance may prompt' '' (citing S. Rep. No. 
752, 79th Cong., 1st Sess. 15 (1946); H.R. Rep. No. 1980, 79th Cong., 
2d Sess. 25 (1946))). Indeed, the Departments have consistently 
communicated an intent to finalize the IFR.\59\ The fact that the IFR's 
effective date was recently stayed \60\ does not change the 
Departments' determination--the brief period between the entry of the 
stay on October 5, 2026, and October 14, 2026, does not alter the fact 
that the public operated under the rule's provisions for more than a 
year and has long been on notice of the Departments' intent to make 
them final.

of this final rule); Def.'s Opp'n to Pls.' Mot. to Compel, Maria L.

    Similarly, the change this final rule makes does not alter the 
calculus merely because it has not been part of the status quo under 
the IFR for the past year. The minor amendment is designed to benefit 
aliens by recognizing that an alien's untimely appeal may nonetheless 
be accepted if the late appeal was caused by a mail delay. See 5 U.S.C.

parties, although it may alter the manner in which the parties present 
themselves or their viewpoints to the agency.'' JEM Broad. Co., Inc. v. 
FCC, 22 F.3d 320, 326 (D.C. Cir. 1994) (quoting Batterton v. Marshall, 
648 F.2d 694, 707 (D.C. Cir. 1980)); see also Mendoza v. Perez, 54 F.3d 
1002, 1023-24 (D.C. Cir. 2014). The amendment in this final rule



does not change an alien's right to appeal a penalty under the IFR's 
15-business day appeal deadline and therefore ``impose[s] no new 
substantive obligations or burdens upon the parties' rights and 
interests.'' Am. Fed'n of Lab. & Cong. of Indus. Organizations v. Nat'l 
Lab. Rels. Bd., 57 F.4th 1023, 1043 (D.C. Cir. 2023) (quoting EPIC v. 
U.S. Dep't of Homeland Sec., 653 F.3d 1, 6 (D.C. Cir. 2011).\61\ 
Rather, while the amendment directs aliens to provide evidence of a 
mail delay in connection with an untimely appeal, this simply 
establishes a clear process for the agency to evaluate such a claim. 
Therefore, this evidentiary requirement is merely a procedural step, 
not a substantive change to the right to appeal itself.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \61\ The Departments further maintain that the 15-day appeal 
deadline is likewise a procedural change, rather than a substantive 
one, for the reasons explained in the IFR. 90 FR 27454.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    In finding good cause to bypass the 30-day delayed effective date 
requirement, the Departments have ``balanc[ed] the necessity for 
immediate implementation against principles of fundamental fairness 
which require that all affected persons be afforded a reasonable 
[amount of] time to prepare for the effective date of [the rule].'' 
Omnipoint Corp. v. FCC, 78 F.3d 620, 630 (D.C. Cir. 1996) (citation 
omitted). Here, the balance tips sharply in favor of immediate 
implementation. The United States Government and the American people 
have a strong interest in making the final rule effective immediately 
to ensure that DHS can continue implementing the IFR's provisions. As 
discussed in Section I.B. of this preamble, the IFR has reduced agency 
resource burdens by streamlining the civil penalty process and has 
allowed DHS to exercise its statutorily authorized civil penalty 
authority at scale in response to the large number of aliens who have 
unlawfully entered the United States or have failed to comply with 
removal and voluntary departure orders in recent years. In turn, this 
has allowed DHS to encourage greater compliance with such orders and 
provides DHS with another tool to disincentive future unlawful entries 
at the border.

B. Executive Order 12866 (Regulatory Planning and Review)

    Executive Order 12866, Regulatory Planning and Review, 58 FR 51735 
(Sept. 30, 1993), and Executive Order 13563, Improving Regulation and 
Regulatory Review, 76 FR 3821 (Jan. 18, 2011), direct agencies to 
assess all costs and benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, 
if regulation is necessary, to select regulatory approaches that 
maximize net benefits. The Office of Management and Budget has 
determined this rule is significant under Executive Order 12866.
    This final rule will allow DHS to more quickly impose a greater 
number of civil penalties on aliens who have unlawfully entered the 
United States and those who remain after a removal or voluntary 
departure order. DHS has not assessed the extent to which this final 
rule will result in an increase in civil penalties collected by the 
Government. DHS believes that this effort will reduce potential agency 
resource burdens by streamlining the process, discourage future 
unlawful entries, and encourage greater compliance with removal and 
departure orders.

C. Executive Order 14192 (Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation)

    This final rule is not an Executive Order 14192 regulatory action 
because it is being issued with respect to an immigration-related 
function of the United States. The rule's primary direct purpose is to 
implement or interpret the immigration laws of the United States (as 
described in section 101(a)(17) of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(17)) or 
any other function performed by the United States Federal Government 
with respect to aliens. See OMB Memorandum M-25-20, Guidance 
Implementing Section 3 of Executive Order 14192, titled ``Unleashing 
Prosperity Through Deregulation'' at 5-6 (Mar. 26, 2025).

D. Regulatory Flexibility Act

    The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980 (``RFA''), 5 U.S.C. 601-612, 
as amended, requires federal agencies to consider the potential impact 
of regulations on small entities during rulemaking. A regulatory 
flexibility analysis is not required when a rule is exempt from notice-
and-comment rulemaking. This final rule finalizes an IFR that was 
exempt from the notice-and-comment rulemaking. Therefore, a regulatory 
flexibility analysis is not required.
    However, even assuming that this rule is not exempt from notice-
and-comment procedures and therefore not exempt from the requirements 
of the RFA, the Departments have reviewed this rule in accordance with 
the RFA. The Secretary of Homeland Security and the Acting Director of 
EOIR certify that this rule will not have a significant economic impact 
on a substantial number of small entities. See 5 U.S.C. 605(b).
    First, aliens are not ``small entit[ies]'' as defined by the RFA. 
See 5 U.S.C. 601(6) (defining ``small entity'' as having the same 
meaning as ``small business,'' ``small organization,'' and ``small 
government jurisdiction'' as defined in 5 U.S.C. 601(3)-(5)).
    Second, to the extent that legal service organizations qualify as 
``small entities,'' any economic effects of this rule on such 
organizations would not be significant under the RFA. The rule will not 
economically impact representatives of aliens in contesting these 
penalties. It does not limit the fees they may charge or the number of 
cases a representative may ethically accept under the rules of 
professional responsibility. For example, the IFR's changes to the 
procedures for contesting a civil penalty do not change the overall 
requirement that aliens must respond to a civil penalty notice to 
challenge the penalty; rather the IFR simply changed the procedures for 
how that appeal is filed, in what time frame, and which U.S. Government 
officials are responsible for adjudicating the appeal. The IFR's 
changes to shorten the appeal period required legal service providers 
to adjust to these new timelines. The Departments expect, however, that 
legal service organizations have quickly acclimated to this change 
without substantial disruption. Indeed, the IFR was in effect for over 
a year, and the appeal rate increased under the IFR compared to the 
pre-IFR process for these civil penalties under 8 CFR part 280. Thus, 
any costs incurred in adapting to the IFR's timelines were not 
significant under the RFA. And the one change in this final rule to the 
IFR's provisions is not expected to increase such costs significantly 
(if at all) given that it discretely applies to demonstrated mail 
delays.
    In any event, this rule does not limit or otherwise dictate the 
fees that legal service providers may charge or the number of civil 
penalty cases the organization may ethically and competently accept. 
See Mid-Tex Elec. Co-op., Inc. v. FERC, 773 F.2d 327, 342-43 (D.C. Cir. 
1985) (concluding ``an agency may properly certify that no regulatory 
flexibility analysis is necessary when it determines that the rule will 
not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of small 
entities that are subject to the requirements of the rule'' and stating 
that legislative history of the RFA ``gives rise to an inference that 
Congress did not intend to require that every agency consider every 
indirect effect that any regulation might have on small businesses in 
any stratum of the national economy'').
    Moreover, any effects this rule may have on legal service 
organizations, other representatives of aliens, or other entities that 
provide services to aliens subject to civil penalty procedures are



indirect. The rule does not impose reporting, recordkeeping, staffing, 
fee, or other compliance requirements on those entities. Rather, it 
establishes procedures governing DHS's issuance and review of civil 
penalties and the process by which an alien may seek administrative 
review of a penalty determination. Although a legal service 
organization or other representative may choose to adjust its internal 
practices in response to procedures or timelines applicable to its 
clients, any such effects result from the entity's provision of 
services to affected aliens and not from a regulatory requirement 
imposed directly on that entity by this rule. The RFA does not require 
an agency to assess indirect effects on small entities that are not 
themselves subject to the rule's requirements. Accordingly, the 
Departments do not treat such indirect effects as regulatory compliance 
costs imposed on small entities by this rule.\62\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \62\ See U.S. Small Business Administration, Office of Advocacy, 
A Guide for Government Agencies: How to Comply with the Regulatory 
Flexibility Act 22-23 (Aug. 2017), https://advocacy.sba.gov/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/How-to-Comply-with-the-RFA.pdf (explaining 
that courts have held that the RFA requires analysis of impacts on 
small entities directly regulated by a rule, rather than indirect 
effects on entities that provide services to or otherwise interact 
with directly affected persons); Mid-Tex Elec. Coop., Inc., 773 F.2d 
at 342-43; see also Am. Trucking Ass'ns, Inc. v. EPA, 175 F.3d 1027, 
1044 (D.C. Cir. 1999).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

E. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995

    This final rule would not result in the expenditure by State, 
local, and Tribal governments, in the aggregate, or by the private 
sector, of $100 million or more in any one year, and it will not 
significantly or uniquely affect small governments. Therefore, no 
actions are deemed necessary under the provisions of the Unfunded 
Mandates Reform Act of 1995.

F. Congressional Review Act

    This final rule is not a ``rule'' as defined by the Congressional 
Review Act, Public Law 104-121. See 5 U.S.C. 804(3)(C) (defining the 
term ``rule'' to exclude ``any rule of agency organization, procedure, 
or practice that does not substantially affect the rights or 
obligations of non-agency parties''). The Departments will nonetheless 
submit this final rule to both houses of Congress and the Comptroller 
General before the rule takes effect.

G. Privacy Act

    In accordance with the Privacy Act of 1974, DHS/ICE-011 Criminal 
Arrest Records and Immigration Enforcement Records (CARIER) System of 
Records Notice provides privacy coverage supporting the final rule 
consistent with system purpose (``To track the process and results of 
administrative and criminal proceedings, including compliance with 
court orders and hearing dates, against individuals who are alleged to 
have violated the INA or other laws enforced by DHS'') and categories 
of records in the system. 89 FR 55638 (July 5, 2024).
    Additionally, DHS/CBP-023 Border Patrol Enforcement Records, System 
of Records Notice provides coverage supporting the final rule 
consistent with system purpose (``Enforcement-related data including: 
Case number, record number, and other data describing an event 
involving alleged violations of criminal, immigration, or other laws 
(location, date, time, event category, types of criminal or immigration 
law violations alleged, types of property involved, use of violence, 
weapons, or assault against DHS personnel or third parties, attempted 
escape, and other related information); CBP encounter management 
information, including: Category (event categories describe broad 
categories of criminal law enforcement, such as smuggling and human 
trafficking), agent or officer, location of officer or officer's 
vehicle, date/time initiated, date/time completed, assets used for 
encounter (bike, horse, vehicle, etc.), results of the encounter, and 
any agent or officer notes and comments.''), 81 FR 72601 (Oct. 20, 
2016).

H. National Environmental Policy Act

    DHS and its components analyze final actions to determine whether 
the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969 (``NEPA''), 42 U.S.C. 
4321 et seq., applies to them and, if so, what degree of analysis is 
required. DHS Directive 023-01 Rev. 01 \63\ and Instruction Manual 023-
01-001-01 Rev. 01 (``Instruction Manual'') establish the policies and 
procedures that DHS and its components use to comply with NEPA.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \63\ DHS, Implementation of the National Environmental Policy 
Act, Directive 023-01, Revision 01 (Oct. 31, 2014).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    NEPA allows Federal agencies to establish categories of actions 
(``categorical exclusions'') that experience has shown do not, 
individually or cumulatively, have a significant effect on the human 
environment and, therefore, do not require an environmental assessment 
(``EA'') or environmental impact statement (``EIS''). An agency is not 
required to prepare an EA or EIS for a proposed action ``if the 
proposed agency action is excluded pursuant to one of the agency's 
categorical exclusions.'' 42 U.S.C. 4336(a)(2). The Instruction Manual, 
Appendix A, lists the DHS Categorical Exclusions. For an action to be 
categorically excluded under DHS's Instruction Manual, the action must 
satisfy each of the following three conditions: (1) the entire action 
clearly fits within one or more of the categorical exclusions; (2) the 
action is not a piece of a larger action; and (3) no extraordinary 
circumstances exist that create the potential for a significant 
environmental effect.
    This final rule is categorically excluded from DHS's NEPA 
implementing procedures, because it satisfies all three relevant 
conditions. First, the Departments have determined that the IFR fits 
clearly within categorical exclusions A3(a) of DHS's Instruction 
Manual, Appendix A, for the promulgation of rules of a ``strictly 
administrative or procedural nature.'' This final rule merely changes 
the procedures that DHS and DOJ apply when assessing civil monetary 
penalties authorized under certain sections of the INA. This change in 
procedures does not result in a change in their environmental effect. 
Second, this final rule is a standalone rule and is not part of any 
larger action. Third, the Departments are not aware of any 
extraordinary circumstances that would cause a significant 
environmental impact. Therefore, this final rule is categorically 
excluded, and no further NEPA analysis or documentation is required.

I. Executive Order 13132 (Federalism)

    This final rule would not have substantial direct effects on the 
States, on the relationship between the national Government and the 
States, or on the distribution of power and responsibilities among the 
various levels of government. Therefore, in accordance with section 6 
of Executive Order 13132, the Departments believe that this FR would 
not have sufficient federalism implications to warrant the preparation 
of a federalism summary impact statement.

J. Paperwork Reduction Act

    This final rule does not impose any new reporting or recordkeeping 
requirements or call for a collection of information under the 
Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, 44 U.S.C. 3501, et seq.

List of Subjects in 8 CFR Part 281

    Administrative practice and procedure, Immigration, Penalties.



Amendments to the Regulations

DEPARTMENT OF HOMELAND SECURITY

    Accordingly, the interim final rule amending 8 CFR part 281, which 
was published at 90 FR 27439 on June 27, 2025, is adopted as final with 
the following change:
title: Imposition and Collection of Civil Penalties for Certain Immigration-Related Violations

PENSION BENEFIT GUARANTY CORPORATION

29 CFR Part 4044


Allocation of Assets in Single-Employer Plans; Interest 
Assumptions for Valuing Benefits

AGENCY: Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation.

ACTION: Final rule.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: This final rule amends the Pension Benefit Guaranty 
Corporation's regulation on Allocation of Assets in Single-Employer 
Plans to prescribe the spreads component of the interest assumption 
under the asset allocation regulation for plans with valuation dates of 
October 31, 2026-January 30, 2027. These interest assumptions are used 
for valuing benefits under terminating single-employer plans and for 
other purposes.

DATES: Effective October 31, 2026.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Jose Singer-Freeman ([email protected]), Attorney, Legislative and Regulatory Division, 
Office of the General Counsel, Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation, 
445 12th Street SW, Washington, DC 20024-2101, 202-229-5432. If you are 
deaf or hard of hearing, or have a speech disability, please dial 7-1-1 
to access telecommunications relay services.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: PBGC's regulation on Allocation of Assets in 
Single-Employer Plans (29 CFR part 4044) prescribes actuarial 
assumptions--including an interest assumption--for valuing benefits 
under terminating single-employer plans covered by title IV of the 
Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 (ERISA). The interest 
assumption is also posted on PBGC's website (www.pbgc.gov).
    PBGC uses the interest assumption in Sec.  4044.54 to determine the 
present value of annuities in an involuntary or distress termination of 
a single-employer plan under the asset allocation regulation. The 
assumptions in part 4044 of PBGC's regulations are also used in other 
situations where it is appropriate for liabilities to align with 
private sector group annuity prices. For example, PBGC's regulations on 
Notice, Collection, and Redetermination of Withdrawal Liability (29 CFR 
part 4219) and Duties of Plan Sponsor Following Mass Withdrawal (29 CFR 
part 4281) provide that these assumptions are used to value liabilities 
for purposes of determining withdrawn employers' reallocation liability 
in the event of a mass withdrawal from a multiemployer



plan. Multiemployer plans that receive special financial assistance 
under the regulation on Special Financial Assistance by PBGC (29 CFR 
part 4262) must, as a condition of receiving special financial 
assistance, use the interest assumption to determine withdrawal 
liability for a prescribed period. Additionally, plan sponsors are 
required to use some, or all of these assumptions for specified 
purposes (e.g., reporting benefit liabilities in filings required under 
PBGC's regulation on Annual Financial and Actuarial Information 
Reporting (29 CFR part 4010) or determining certain amounts to transfer 
to PBGC's Missing Participants Program on behalf of a missing 
participant of a terminating defined benefit plan under PBGC's 
regulation on Missing Participants (29 CFR part 4050)) and may use them 
for other purposes (e.g., to ensure that plan spinoffs comply with 
section 414(l) of the Internal Revenue Code).
    Part 4044 of PBGC's regulations provides that the interest 
assumption for part 4044 purposes is a yield curve (i.e., the ``4044 
yield curve'') that is based on a blend of two publicly available bond 
yield curves that is adjusted to the extent necessary so that the 
resulting liabilities align with group annuity prices. The adjustments 
are referred to as ``spreads.'' PBGC determines and publishes spreads 
quarterly based on survey data on pricing of private-sector group 
annuities. PBGC posts the 4044 yield curve on its website at 
www.pbgc.gov each month shortly after its underlying data becomes 
available. In addition, practitioners are able to determine the 4044 
yield curve as of the end of any month using the publicly available 
bond yield curves and the spreads specified in the regulation.
    This rule amends the regulation to specify the spreads used to 
determine the 4044 yield curve as of the last days of October, 
November, and December of 2026 (i.e., the ``fourth quarter 2026 
spreads''). Due to space constraints, table 1 to paragraph (e) shows 
spreads only for the most recent four quarters. Historical spreads are 
available on www.pbgc.gov, along with more recent spreads.

Need for Immediate Guidance

    PBGC has determined that notice of, and public comment on, this 
rule are impracticable, unnecessary, and contrary to the public 
interest. PBGC routinely updates the spreads component of the interest 
assumption in the asset allocation regulation so that the 4044 yield 
curve may be determined as soon as the underlying bond yield curves 
become available. These amendments are merely technical; they ensure 
that use of PBGC's interest assumption continues to yield liabilities 
in line with group annuity prices. Accordingly, PBGC finds that the 
public interest is best served by issuing this rule expeditiously, 
without an opportunity for notice and comment, and that good cause 
exists for making the assumptions set forth in this amendment effective 
less than 30 days after publication.
    PBGC has determined that this action is not a ``significant 
regulatory action'' under the criteria set forth in Executive Order 
12866.
    Because no general notice of proposed rulemaking is required for 
this amendment, the Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980 does not apply. 
See 5 U.S.C. 601(2).

List of Subjects in 29 CFR Part 4044

    Employee benefit plans, Pension insurance, Pensions.

    For the reasons stated in the preamble, PBGC amends 29 CFR part 
4044 as follows.
title: Allocation of Assets in Single-Employer Plans; Interest Assumptions for Valuing Benefits

AGENCY: Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), DOT.

ACTION: Final rule.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: The FAA is adopting a new airworthiness directive (AD) for 
certain Bombardier, Inc., Model BD-700-2A12 airplanes. This AD was 
prompted by



reports of low clearance in the right wing between the fuel line 
flexible coupling and the harness support bracket clip-nut, between the 
fuel line flexible coupling and hydraulic system, and between the 
hydraulic system and fuel vent tube. This AD requires rectifying the 
low clearance condition between the fuel line flexible coupling and the 
harness support bracket clip-nut, rectifying the low clearance 
condition between the fuel line flexible coupling and the hydraulic 
system, and doing an inspection for adequate clearance between the 
hydraulic system and the fuel vent tube and applicable on-conditions 
actions. The FAA is issuing this AD to address the unsafe condition on 
these products.

DATES: This AD is effective November 18, 2026.
    The Director of the Federal Register approved the incorporation by 
reference of a certain publication listed in this AD as of November 18, 
2026.

ADDRESSES: 
    AD Docket: You may examine the AD docket at regulations.gov under 
Docket No. FAA-2026-2289; or in person at Docket Operations between 9 
a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays. The AD 
docket contains this final rule, the mandatory continuing airworthiness 
information (MCAI), any comments received, and other information. The 
address for Docket Operations is U.S. Department of Transportation, 
Docket Operations, M-30, West Building Ground Floor, Room W12-140, 1200 
New Jersey Avenue SE, Washington, DC 20590.

     For Transport Canada material identified in this AD, 
contact Transport Canada, Transport Canada National Aircraft

Transport Canada website at tc.canada.ca/en/aviation.
     You may view this material at the FAA, Airworthiness

FAA, call 206-231-3195. It is also available at regulations.gov under

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: Joseph Catanzaro, Aviation Safety
