Trichloroethylene (TCE); Regulation Under the Toxic Substances 
Control Act (TSCA); Compliance Date Extensions

AGENCY: Environmental Protection Agency (EPA).

ACTION: Proposed rule.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA or Agency) is 
proposing to extend certain compliance dates applicable to certain 
entities subject to the regulation of trichloroethylene (TCE) under the 
Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) until December 31, 2027, including 
for certain chemical processors in meeting the prohibition compliance 
deadline for the processing of TCE, industrial and commercial use of 
TCE as a processing aid, and associated wastewater disposal; and for 
refrigerant manufacturers in meeting the compliance deadline for 
phasing down



TCE feedstock in the production of HFC-134a. This proposed compliance 
extension would allow for necessary and reasonable transition periods 
for regulated entities under TSCA section 6(d).

DATES: Comments must be received on or before November 13, 2026.

ADDRESSES: Submit your comments, identified by docket identification 
(ID) number EPA-HQ-OPPT-2026-7327, using the Federal eRulemaking Portal 
at https://www.regulations.gov. As required by the Administrative 
Procedure Act at 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(4), a plain language summary of the 
rule is available at https://www.regulations.gov. Follow the online 
instructions for submitting comments. Do not submit electronically any 
information you consider to be Confidential Business Information (CBI) 
or other information whose disclosure is restricted by statute. 
Additional instructions on commenting or visiting the docket, along 
with more information about dockets generally, is available at https://www.epa.gov/dockets/.

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT: 
    For technical information contact: Simon Regenold, Existing 
Chemicals Risk Management Division, Office of Pollution Prevention and 
Toxics, Environmental Protection Agency, 1200 Pennsylvania Ave. NW, 
Washington, DC 20460-0001; telephone number: (202) 566-1537; email 
address: [email protected].
    For general information contact: The TSCA Assistance Information 
Service Hotline, Goodwill Vision Enterprises, 422 South Clinton Ave., 
Rochester, NY 14620; telephone number: (800) 471-7127 or (202) 554-
1404; email address: [email protected].

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:

I. Executive Summary

A. Does this action apply to me?

    You may be potentially affected by this rule if you manufacture, 
process, distribute in commerce, use, or dispose of TCE, or products 
containing TCE. TSCA section 3(9) defines the term ``manufacture'' to 
mean ``to import into customs territory of the United States (as 
defined in general note 2 of the Harmonized Tariff Schedule of the 
United States), produce, or manufacture.'' Therefore, unless expressly 
stated otherwise, importers of TCE are subject to provisions regulating 
manufacture of TCE once the chemical enters the customs territory of 
the United States. Potentially affected entities may be included in the 
following lists of North American Industrial Classification System 
(NAICS) codes:
     Wood Window and Door Manufacturing (NAICS code 321911);
     Other Basic Inorganic Chemical Manufacturing (NAICS code 
325180);
     Medicinal and Botanical Manufacturing (NAICS code 325411);
     All Other Miscellaneous Chemical Product and Preparation 
Manufacturing (NAICS code 325998);
     Rubber and Plastics Hoses and Belting Manufacturing (NAICS 
code 326220);
     Rubber Product Manufacturing for Mechanical Use (NAICS 
code 326291); and
     Storage Battery Manufacturing (NAICS code 335911).

B. What is the agency's authority for taking this action?

    Under TSCA section 6(a) (15 U.S.C. 2605(a)), if EPA determines 
through a TSCA section 6(b) risk evaluation that a chemical substance 
presents an unreasonable risk of injury to health or the environment 
under the conditions of use, EPA must by rule apply one or more 
requirements listed in TSCA section 6(a) to the extent necessary so 
that the chemical substance or mixture no longer presents such risk 
under the conditions of use. EPA must specify compliance dates under 
TSCA section 6(d) (15 U.S.C. 2605(d)) for any TSCA section 6(a) rule. 
For TCE, EPA promulgated a final risk management rule under TSCA 
section 6(a) in 2024 (``2024 TCE Final Rule'') (Ref. 1) and an interim 
final rule extending compliance dates for two specific TCE conditions 
of use in 2025 (``2025 TCE Interim Final Rule'') (Ref. 2). Each of 
these TSCA section 6(a) actions include compliance dates pursuant to 
TSCA section 6(d). This action proposes to alter some of the compliance 
dates finalized in 2024 or finalized in subsequent amended rulemakings. 
Unless provided otherwise by law, agencies may change existing 
positions (e.g., reconsider, revise, or rescind prior rules) provided 
that they acknowledge the change in position, offer a reasoned 
explanation for the change, and take any serious reliance interests 
into account. See, e.g., FDA v. Wages & White Lion Invs., L.L.C., 145 
S. Ct. 898, 917 (2025); Encino Motorcars v. Navarro, 579 U.S. 211, 221 
(2016); FCC v. Fox Television Stations, Inc., 556 U.S. 502, 515 (2009); 
Motor Vehicle Mfrs. Ass'n v. State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co., 463 U.S. 
29 (1983). For the reasons set out in Units II and III of this 
preamble, EPA is proposing to revise select compliance dates. EPA is 
not aware of any serious reliance interests regarding this proposal.

C. What action is the agency taking?

    EPA is proposing to amend 40 CFR 751.305 and 40 CFR 751.313 to 
extend the prohibition compliance dates for processing TCE as a 
reactant/intermediate, processing for and industrial and commercial use 
of TCE as a processing aid in: process solvent used in battery 
manufacture, process solvent used in polymer fiber spinning, 
fluoroelastomer manufacture and Alcantara manufacture, extraction 
solvent used in caprolactam manufacture, precipitant used in beta-
cyclodextrin manufacture (hereinafter referred to as ``industrial and 
commercial use of TCE as a processing aid''), and the disposal of TCE 
from such processing or uses to industrial pre-treatment, industrial 
treatment, or publicly owned treatment works from December 18, 2026, to 
December 31, 2027.
    EPA is also proposing to amend 40 CFR 751.307 to extend the 
compliance timeframe for a step in the phase-out of processing TCE as 
an intermediate to manufacture HFC-134a. Specifically, EPA is proposing 
to extend the compliance deadline from June 7, 2027, to December 31, 
2027, for each manufacturer of HFC-134a via processing TCE as an 
intermediate to process TCE at an annual volume no greater than 75 
percent of the baseline.
    EPA is also proposing to amend 40 CFR 751.321 to amend the 
compliance deadline for downstream notification, and the text required 
to be present in the SDS, to accurately reflect the new prohibition 
compliance deadline for processing TCE as a reactant/intermediate, 
processing for and industrial and commercial use of TCE as a processing 
aid, and the disposal of TCE from such processing or uses to industrial 
pre-treatment, industrial treatment, or publicly owned treatment works. 
The new text would be required to be updated 30 days after the 
publication of the final rule.

D. Why is the Agency taking this action?

    EPA is proposing to address ongoing difficulties associated with 
compliance dates for the 2024 TCE Final Rule and 2025 Interim Final 
Rule for certain chemical processors and refrigerant manufacturers due 
to challenges with the implementation of the respective prohibition and 
phaseout, in order to provide a reasonable transition period to no 
longer process TCE. As detailed further in Unit III.A.1, soon after 
publication of the 2024 TCE Final Rule, chemical processors and 
chemical manufacturers explained to EPA that the prohibition on 
processing TCE as a



reactant/intermediate, and associated wastewater disposal, would cause 
significant hardships to the chemical manufacturing sector because 
byproduct TCE at levels above the regulatory threshold is regularly 
transferred between sites during the manufacture of other chemicals 
(Refs. 3, 4 and 5).
    EPA is also concerned about the prohibition on the processing for 
and industrial and commercial use of TCE as a processing aid with the 
same compliance date, as EPA believes it may also warrant a more 
reasonable compliance timeframe for chemical processing. Due to the 
regular transfer of byproduct TCE between sites during the manufacture 
of other chlorinated solvents, a prohibition on processing TCE on 
December 18, 2026, could have significant negative impacts on the 
production of other chlorinated solvents in the United States (Ref. 3).
    Separately, after publication of the 2024 TCE Final Rule, EPA 
received information from processors of TCE who manufacture HFC-134a 
about the continued need for high production of the refrigerant past 
the 2024 Final Rule's phaseout compliance dates (Ref. 6). As discussed 
further in Unit III.A.2, HFC-134a manufacturers now need a longer 
transition period so they can continue using a higher volume of TCE 
feedstock in order to meet demand for national security and critical 
infrastructure (Ref. 6). EPA's proposed amendment to the compliance 
deadline for downstream notification, and the text required to be 
present in SDSs, is being modified to accurately reflect the new 
prohibition compliance deadlines for processing being proposed in this 
action.

E. What are the incremental economic impacts?

    EPA evaluated the potential incremental economic impacts and 
determined that these changes would have minimal impacts on the 
estimated costs and benefits of the existing actions and would 
primarily result in a delay when those costs and benefits begin 
accruing. Quantified costs are expected to be the same as estimated in 
the 2024 TCE Final Rule but will not be incurred until the proposed 
compliance date extensions expire. Relying on the cost estimates in 
section 7 of the economic analysis of the TCE Final Rule (Ref. 7), EPA 
estimates that the proposed extension of compliance dates would result 
in present value cost savings of $0.62-0.65 million (2024$ in 2026), 
forgone health benefits of $3,795 to $7,844 (2025$), and annualized 
cost savings of $ 0.04-0.06 million (2024$ in 2026, 3%-7% discount rate 
respectively, 20-year time horizon). EPA notes that, in the event that 
alternative compliance timeframes are finalized in response to comments 
received on this proposal, these impacts would be modified accordingly 
(e.g., cost savings likely increase as the duration of the compliance 
timeframe extension increases).

II. Background

    On December 17, 2024, EPA published the 2024 TCE Final Rule under 
TSCA section 6(a) to address unreasonable risk to human health (89 FR 
102568) (FRL-8317-02-OCSPP). The 2024 TCE final rule prohibits the 
manufacture (including import), processing, and distribution in 
commerce of TCE for all uses (industrial, commercial, and consumer), 
while including longer compliance timeframes with reasonable worker 
protections for some processing and industrial and commercial uses 
until the prohibitions come into effect, so that TCE no longer presents 
an unreasonable risk to workers, occupational non-users, consumers, and 
bystanders.
    After publication of the 2024 TCE Final Rule, EPA was made aware of 
a previously unidentified use of TCE as a processing aid in the 
manufacture of nuclear fuel and promulgated an interim final rule in 
September of 2025 to amend the prohibition compliance deadlines until 
September 15, 2028, to provide a reasonable transition period for that 
use (Ref. 2). EPA additionally extended the deadlines for disposal of 
TCE to wastewater for processors of TCE as a reactant/intermediate and 
certain processors and industrial and commercial users of TCE as a 
processing aid to December 18, 2026, to match the prohibition 
compliance date for these processing conditions of use.
    EPA received three TSCA section 21 petitions concerning the 2024 
TCE Final Rule: from American Chemistry Council (ACC) on May 29, 2025 
(withdrawn September 19, 2025) (Refs. 3 and 8); from PPG Industries, 
Inc. on March 24, 2025 (withdrawn June 11, 2025) (Refs. 4 and 9); and 
from the Alliance for a Strong U.S. Battery Sector and Microporous on 
April 30, 2025 (withdrawn July 25, 2025) (Refs. 5 and 10). While these 
petitions were withdrawn, EPA recognizes the potential merits of 
certain requests contained in these petitions and is planning to 
address them in amendments to the rule through a future notice-and-
comment rulemaking.
    After issuing the TCE Final Rule, EPA received petitions for review 
that were consolidated in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third 
Circuit. EPA has since announced its intention to reconsider the TCE 
Final Rule.

III. Provisions of This Proposed Rule

    For any TSCA section 6(a) rule, EPA must specify mandatory 
compliance dates that are ``as soon as practicable,'' while allowing 
for ``a reasonable transition period.'' 15 U.S.C. 2605(d)(1)(B) and 
(E). EPA acknowledges that it is proposing a change in position from 
the 2024 TCE Final Rule and the 2025 TCE Interim Final Rule. EPA 
intended that the compliance timeframes in these rules would be as soon 
as practicable while allowing for a reasonable transition period (see 
Unit I.E of the 2024 TCE Final Rule, and Unit III of the 2025 TCE 
Interim Final Rule). However, the Agency did not fully anticipate the 
challenges that certain entities are now experiencing: for chemical 
processors in meeting the prohibition compliance deadline for the 
processing of TCE, industrial and commercial use of TCE as a processing 
aid, and associated wastewater disposal (Unit III.A); and for 
refrigerant manufacturers in meeting the compliance deadline for 
phasing down TCE feedstock in the production of HFC-134a (Unit III.B). 
Accordingly, EPA proposes that the compliance dates detailed in this 
Unit would be more feasible and workable, and compliant with EPA's 
obligations under TSCA section 6(d) for TCE, than those finalized in 
2024 or amended in 2025.

A. Processing TCE as a Reactant/Intermediate, Industrial and Commercial 
Use of TCE as a Processing Aid, and Their Associated Wastewater 
Disposal

    EPA is proposing to amend the compliance deadline for the 
prohibition on processing TCE as a reactant/intermediate and the 
industrial and commercial use of TCE as a processing aid in certain 
chemical manufacturing to December 31, 2027. EPA is also proposing to 
amend the compliance deadline for the prohibition on the associated 
disposal of TCE to wastewater by processors of TCE and processors and 
industrial and commercial users of TCE as a processing aid to December 
31, 2027.
    In the 2024 TCE Final Rule, EPA finalized a prohibition on 
processing and distributing in commerce (including making available) of 
TCE as of June 16, 2025 (40 CFR 751.305(b)(2)). EPA also finalized 
extended phaseouts for processing of TCE as a reactant/intermediate and 
processing for and the industrial and commercial use of TCE as a 
processing aid to continue until December 2026 (40 CFR



751.305(b)(9)(i)), and an exclusion from all prohibitions and 
restrictions for processing (including reuse) of TCE as a byproduct 
when that TCE byproduct is processed within a site-limited, physically 
enclosed system that is part of the same overall manufacturing process 
from which the byproduct TCE was generated (40 CFR 751.301(c)).
    After the publication of the 2024 TCE Final Rule, EPA received a 
Section 21 petition from the ACC regarding the exclusion on byproduct 
reprocessing and the wastewater disposal associated with processing TCE 
(Ref. 3). In response, in the 2025 TCE Interim Final Rule EPA amended 
the compliance deadline from September 15, 2025, to December 18, 2026, 
for the prohibition on disposal of TCE to wastewater for processors of 
TCE as a reactant/intermediate and processors for and industrial and 
commercial users of TCE as a processing aid for certain industrial 
sectors. This action aligned the disposal prohibition with the December 
18, 2026, prohibition on such uses in the 2024 Final Rule. This change 
responded to the concerns raised to EPA that processing conditions of 
use also involve disposal of TCE to wastewater that inadvertently was 
not similarly subject to the same compliance deadline (Ref. 2).
    Through the Section 21 Petition and subsequent engagement, EPA was 
made aware after the 2024 final rule that byproduct TCE that is present 
in feedstock streams is sent by railcar between facilities to be 
further processed. This usually occurs between facilities of the same 
company, where one site has chemical manufacturing capabilities that 
another does not (Refs. 3, 8, 11 and 13). If the prohibition on 
processing TCE goes into effect on December 18, 2026, then the 
processing of byproduct TCE that travels between sites will be 
prohibited, along with disposal of this byproduct TCE to wastewater. 
Disposal of this byproduct TCE would therefore require incineration; if 
all byproduct TCE that is currently reused in a different facility must 
be incinerated, it would cause significant implementation concerns, 
including exceeded permit limitations and potential facility closures. 
Petitioners have indicated that the inability to send unpurified 
chlorinated solvent product streams with byproduct TCE between 
facilities would significantly disrupt the national supply chain by 
disproportionately impacting operations in the manufacture of other 
chlorinated solvents which unintentionally produce TCE as a byproduct 
(importantly perchloroethylene, carbon tetrachloride, methylene 
chloride, and 1,2-dichloroethane) in the United States (Refs. 3, 8, 11 
and 13). In the 2024 TCE Final Rule and 2025 TCE Interim Final Rule EPA 
did not anticipate these implications.
    As such, EPA is proposing to amend the compliance deadline for the 
prohibition on processing TCE as a reactant/intermediate and the 
wastewater disposal associated with such processing TCE until December 
31, 2027, so that regulated entities would not be held in non-
compliance with the relevant requirements in the 2024 TCE Final Rule 
and the 2025 TCE Interim Final Rule. EPA is also proposing to amend the 
compliance deadline for the prohibition on industrial and commercial 
use of TCE as a processing aid because EPA believes, based on ACC's 
comments, that this condition of use also needs a longer transition 
period. These ongoing difficulties (see Unit I.D.2) in complying with 
the prohibitions and restrictions of the TCE final rule, particularly 
the need to transfer byproduct chemicals off site, warrant a longer 
reasonable transition period for this group of uses than EPA expected 
in 2024 or 2025. Given the two years provided for this compliance date 
in the 2024 TCE rule, EPA considers this extension of no more than one 
year to be appropriate because it is ``as soon as practicable,'' while 
allowing for ``a reasonable transition period'' (15 U.S.C. 
2605(d)(1)(B) and (E)). Separately, EPA has initiated a rulemaking 
under RIN 2070-AL41 through which the Agency is reconsidering various 
elements of the 2024 TCE Final Rule, including various workplace 
exposure controls and prohibitions on certain industrial and commercial 
uses.

B. Processing TCE as an Intermediate for the Manufacture of HFC-134a

    EPA is proposing to amend the compliance deadline for the first 
phaseout reduction of the processing of TCE as an intermediate for the 
manufacture of HFC-134a (1,1,1,2-tetrafluroethane; CASRN 811-97-2). 
Under the 2024 TCE Final Rule, stakeholders processing TCE to 
manufacture HFC-134a would have to cut the amount of TCE feedstock they 
use to 75% of their baseline by June 7, 2027. EPA is proposing to amend 
the compliance deadline so that this reduction in TCE feedstock would 
instead occur by December 31, 2027.
    At the time of publication of the 2024 TCE Final Rule, the public 
comments EPA had received from the regulated community supported this 
phaseout schedule. After the publication of the 2024 TCE Final Rule, 
EPA received new information from Orbia Fluor & Energy Materials 
(Orbia) regarding the continued need for HFC-134a for military, 
industrial, and medical applications at rates higher than the 2024 TCE 
final rule phaseout accounted for (Refs. 6 and 12). Since the 
publication of the 2024 TCE Final Rule, the 2024 TCE final rule 
phaseout is no longer in alignment with the AIM Act phasedown because 
Orbia has received more allowances and anticipates receiving further 
allowances under the AIM Act to manufacture HFC-134a than initially 
anticipated (Ref. 6). The demand for HFC-134a from users in critical 
infrastructure and national security applications is now expected to 
remain significant through the early 2030s (Ref. 12).
    By proposing to amend the compliance deadline for the first 
phasedown reduction in TCE feedstock volume to be in December instead 
of June 2027, EPA intends to allow time for a reasonable transition 
period given the changes in AIM Act allowances received for HFC-134a 
manufacture. This new compliance deadline will allow manufacturers of 
HFC-134a to meet needs from critical infrastructure and national 
security users while allowing for a transition that has a reasonable 
timeframe and will not produce unintended negative consequences. It is 
important to amend this compliance date because if the June 2027 date 
is not changed, HFC-134a manufacturers must otherwise begin curtailing 
their production of the refrigerant before the demand abates, 
negatively impacting critical infrastructure and national security 
application needs. Given the two and a half years provided for this 
compliance date in the 2024 TCE rule, EPA considers this extension of 
no more than 6 and a half months to be appropriate because it is ``as 
soon as practicable,'' while allowing for ``a reasonable transition 
period'' (15 U.S.C. 2605(d)(1)(B) and (E)).
    Separately, EPA has initiated a rulemaking under RIN 2070-AL41 
through which the Agency is reconsidering various elements of the 2024 
TCE final rule, including stakeholders' larger issues with the use of 
TCE for HFC-134a manufacturing.

C. Downstream Notification

    In keeping with the proposed new prohibition compliance deadline 
for processing TCE as a reactant/intermediate in chemical 
manufacturing, processing for and industrial and commercial use of TCE 
as a processing aid in certain chemical manufacturing, and the disposal 
of TCE



from such processing or uses to industrial pre-treatment, industrial 
treatment, or publicly owned treatment works, EPA also proposes to 
amend the downstream notification requirements of the 2024 TCE Final 
Rule to accurately reflect the restrictions on TCE. Accurate downstream 
notification is necessary to spread awareness throughout the supply 
chain of the restrictions on use of TCE under TSCA, as well as provide 
information to commercial end users about allowable uses of TCE until 
the prohibition compliance dates. EPA recognizes that the 2024 TCE 
Final Rule and 2025 Interim Final Rule compliance deadlines for 
updating the SDS of June 16, 2025, and December 16, 2025, respectively, 
have already passed and as such, manufacturers, processors, and 
distributors in commerce of TCE would need to update or amend their SDS 
shortly after doing so already. EPA proposes that 30 days from the 
publication of the final rule is a practicable time to update the SDS 
for manufacturers, processors, and distributors in commerce of TCE.

IV. Requests for Comment

    EPA is requesting public comment on all aspects of this proposal. 
EPA notes that the proposed compliance dates may be subject to change 
depending on the timing of the final rulemaking and public comment.
    1. EPA requests comment on the changes proposed in this action, 
including whether stakeholders have any serious reliance interests that 
may be impacted and, if so, how such interests should be accounted for 
in any final action.
    2. EPA requests comment on a stakeholder requested alternative 
compliance deadline of December 18, 2028, for the TCE uses that this 
rule proposes to extend, and whether there is a basis that this longer 
deadline, compared to the proposed date of December 31, 2027, would be 
``as soon as practicable,'' while allowing for ``a reasonable 
transition period.'' (15 U.S.C. 2605(d)(1)(B) and (E)) (Ref. 13).
    3. EPA requests comment on an expedited (e.g., 14 day) or immediate 
effective date of this extension rule because the December 18, 2026, 
compliance deadline is fast approaching.

VI. Statutory and Executive Order Reviews

    Additional information about these statutes and Executive Orders 
can be found at https://www.epa.gov/laws-regulations/laws-and-executive-orders.

A. Executive Order 12866: Regulatory Planning and Review and Executive 
Order 13563: Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review

    This action is a significant regulatory action that was submitted 
to the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review under Executive 
Orders 12866 (58 FR 51735, October 4, 1993) and 13563 (76 FR 3821, 
January 21, 2011). Any changes made in response to Executive Order 
12866 review have been documented in the docket.

B. Executive Order 14192: Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation

    This action is expected to be an Executive Order 14192 deregulatory 
action because the action is expected to result in cost savings, as 
discussed in Unit I.E.

C. Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA)

    This action does not impose any new information collection 
activities or burden subject to OMB review and approval under the PRA, 
44 U.S.C. 3501 et seq. However, this action defers the costs associated 
with paperwork and



recordkeeping burden for an existing information collection because the 
delayed compliance dates alter the time horizon of the collection's 
analysis. Burden is defined in 5 CFR 1320.3(b). OMB has previously 
approved the information collection activities contained in the 
existing regulations and associated burden under OMB Control No. 2070-
0232 (EPA ICR No. 2775.02). An agency may not conduct or sponsor, and a 
person is not required to respond to a collection of information that 
requires OMB approval under PRA, unless it has been approved by OMB and 
displays a currently valid OMB control number. The OMB control numbers 
for EPA's regulations in title 40 of the CFR, after appearing in the 
Federal Register, are listed in 40 CFR part 9, and included on the 
related collection instrument or form, if applicable.

D. Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA)

    I certify that this action will not have a significant economic 
impact on a substantial number of small entities under the RFA, 5 
U.S.C. 601 et seq. In making this determination, EPA concludes that the 
impact of concern for this action is any significant adverse economic 
impact on small entities, and the Agency is certifying that this rule 
will not have a significant economic impact on a substantial number of 
small entities because the rule relieves regulatory burden on the small 
entities subject to the rule. This action would extend the compliance 
date for the prohibition on processing TCE as a reactant/intermediate 
and the industrial and commercial use of TCE as a processing aid and 
their associated disposal until 2028, the compliance date for the first 
phase of the phaseout of TCE processing in the manufacture of HFC-134a 
until 2028, and the compliance deadline for downstream notification and 
the text required to be present in SDSs for TCE starting 30 days after 
publication of the final rule. We have therefore concluded that this 
action will relieve regulatory burden for all directly regulated small 
entities.

E. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (UMRA)

    This action does not contain an unfunded mandate as described in 
UMRA, 2 U.S.C. 1531-1538, and does not significantly or uniquely affect 
small governments. The costs involved in this action are estimated not 
to exceed $187 million in 2024$ ($100 million in 1995$, adjusted for 
inflation using the GDP implicit price deflator) or more in any one 
year. EPA estimates the annualized cost savings of extending compliance 
dates in this action to be $0.04-0.06 million.

F. Executive Order 13132: Federalism

    This action does not have federalism implications as specified in 
Executive Order 13132 (64 FR 43255, August 10, 1999) because it will 
not have substantial direct effects on the States, on the relationship 
between the national government and the States, or on the distribution 
of power and responsibilities among the various levels of government.

G. Executive Order 13175: Consultation and Coordination With Indian 
Tribal Governments

    This action does not have Tribal implications as specified in 
Executive Order 13175 (65 FR 67249, November 9, 2000) because it does 
not have substantial direct effects on one or more Indian Tribes, on 
the relationship between the Federal Government and Indian Tribes, or 
on the distribution of power and responsibilities between the Federal 
Government and Indian Tribes. Thus, Executive Order 13175 does not 
apply to this action.

H. Executive Order 13045: Protection of Children From Environmental 
Health Risks and Safety Risks

    Executive Order 13045 (62 FR 19885, April 23, 1997) directs federal 
agencies to include an evaluation of the health and safety effects of 
the planned regulation on children in federal health and safety 
standards and explain why the regulation is preferable to potentially 
effective and reasonably feasible alternatives. This action is not 
subject to Executive Order 13045 because it is not a significant 
regulatory action under section 3(f)(1) of Executive Order 12866, and 
because the EPA does not believe the environmental health or safety 
risks addressed by this action present a disproportionate risk to 
children.
    Nevertheless, as in the 2024 TCE final rule, EPA's Policy on 
Children's Health applies to this action. The environmental health or 
safety risks addressed by the 2024 TCE final rule present a 
disproportionate risk to children due to TCE's developmental toxicity, 
as described in Unit VIII.G of that rule. However, this action would 
not alter the requirements of the final rule promulgated in 2024 that 
addresses the unreasonable risks presented by TCE under its conditions 
of use. Rather, this action would delay when entities must comply with 
certain provisions in order to provide a reasonable transition period 
for compliance as required under TSCA section 6(d)(1)(E). Information 
on how the Policy was applied in the 2024 TCE final rule and on that 
action's health and risk assessments is available under Units II.C., 
II.D. and IV.A of the final rule as well as in the 2020 Risk 
Evaluation, and the Economic Analysis for the final rule.

I. Executive Order 13211: Actions Concerning Regulations That 
Significantly Affect Energy Supply, Distribution, or Use

    This action is not a ``significant energy action'' as defined in 
Executive Order 13211 (66 FR 28355, May 22, 2001) because it is not 
likely to have a significant adverse effect on the supply, distribution 
or use of energy.

J. National Technology Transfer and Advancement Act (NTTAA)

    This action does not involve technical standards under NTTAA 
section 12(d), 15 U.S.C. 272. EPA determined that the 2024 TCE final 
rule involves environmental monitoring or measurement for occupational 
inhalation exposures and, consistent with the Agency's Performance 
Based Measurement System, decided not to require the use of specific, 
prescribed analytic methods. However, this action would simply extend 
compliance dates as described in Unit III.

There is no appeal under this chapter from the termination of refugee status by USCIS. Upon termination of refugee status, USCIS will process the alien under sections 235, 240, and 241 of the Act. Removing 30-Day Refugee Termination Notice

AGENCY: U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, Department of 
Homeland Security (DHS).

ACTION: Interim final rule.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------

SUMMARY: This interim final rule (IFR) amends Department of Homeland 
Security (DHS) regulations to expedite termination of refugee status 
when DHS determines an alien was not a refugee within the meaning of 
section 101(a)(42) of the Immigration and Nationality Act at the time

changes aim to restore integrity to the immigration system, mitigate 
risks to national security and public safety, and prevent fraud and 
exploitation.

II. Executive Summary

A. Purpose of the Regulatory Action

    The purpose of this rulemaking is to shorten the termination notice 
period in order to mitigate potential risks posed by aliens admitted to 
the United States as refugees when, in fact, they were not eligible for 
refugee classification at the time of admission. Those who are 
improperly admitted may not have their identity fully confirmed and 
vetted due to an incomplete record, and as such pose a risk to program 
integrity and may pose a risk to national security and public safety. A 
review of refugee processing policies and procedures implemented under 
the Biden administration indicates an alarming erosion of integrity 
leading to aliens being admitted to the United States as refugees when 
their identities, eligibility for refugee classification, and 
admissibility were determined based on incomplete records.\1\ 
Operational guidance implemented during this period allowed officers to 
forgo typical lines of inquiry, sacrificing the caliber and efficacy of 
the refugee interview, a critical screening component of the refugee 
adjudication process.\2\ The priority of expediency over quality 
encouraged a lack of robust interviews. Certain questions to ensure 
that aliens were eligible for refugee status prior to admission to the 
United States were omitted and this increased the risk of ineligible 
aliens being approved for refugee classification and subsequently 
admitted to the United States. This is supported by a recent 
preliminary review of admitted refugees residing in Minnesota who were 
interviewed, approved, and admitted during the Biden administration. 
For the majority of these reviewed cases, the evidence was insufficient 
to establish that the principal applicant met all of the required 
elements of the refugee definition.\3\ The goal was to have as many 
refugees as practicable enter the United States to meet President 
Biden's ceiling for refugee admissions and in order to accomplish this, 
a number of requirements for ensuring a thorough examination and 
assessment of eligibility were reduced or removed.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \1\ Refugee applicants have the burden to establish their 
identity for purposes of immigration benefits. Identity is a 
critical element in refugee adjudications because it helps verify 
that the applicant is who they say they are. Identity can be 
established through the collection of biometrics, documentary 
evidence, and testimony. In the refugee context, testimony is a 
primary source of evidence. It provides valuable information about 
the applicant's background, familial relations, past experiences, 
and associations which provide context in establishing who the 
applicant is as a person and whether they are eligible for the 
benefit sought. An applicant's capacity to demonstrate their 
identity to the satisfaction of the U.S. Government, ensuring that 
officials are confident in the applicant's identity, is a necessary 
step in determining eligibility for the immigration benefit 
requested.
    \2\ Cases of resettled refugees residing in Minnesota were 
reviewed as part of an initial pilot operation cohort to reinforce 
recent joint antifraud enforcement actions, such as Operation Twin 
Shield, conducted with other law enforcement partners including ICE 
and the FBI.
    \3\ See USCIS Announces Results of Operation Twin Shield, a 
Large-Scale Immigration Fraud Investigation (Sept. 30, 2025), 
https://www.uscis.gov/newsroom/news-releases/uscis-announces-results-of-operation-twin-shield-a-large-scale-immigration-fraud-investigation.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    This raises concerns about the integrity of the refugee program and 
calls into question the eligibility for refugee status of aliens 
admitted to the United States during this time. As detailed below in 
this preamble, several policy decisions were implemented that 
significantly reduced the integrity measures within the refugee 
program. These changes resulted in an increase in the number of refugee 
interviews conducted per officer each day, with less comprehensive 
elicitation of testimony from applicants. These adjustments limited the 
ability of refugee officers, and the U.S. government to accurately 
determine whether an applicant's identity was properly established, 
assess potential national security or public safety concerns, and 
verify whether the applicant met the definition of a refugee.
    To protect U.S. interests and public safety, USCIS must act swiftly 
when DHS determines that an alien did not meet the refugee definition 
and was not entitled to refugee status at the time of admission. 
Shortening the NOIT response period enables DHS to respond rapidly to 
such findings. Allowing a longer notice period could provide 
opportunities for aliens to evade enforcement or engage in harmful 
activities. For example, the Fraud Detection and National Security 
(FDNS) Directorate investigated cases where refugees were later 
identified as members of armed groups or had concealed extremist 
affiliations. In one case, a refugee was found to have participated in 
human rights abuses with the Liberian Armed Forces during the Liberian 
Civil War. In another case, a refugee was found to have misrepresented 
his involvement with the Oromo Liberation Front (OLF), an armed group 
in Ethiopia. Social media checks indicated numerous pro-OLF activities 
and pro-OLF and radical violent rhetoric posted prior to his admission 
to the United States as a refugee. These cases demonstrate that when 
credible evidence of national security or public safety concerns arises 
after a refugee's admission, USCIS may be unable to initiate removal 
proceedings until the termination process is complete. Therefore, 
reducing the response period to ten days after issuance of a NOIT 
allows USCIS to address such threats more quickly and effectively, 
restoring integrity to the immigration system.
    To be eligible for admission to the United States as a refugee, an 
alien must establish, among other things, that they meet the definition 
of ``refugee'' as defined in section 101(a)(42)(A) and (B)



of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42)(A) and (B), which includes the 
requirement that they are not a persecutor. When USCIS discovers after 
an alien's admission to the United States that they should not have 
been admitted because they did not meet the refugee definition and 
therefore the eligibility requirements for refugee classification at 
the time of admission, it is important to protect the integrity of the 
American immigration system by taking whatever steps are legally 
available, including ensuring that the alien is removed from the United 
States as quickly as possible where there is a legal basis to do so. 
There is an inherent risk to national security and public safety when 
an alien's identity has not been fully established. Therefore, the 
ability to streamline refugee status termination, where appropriate, 
contributes immediately to the safety of the American people and the 
integrity of the lawful U.S. immigration system.
    The current notice and response process for terminating refugee 
status upon determination that the alien was not a refugee at the time 
of their admission is inefficient and compromises the security and 
safety of the United States. Providing 30 days to respond to a NOIT, 
instead of a 10-day response period, allows ineligible aliens more time 
to retain immigration benefits to which they are not entitled, 
undermining the integrity of the U.S. immigration system and national 
interests of the United States. Moreover, when an alien retains a 
status he or she is not entitled to, while also being inadequately 
vetted with insufficient information as to their true identity, there 
is a risk to American society's safety and security.

B. Legal Authority

    The Secretary of Homeland Security's (Secretary) authority for the 
regulatory amendment made in this IFR is found in various provisions of 
the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), 8 U.S.C. 1101 et seq., and 
the Homeland Security Act of 2002 (HSA), Public Law 107-296, 116 Stat. 
2135 (codified in part at 6 U.S.C. 101 et seq.). Under the INA, the 
Secretary has authority over the admission, termination of status, 
removal, and adjustment of status of refugees. See, e.g., INA 207, 209, 
8 U.S.C. 1157, 1159.\4\ Most importantly, section 207(c)(4) of the INA, 
8 U.S.C. 1157(c)(4), allows the Secretary to terminate the refugee 
status of any alien and the alien's spouse or children if the Secretary 
determines that the alien ``was not in fact a refugee . . . at the time 
of the alien's admission'' and expressly authorizes the Secretary to 
issue regulations governing the procedures for such terminations. The 
Secretary has delegated the authority to grant refugee status and to 
adjust or terminate such status to USCIS.\5\

C. Summary of the Regulatory Action

    Through this IFR, DHS is amending 8 CFR 207.9 to change the 30-day

terminated by USCIS to a 10-day notice-and-response period.

III. Background and Purpose

A. Initial Refugee Processing

    Refugee status in the United States is a highly sought after 
immigration benefit for displaced persons throughout the world due in 
part to the benefits it bestows as well as a pathway to permanent 
status. Resettlement to the United States through the United States 
Refugee Admissions Program (USRAP) is a multi-step process involving 
several agency partners. The U.S. Department of State (State) leads the 
annual



consultations process, funds and oversees refugee resettlement 
activities, contracts with the non-governmental organizations that 
provide pre- and post-USCIS interview support, and facilitates the 
Priority 1 referrals to the USRAP process. After an alien is determined 
to have access to the USRAP, they may file a Form I-590, Registration 
for Classification as Refugee.\10\ Applications for refugee 
classification are primarily processed overseas and adjudicated by 
USCIS Refugee Officers who determine whether an alien meets the refugee 
definition and is otherwise eligible for resettlement to the United 
States. Under United States law, to be eligible for refugee 
classification an applicant must establish that he or she:
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \10\ Form I-590, Registration for Classification as Refugee, OMB 
No. 1615-0068 (Nov. 3, 2025), available at https://www.uscis.gov/sites/default/files/document/forms/i-590.pdf.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

     is located outside the country of his or her nationality; 
\11\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \11\ The Refugee Act of 1980 amended this requirement and 
allowed for in-country processing for certain refugees that the 
President specifies.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

     is of special humanitarian concern to the United States;
     was persecuted or fears persecution due to race, religion, 
nationality, political opinion, or membership in a particular social 
group;
     is not firmly resettled in another country; and
     is admissible as an immigrant to the United States.
    See INA 101(a)(42), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42); INA 207(c)(1), 8 U.S.C. 
1157(c)(1).
    A refugee does not include anyone who ordered, incited, assisted, 
or otherwise participated in the persecution of any person on account 
of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social 
group, or political opinion. Id. USCIS officers make a determination of 
eligibility for refugee classification based on the above elements of 
eligibility.
    USCIS approval of an application for refugee classification 
authorizes U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) to admit the alien 
``conditionally'' as a refugee upon arrival at a U.S. port of entry 
within four months of the date of such approval.\12\ U.S. Department of 
Health and Human Services, the Office of Refugee Resettlement provides 
resettlement assistance, that includes employment training, English 
language training, cash assistance (in a manner that promotes early 
self-sufficiency), and job placement, to the aliens admitted as 
refugees to the United States.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \12\ 8 CFR 207.4 (authority for CBP to admit aliens approved for 
refugee classification).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Derivatives of the principal refugee applicant may include the 
spouse of a principal refugee and their unmarried children under the 
age of 21.\13\ Derivative family members may be included in the initial 
application for refugee status or petitioned for after the principal 
refugee's arrival to the United States. Id. For derivatives to be 
admitted to the United States as refugees, they must establish that 
they are admissible and not subject to the persecutor bar but are not 
required to prove that they meet the refugee definition or any of its 
elements, such as past persecution or a well-founded fear of future 
persecution.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \13\ INA 207(c)(2), 8 U.S.C. 1157(c)(2).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    In addition to resettlement in the United States, refugees receive 
employment authorization as soon as they arrive in the United 
States.\14\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \14\ 8 CFR 274a.12(a)(3).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

B. Termination of Refugee Status

    The sole basis for USCIS to terminate the status of an alien 
conditionally admitted to the United States as a refugee is if USCIS 
determines that the alien did not meet the definition of a refugee at 
the time of admission to the United States.\15\ No other ground of 
termination is specified under the law. An alien who did not, in fact, 
meet the refugee definition at the time of admission would have been 
inadmissible, and once that status is terminated, will generally lack 
legal grounds to remain in the United States.\16\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \15\ INA 207(c)(4), 8 U.S.C. 1157(c)(4).
    \16\ See 8 CFR. 207.9 (permitting termination of refugee status 
only if USCIS determines the alien ``was not a refugee'' within the 
meaning of INA section 101(a)(42) at the time of admission); INA 
section 237(a)(1)(A), 8 U.S.C. 1227(a)(1)(A) (making deportable any 
noncitizen who was inadmissible ``at the time of entry''), 
incorporating, inter alia, INA section 212(a)(7)(A)(i)(I), 8 U.S.C. 
1182(a)(7)(A)(i)(I) (inadmissibility for lack of valid immigrant 
entry document).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    The determination to terminate refugee status because the alien did 
not meet the definition of a refugee at the time of his or her 
admission to the United States applies solely to principal refugees and 
not to derivative refugees. In order to be eligible for refugee status, 
principal applicants must meet the requirements of the refugee 
definition in INA 101(a)(42), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42), must be admissible 
to the United States, and must qualify under one of the designated 
USRAP processing priorities.\17\ USCIS may in turn terminate a 
derivative refugee's status if the principal's status is 
terminated.\18\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \17\ INA 291, 207(c)(1), 8 U.S.C. 1361, 1157(c)(1).
    \18\ See 8 CFR 207.7(d) and 207.9, see also INA 207(c)(4), 8 
U.S.C. 1157(c)(4) providing that the ``refugee status of any alien 
(and of the spouse or child of the alien), may be terminated'' 
(emphasis added).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Refugee status can only be terminated while the alien remains in 
refugee status and has not yet adjusted to lawful permanent resident 
(LPR) status or naturalized.\19\ However, if USCIS has rescinded an 
alien's LPR status under INA 246, 8 U.S.C. 1156, an alien admitted as a 
refugee reverts to the prior refugee status and his or her refugee 
status can be terminated if the basis for termination meets the 
statutory requirements.\20\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \19\ Matter of D-K-, 25 I&N Dec. 761 (BIA 2012); Matter of 
Smriko, 23 I&N Dec. 836 (BIA 2005).
    \20\ USCIS Policy Manual, Volume 7, Part Q, Rescission of Lawful 
Permanent Residence, https://www.uscis.gov/policy-manual/volume-7-part-q (last visited Jan. 22, 2026).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    When USCIS determines that a principal refugee was not a refugee as 
defined in INA 101(a)(42), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(42), at the time of 
admission, USCIS initiates termination of refugee status. The former 
Immigration and Naturalization Service first implemented regulations 
governing the termination of refugee status following the enactment of 
the Refugee Act of 1980, and the process has remained substantively 
unchanged in the 45 years since then.\21\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \21\ 45 FR 37392 (June 2, 1980) (interim final rule); 46 FR 
45116 (Sept. 10, 1981) (final rule). INS and DHS have made only 
minimal changes to 8 CFR 207.9 since it was first published. 
Following the enactment of IIRIRA, INS updated the references to the 
types of removal proceedings that may apply following a termination 
of refugee status. See also, Inspection and Expedited Removal of 
Aliens; Detention and Removal of Aliens; Conduct of Removal 
Proceedings; Asylum Procedures, 62 FR 10312, 10337 (Mar. 6, 1997). 
Other minor changes included renumbering from 207.8 to 207.9 and 
including updated DHS service procedures. Procedures for Filing a 
Derivative Petition (Form I-730) for a Spouse and Unmarried Children 
of a Refugee/Asylee, 63 FR 3792 (Jan. 27, 1998); Immigration 
Benefits Business Transformation, Increment I, 76 FR 53764, 53784 
(Aug. 29, 2011).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    USCIS issues a Notice of Intent to Terminate (NOIT) prior to 
termination.\22\ In the NOIT, USCIS outlines the specific basis or 
bases for the termination, such as a determination by USCIS that the 
harm the alien experienced or feared was not on account of a protected 
ground or, for example, that the alien had another nationality or legal 
status in another country such that they did not qualify as a refugee 
from the claimed country. The NOIT further informs the alien of his or 
her right to offer written or oral evidence in support of his or her 
refugee claim and in opposition to the proposed termination. Prior to 
this IFR, 8 CFR 207.9 provided that the alien has a 30-day period to

Errant Refugee Admissions

Refugee Act of 1980. INA 207(a)(2), 8 U.S.C. 1157(a)(2). During 
President Trump's first term he reduced the number each fiscal year 
(FY) (and additionally COVID-19 drastically reduced actual admissions) 
in order to review the program's integrity and make sure proper 
screening and vetting measures were in place and in order to shift 
resources to deal with the crisis at the U.S. southern border.\28\

    The majority of these changes impacted the quality of the refugee 
interview required under regulation.\33\ The main reasons officers 
elicit information during an interview are to: verify the identity of 
those present at the interview; determine whether to proceed with the 
interview; determine eligibility for a benefit being sought (if the 
interview relates to an application for a benefit); determine whether 
the individual being interviewed is subject to any bars or grounds of 
inadmissibility; evaluate the credibility; and identify whether fraud 
may be involved.\34\ Accordingly, the refugee interview is an 
instrumental component of robustly screening a refugee applicant. More 
truncated, less thorough interviews under the Biden administration 
damaged the integrity of refugee processing by hindering the officers' 
ability to appropriately gather sufficient information related to the 
aforementioned purposes of the refugee interview and to make an 
appropriate and legally sufficient decision. Consequently, these 
changes enabled ineligible aliens to exploit the refugee program to 
resettle in the United States,



where they then have a path to permanent status, including citizenship.

    USCIS further instructed its adjudicators that it was no longer 
necessary to ask additional detailed questions to identify and explore 
inadmissibility grounds, including security-related inadmissibility 
grounds, absent a clear indication of a concern. For example, per 
internal guidance, if an alien was transported across a border by 
smugglers, or an alien's home was attacked by an armed group, absent 
additional information in the record or in country conditions 
information indicating possible security-related concerns with respect 
to these incidents (e.g., material support to a terrorist 
organization), officers were not required to follow up or explore if 
the individual was potentially inadmissible, or if these interactions 
raised other concerns. Officers were discouraged from investigating 
potential concerns or delving into an applicant's background or past 
experiences unless referral documents, such as the U.N. High 
Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) Resettlement Registration Form (RRF), 
explicitly noted concerns. In other words, officers were discouraged 
from seeking or obtaining additional information beyond what was 
provided in the record, already provided by non-U.S. government 
entities, such as UNHCR or the Resettlement Support Center.
    With respect to country of origin information (COI), rather than 
using COI to inform their interviews and adjudications, USCIS, under 
the Biden administration, trained refugee officers that for certain 
populations, they could rely on COI ``profiles'' (e.g., ``Venezuelans 
who oppose the government of Venezuela'') to establish various elements 
of refugee eligibility once an alien indicated they were part of a 
group of individuals for which COI supported a finding of well-founded 
fear. Officers shifted from individualized, more detailed assessments 
of refugee eligibility to confining interviews to review of the Form I-
590 and an alien's affirmation of belonging to a designated group 
(e.g., Rohingya), rather than exploring and evaluating an alien's 
unique experiences of past persecution or fears. In doing so, they 
bypassed in-depth interviews exploring an alien's background, 
experiences of past persecution in their home country, affiliations and 
relationships, if the alien in fact had a well-founded fear of future 
persecution in their home country, and other relevant details.
    In 2017, President Trump issued Executive Order 13769, Protecting 
the Nation from Foreign Terrorist Entry into the United States, 
restricting entry to the U.S. by certain foreign nationals and 
temporarily suspending the USRAP.\35\ During this suspension of refugee 
processing agencies were directed to review and strengthen vetting 
procedures. As a result of the review, USCIS clarified and confirmed 
that as a matter of policy, officers interviewing refugee applicants 
were required to elicit sufficient information to make a determination 
on both the past persecution and well-founded fear of future 
persecution claims. Gathering testimony on both past persecution and 
well-founded fear ensures a thorough and accurate evaluation of the 
applicant's eligibility and prevents overlooking critical facts that 
could substantiate, or call into question, their claim. For example, 
thorough elicitation of testimony regarding past and future harm may 
help identify inconsistencies and potential fraud by allowing 
adjudicators to probe the alien's narrative for credibility by ensuring 
it is internally consistent and consistent with statements the alien 
may have provided to processing partners prior to interview. Most 
importantly, it requires officers to probe more thoroughly into an 
applicant's background and experiences, helping to establish his or her 
identity, and further ensure that the correct decision is made in his 
or her case. Although eliciting testimony about both past persecution 
and well-founded fear helps develop a fuller picture of the alien and 
better assess eligibility--ensuring that protection is granted to those 
who genuinely qualify under the law--during the Biden administration 
this policy was rescinded. Refugee officers were no longer required to 
elicit testimony on both past persecution and well-founded fear claims, 
and were instead instructed to only pursue one or the other, once one 
had been established, precluding opportunities to identify critical 
information and concerns related to an alien's eligibility.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \35 \ Protecting the Nation From Foreign Terrorist Entry Into 
the United States, 82 FR 8977 (Feb. 1, 2017).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    In addition to the relaxed requirements for principal refugee 
applicants, USCIS changed policies regarding derivative applicants. The 
first Trump administration issued guidance emphasizing the importance 
of eliciting testimony from derivative I-590 applicants apart from the 
principal refugee applicant to further explore potential national 
security, identity, inadmissibility, and credibility issues. However, 
USCIS subsequently rescinded this guidance under the Biden 
administration and provided refugee officers the sole discretion on 
when to interview derivative applicants separately. The purpose of this 
change was to reduce the amount of questions and time spent with 
derivatives in an interview, thus not thoroughly vetting and 
identifying potential issues of all members of a case who, upon case 
approval, were eligible to travel to the United States as refugees 
along with the principal applicant.
    Compounding the issue, marriage guidance under the previous 
administration relaxed the criteria for adding a derivative spouse to a 
case. Although intended to accommodate couples who genuinely acted as 
spouses but could not formalize their union due to local restrictions, 
the standards were misapplied, allowing individuals with minimal or 
short-term connections to be classified as spouses and included on 
cases. This practice, combined with lowered interview standards and 
increasingly brief, less detailed case reviews in the name of 
streamlining, increased the risk of approving applicants with only 
tenuous relationships with the principal applicant.
    In parallel with this minimized focus on eliciting substantive 
information to comprehensively understand an alien's background and 
identify potential issues of concern, the increased interview quotas 
made it more difficult for officers to explore important issues, fully 
probe the alien's credibility, and still meet their productivity 
expectations. During the first Trump administration, USCIS reduced the 
number of refugee interviews conducted per day per officer for certain 
cases to allow for further exploration of potential national security, 
inadmissibility, and credibility issues at interviews for refugee 
adjudications. Notwithstanding, USCIS under the Biden administration, 
in their effort to streamline interviews and increase the volume of 
refugee cases that could be processed, increased the number of cases an 
officer was expected to interview and adjudicate in a day for certain 
cases, again pressuring officers to at times scale back interviews to 
comply with the expectations.
    This shift away from in-depth, thorough interviews in order to 
streamline and expedite admission of aliens to the United States as 
refugees shut down important lines of questioning to identify potential 
national security, public safety, and other concerns to accurately 
assess eligibility, illustrating the program's emphasis on the volume 
of refugee case completions rather than the quality of interviews or 
the integrity of



adjudications. Refugee officers potentially missed vital information 
that could impact an applicant's eligibility, including issues related 
to fraud, public safety, and national security, and discretionary 
factors. USCIS, under the Biden administration, failed to fulfill its 
responsibility to ensure that its officers thoroughly assessed 
applicants, potentially resulting in an influx of ineligible aliens 
into the country that may pose a risk to the national interests of the 
United States.
    Moreover, USCIS under the Biden administration decreased 
requirements for supervisory review of refugee cases by only requiring 
review of the assessment in lieu of reviewing the entire case contents. 
This limited supervisor oversight to ensure cases were thoroughly and 
accurately adjudicated, increased the risk that important information 
about an alien was overlooked.
    An overarching desire to approve as many refugee cases as possible 
to meet the refugee ceiling set by the Biden administration contributed 
to a culture in which the expectation appeared to be to approve cases, 
even where egregious concerns may have existed. For instance, in one 
processing location, a number of aliens identified as having defrauded 
the U.S. government or submitting fraudulent documentation were found 
inadmissible pursuant to the INA provisions related to fraud and 
misrepresentation. Despite clear evidence of misrepresentation, 
including falsification of identity and key information relevant to 
their access to the USRAP, USCIS almost universally approved waivers of 
the misrepresentation or fraud. This pattern demonstrates a troubling 
disregard for the integrity of the refugee program, as individuals who 
had already demonstrated a willingness to engage in fraud and 
misrepresentation of their identities to U.S. government officials, 
were nonetheless permitted to proceed with resettlement to the United 
States, undermining both the security and credibility of the admissions 
process.
    The persistent presence of individuals, both in the United States 
and overseas, attempting to exploit and defraud the U.S. humanitarian 
programs, poses risks to national security, public safety, and the 
integrity of the U.S. immigration system. Historically, DHS and State

Service and the DHS Office of the Inspector General, which uncovered a 
fraud scheme related to the program.\36\ According to the indictment

IV. Discussion of Interim Final Rule

    Previous administrations' prioritization of the admissions of large 
numbers of refugees over homeland



security blatantly overlooked essential components of eligibility and 
put at risk the national security, public safety and other interests of 
the U.S. citizenry. Safeguarding national security and public safety 
remains the foremost priority of the country's immigration programs, 
taking precedence over numerical admission targets. The agency stands 
committed to conducting rigorous vetting of all aliens and to the 
detection and prevention of fraud and other serious threats, ensuring 
the safety of all Americans prior to admission of an alien to the 
United States.
    Accordingly, this IFR shortens the amount of time that refugees are 
provided to respond to a NOIT in order to ensure that terminations of 
refugee status can occur as expeditiously as possible to protect 
national security and public safety, given the risks created by the 
deficient vetting described above in Section III.C. Under this IFR, 
refugees will continue to receive a NOIT, which will specify DHS's 
intent to terminate their refugee status based on a determination that 
they did not meet the refugee definition at the time of admission. DHS 
will provide the specific reason or reasons why USCIS found the refugee 
failed to meet the refugee definition at the time of admission (e.g., 
failure to establish that past harm experienced was serious enough to 
rise to the level of persecution, a determination that the alien's harm 
was not on account of a protected ground, failure to provide credible 
testimony as to any or all of the elements of the refugee definition, 
etc.). However, this rule will provide such aliens with ten days 
(rather than 30 days) to respond (provide documentary evidence or 
indicate a desire to provide oral evidence) if they choose. If the 
deadline to reply to the NOIT passes without a response, the refugee is 
considered to have forfeited his or her right to rebut the allegations 
in the NOIT, and DHS will terminate his or her refugee status.
    By regulation, the response period begins either upon personal 
service of the NOIT directly to the alien or, if sent by mail, upon 
mailing of the NOIT.\52\ When calculating the response deadline, all 
days, including Saturdays, Sundays, and federal holidays, are 
counted.\53\ However, if the final day falls on a Saturday, Sunday, or 
federal holiday, the deadline is extended to the next business day.\54\ 
Per 8 CFR 103.8(b), if the notice is served by mail, three days are 
added to the response period, with service considered complete on the 
date the notice is mailed.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \53\ See 8 CFR 1.2 (definition of ``day'').
    \54\ Id.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    DHS's foremost priority is the safety and security of American 
citizens and residents. At the same time, DHS is committed to ensuring 
that refugees who receive a NOIT are afforded a meaningful opportunity 
to respond or provide a rebuttal. To enhance mail service reliability 
and afford refugees the full response period, DHS will utilize express 
delivery service providers, which guarantee a three-day delivery window 
and offer tracking and confirmation of both the NOIT's departure from 
DHS custody and its delivery to the recipient.\55\ This approach 
ensures that refugees receive their NOIT promptly and can exercise 
their right to respond. The NOIT will be dated on the day it is mailed, 
and the 10-day response period for the refugee will begin from that 
date. If the refugee wishes to request an opportunity to provide oral 
testimony in lieu of responding to each point or points in the NOIT, 
such a request would be considered a timely response by DHS. As 
explained above, in accordance with 8 CFR 103.8(b), when a notice is 
served by mail, three additional days are added to the response period, 
with service considered complete on the date the notice is mailed. 
Therefore, applicants who are mailed notices are afforded a total of 13 
days to respond, accounting for this regulatory provision.

    Reducing the 30-day response timeframe for NOITs issued in refugee 
terminations to a 10-day response timeframe allows DHS to take swifter 
action in cases where aliens did not meet the definition of a refugee 
when admitted to the United States. USCIS needs the ability to 
terminate refugee status in such cases in order to more quickly begin 
the removal process for aliens who should never have been admitted to 
the United States as refugees in the first place, including aliens 
similarly situated to those discussed above in Section III.C, who also 
pose a national security or public safety risk. While termination of 
refugee status is not a precondition for initiation of removal 
proceedings, the termination of refugee status gives DHS a statutory 
basis for removal, and in some cases, no other removal grounds apply, 
so this termination is needed.\56\ Accordingly, promptly terminating 
refugee status in cases where the alien was clearly ineligible at the 
time of admission facilitates DHS's ability to process the alien for 
removal under sections 235, 240, and 241 of the INA, and to remove the 
alien if they do not qualify for relief from removal.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \56\ In Matter of Smriko, 23 I&N Dec. 836 (BIA 2005), the Board 
of Immigration Appeals held that termination of an alien's refugee 
status under section 207 of the INA is not a precondition to the 
initiation of section 240 removal proceedings, but only because the 
alien in that case was removable on the basis of certain criminal 
conduct that independently qualified him for removal irrespective of 
refugee status. See id. at 837-838; compare Matter of D-K-, 25 I&N 
Dec. 761 (BIA 2012) (affirming that DHS need not terminate refugee 
status prior to commencing section 240 removal proceedings but 
determining that the alien was not removable under the grounds 
charged by DHS). On January 21, 2026, the DHS Secretary formally 
referred the BIA's decision in Matter of D-K- to the Attorney 
General for review. In that referral, DHS asked the Attorney General 
to vacate the BIA's decision insofar as it erroneously holds that 
aliens admitted as refugees may not be taken back into DHS custody 
under section 209(a)(l) of the INA, charged with inadmissibility 
under section 212(a) of the INA, and promptly removed.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    More broadly, timely termination of their refugee status is 
critical to the integrity of the country's immigration programs, 
considering the risks they may pose to the United States. As USCIS 
continues to encounter aliens admitted as refugees who did not meet the 
definition of refugee at the time of admission, termination of refugee 
status in as prompt and efficient manner as possible ensures USCIS can 
best protect the safety and security of Americans and continue 
complying with E.O.s 14161 and 14163. By shortening the 30-day period 
for an alien to respond to a NOIT to 10 days, USCIS is exercising its 
authority to expeditiously terminate the status of refugees who did not 
meet the refugee definition at the time of their admission to the 
United States. Streamlining the termination process additionally 
ensures that ineligible aliens who were erroneously allowed to enter 
the United States as refugees lose their authorization to work in as 
timely a manner as possible since termination of refugee status also 
results in termination of employment authorization.
    DHS believes that reducing the NOIT response period from 30 days to 
10 days maintains adequate procedural safeguards for aliens by 
affording them an opportunity to respond to the NOIT while also 
balancing the government's interests in national security and public 
safety and in protecting the integrity of the refugee program. The NOIT 
will inform the alien the basis for termination and explain that they 
may submit evidence to contest termination, and/or request an 
interview. An alien does not need to submit evidence or a full response 
within the 10 days, and may instead opt for an interview, but must make 
the interview request to USCIS within the response period.



Aliens who receive a NOIT under the proposed process therefore will 
continue to receive a meaningful opportunity to respond to the 
allegations in the notice--the alien can submit a written response to 
the NOIT within the deadline and/or request an interview with USCIS 
where their refugee claim can be heard. The abbreviated time period to 
respond to the NOIT will in turn allow the government to more 
efficiently process cases where aliens did not meet the refugee 
definition at the time of admission to the United States, and who were 
from the outset, never eligible for the benefit they received. Instead 
of waiting 30 days for an alien to respond to a NOIT before scheduling 
an interview if requested by the alien or taking other action, this 
rule will allow USCIS to act as soon as 10 days after service of the 
NOIT. For aliens who do not respond timely, the 10-day response period 
will allow USCIS to finalize termination much more quickly. 
Furthermore, each alien whose refugee status is terminated will be 
processed under INA sections 235, 240, or 241 and may seek other forms 
of relief or protection from removal as permitted in those proceedings. 
For example, aliens in section 240 removal proceedings may seek other 
forms of relief in a hearing before an immigration judge where the 
interests of the U.S. Government are properly represented by an 
attorney from the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Office 
of the Principal Legal Advisor (OPLA).
    The regulatory amendment being made in this IFR is clearly 
authorized by INA 207(c)(4), 8 U.S.C. 1157(c)(4), which gives 
discretion to the Secretary to ``prescribe'' regulations governing 
termination of aliens who were ``not in fact a refugee within the 
meaning of section 101(a)(42) . . . at the time of the alien's 
admission.''

V. Statutory and Regulatory Requirements

A. Administrative Procedures Act (APA)

    DHS is issuing this IFR without prior notice or public procedure 
because DHS is invoking the ``good cause'' and foreign affairs 
exceptions of the APA. See 5 U.S.C. 553(a)(1), (b)(B). For the same 
reasons, a delayed effective date of no less than 30 days is not 
required under 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3). DHS has also considered potential 
reliance interests and discusses them below.
a. Good Cause
    An agency may forgo notice-and-comment rulemaking and a delayed 
effective date when the agency ``for good cause finds . . . that notice 
and public procedure thereon are impracticable, unnecessary, or 
contrary to the public interest.'' See 5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B). Likewise, 
section 553(d)'s requirement of 30-day advance publication may be 
waived by the agency for good cause found and published with the rule. 
See 5 U.S.C. 553(d)(3).
    The ``impracticable'' prong of the good cause exception excuses 
notice and comment in emergency situations, or where the delay caused 
by the APA's notice-and-comment procedures would result in serious harm 
to life, property, or an immediate threat to public safety.\57\ 
Although the good cause exception is ``narrowly construed and only 
reluctantly countenanced,'' \58\ it is an important safety valve to be 
used where delay caused by notice and comment would do real harm (even 
absent an emergency situation).\59\ An agency may find that advance 
notice and comment or a delayed effective date is ``impracticable'' 
when undertaking such procedure would impede due and timely execution 
of an important agency function.\60\ For example, courts have explained 
that notice-and-comment rulemaking may be impracticable where, for 
instance, air travel security would be unable to address threats posing 
a ``possible imminent hazard to aircraft, persons and property within 
the United States;'' \61\ if a rule was of life-saving importance to 
mine workers in the event of a mine explosion; \62\ if public safety is 
jeopardized; \63\ or in case of an urgency related to an international 
crisis and national security.\64\ Impracticability is inevitably a 
fact-or-context dependent inquiry.\65\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \57\ See Nat. Res. Def. Council v. Nat'l Highway Traffic Safety

    \58\ See State of New Jersey v. EPA, 626 F.2d 1038, 1045 (D.C.

    The good cause exception may also apply when affording prior notice 
and comment would be contrary to the public interest. See 5 U.S.C. 
553(b)(B). The question is not whether dispensing with notice and 
comment would be contrary to the public interest, but whether providing 
notice and comment would be contrary to the public interest.\66\ This 
prong is met when the ordinary procedures under the APA--generally 
presumed to serve in the public interest--would in fact harm the 
interest of the public.\67\ The exception is appropriately invoked when 
the timing and the disclosure requirement of the usual procedures would 
defeat the purpose of the proposal and harm the public interest.\68\ 
This prong of the good cause exception is closely related to the 
impracticable prong.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \66\ Mack Trucks, Inc. v. EPA, 682 F.3d 87, 95 (D.C. Cir. 2012).
