---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    For the reasons explained below, DHS believes that, based on the 
totality of the circumstances, it has good cause to bypass ordinary 
notice-and-comment procedures because following these public procedures 
is impracticable and moving expeditiously is in the best interest of 
the public. As discussed in the preamble, streamlining the process to 
terminate refugee status in cases where the alien is determined to not 
have met the refugee definition at the time of admission to the United 
States is consistent with DHS's mission and responsibilities to ensure 
national security and public safety, and to



protect the immigration system from fraud and exploitation. DHS is 
immediately taking measures to implement a process that changes the 30-
day response timeframe in refugee termination cases to 10 days, thereby 
expediting terminations in a manner that averts harm to the public.
    Engaging in the APA's notice-and-comment requirement under 5 U.S.C. 
553(b) would impede DHS's duties as outlined in E.O. 14161, requiring 
that sufficient safeguards are in place to prevent any refugee from 
being admitted to the United States without undergoing stringent 
vetting, and E.O. 14163, permitting admission of refugees on a case-by-
case basis only so long as it is determined to be in the national 
interest and the alien does not pose a threat to the security and 
welfare of the United States.
    Thus, in accordance with President Trump's policy determinations 
related to foreign nationals, DHS is taking, without delay, immediate 
action to ensure that aliens who did not meet the refugee definition at 
the time of admission to the United States are vetted and screened to 
the maximum degree possible to ensure they do not receive significant 
benefits, including employment authorization, permanent legal status, 
and other federal, state, and local benefits. Furthermore, unless DHS 
acts immediately, there is a risk that aliens who were not eligible for 
admission as refugees could present harm to the public interest.
    As explained in detail in Section IV of this preamble, DHS 
reasonably believes, based on a review of prior refugee approvals and 
internal procedures, policies, and directives, that the lack of 
detailed refugee interviews and insufficient inquiry into critical 
matters such as inadmissibilities or terrorism-related grounds, coupled 
with the prioritization of admission numbers over legally sufficient 
decisions and other programmatic issues like over-reliance on COI, have 
resulted in aliens receiving refugee status when they were not 
eligible. These practices have compromised the integrity of the refugee 
program.
    In Operation PARRIS, DHS has further identified similar issues 
regarding the quality of refugee interviews after reviewing a subset of 
cases, where in some instances populations from specific countries were 
processed and approved with minimal lines of questioning. This rule 
amends the 30-day period to 10 days for aliens to respond to a NOIT so 
that the agency can expeditiously issue terminations in cases where, 
after a thorough review of the case and comprehensive vetting, USCIS 
determines that the alien did not meet the refugee definition at the 
time of admission. In such cases, an alien will not maintain valid 
refugee status a day longer than legally required. This IFR would 
accordingly more quickly eliminate a pathway to permanent status used 
by aliens with falsified claims or malevolent intent, including those 
who may pose an ongoing and imminent threat to public safety and 
national security such as the refugee cases reviewed and terminated by 
the USCIS Vetting Center outlined above.
    Therefore, if DHS had to engage in advance notice-and-comment 
procedures, it would continue to allow aliens who should have never 
been admitted to the United States as refugees to remain present longer 
than necessary, potentially putting at risk the safety and security of 
the United States and compromising the integrity of the U.S. 
immigration system. For example, in one case, after admission to the 
U.S. it was later discovered that the refugee was a war criminal who 
should have been subject to the persecutor bar and not allowed into the 
country. In another case listed above, the refugee was not admissible 
due to a lack of credibility with regard to both participation in and 
sending money to the OLF (a Tier III terrorist organization at the time 
of the alien's involvement) as well as his father's status as a well-
known OLF member. In these circumstances, providing advance notice-and-
comment procedures is impracticable and not in the public interest.
    Finally, DHS finds that it is unnecessary to delay this final 
rule's effective date under 5 U.S.C. 553(d). There is no need to give 
affected parties additional time to adjust their behavior before this 
final rule takes effect because DHS believes there are likely no 
behavioral adjustments to make. The aliens who would be affected by 
this rule have already entered the United States.\69\ In other words, a 
delay in the rule's effective date would be unlikely to have an impact 
on an alien's choice to seek to enter the United States as a refugee or 
not and would not impact whether or not they were eligible for such 
status at the time of admission. A delayed effective date would serve 
no purpose but create further harm to the public, as exemplified by the 
cases that, upon review and additional vetting, have resulted in the 
issuance of NOITs because the record indicated the alien was not a 
refugee at the time of admission.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \69\ DHS recognizes that there are some ongoing case-by-case 
admissions of refugees and that, as a result, there may be a small 
number of aliens admitted as refugees during what would have been 
the 30-day delayed effective date period. DHS does not believe, 
however, that these aliens would likely be subject to a later 
termination of their refugee status and subject to this rule given 
the actions taken as discussed above to strengthen refugee vetting 
and processing.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    For the reasons outlined above, DHS believes that bypassing the 
ordinary notice-and-comment procedures and the delayed effective date 
requirement is justified, under the totality of circumstances, and 
given that immediate action is necessary, is consistent with DHS's 
statutory mission to take regulatory action to administer the refugee 
program effectively, as well as the President's directives in E.O. 
14161 and E.O. 14163. Nevertheless, recognizing the value of public 
comments, DHS is publishing this rule as an IFR with a request for 
public comment.
b. Foreign Affairs Exception
    Agencies may forgo notice-and-comment rulemaking and a delayed 
effective date when the rulemaking involves a ``military or foreign 
affairs function of the United States.'' 5 U.S.C. 553(a)(1). The 
Secretary of State, on February 21, 2025, determined that:

    all efforts, conducted by any agency of the federal government, 
to control the status, entry, and exit of people and the transfer of 
goods, services, data, technology, and any other items across the 
borders of the United States, constitutes a foreign affairs function 
of the United States under the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 
U.S.C. 553, 554.\70\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \70\ Determination: Foreign Affairs Functions of the United 
States, 90 FR 12200 (Mar. 14, 2025).

    This rulemaking is connected to an alien's status as a refugee 
admitted into the United States, which directly stems from the conduct 
of international relations of the United States. Therefore, it 
constitutes a foreign affairs function. U.S. refugee law is rooted in 
international law. In 1968, the United States acceded to the 1967 
United Nations Protocol Relating to the Status of Refugees (Refugee 
Protocol) \71\, which incorporates the 1951 United Nations Convention 
Relating to the Status of Refugees (Refugee Convention). The Refugee 
Convention sets out the rights of refugees and establishes the 
standards for their treatment in the countries that receive them, 
providing the most comprehensive codification of refugee rights at the 
international level. State



signatories to the 1951 Convention and the 1967 Protocol are bound by 
international obligations to provide for the protection of refugees 
whether such States are countries of first asylum or of resettlement. 
Refugee status is a product of statutorily mandated foreign affairs 
considerations and U.S. foreign policy commitments. With respect to 
refugee admissions, the relevant Departments must consider conditions 
within the specific countries, ``the extent to which other countries 
will admit and assist'' in resettlement, and ``the impact of the 
participation of the United States in the resettlement of such refugees 
on the foreign policy interests of the United States''. INA sec. 207; 8 
U.S.C. 1157(e). Refugee determinations require diplomatic relationships 
with countries of origin, transit, and habituation as well as ongoing 
assessments of foreign governments' conduct, stability, and human 
rights practices.\72\ The United States' management of its refugee 
program and immigration enforcement strategies is predicated on the 
belief that migration is a shared responsibility among all countries 
with which the United States has ongoing diplomatic relations and 
negotiations. The common thread in these engagements is the United 
States' commitment to provide protection to refugees who clearly 
qualify, while enforcing national immigration laws, and that addressing 
this challenge requires a multinational response. As such, this is a 
function of foreign affairs.

c. Reliance Interests
    DHS has considered potential reliance interests regarding this IFR. 
DHS recognizes the difficulty aliens may face if their refugee status 
is terminated, but DHS believes the significant public safety, national 
security, and integrity benefits described in detail above heavily 
outweigh any potential reliance interest and adverse impacts. DHS 
notes, however, that aliens will continue to receive an opportunity to 
respond to the NOIT and overcome the reasons for termination, if 
merited. With this IFR, DHS is merely ensuring that aliens who were 
never eligible for refugee status do not receive the attendant benefits 
of being a refugee admitted into the United States for as long as they 
could have without this rule. This IFR does not remove the ability of 
aliens who legitimately qualify for refugee status to obtain employment 
authorization, permanent residency, and any other available benefits. 
Aliens whose refugee status is terminated may be able to seek 
protection or other relief in proceedings under sections 235, 240, or 
241 of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1225, 1229a, or 1231, which would mitigate any 
potential reliance interests.\74\

B. Executive Orders 12866 (Regulatory Planning and Review), 13563 
(Improving Regulation and Regulatory Review), and 14192 (``Unleashing 
Prosperity Through Deregulation'')

    E.O.s 12866 and 13563 direct agencies to assess the costs and 
benefits of available regulatory alternatives and, if a regulation is 
necessary, to select regulatory approaches that maximize net benefits. 
E.O. 13563 emphasizes the importance of quantifying both costs and 
benefits, of reducing costs, of harmonizing rules, and of promoting 
flexibility. E.O. 14192 directs agencies to significantly reduce the 
private expenditures required to comply with Federal regulations and 
provides that ``any new incremental costs associated with the new 
regulations shall, to the extent permitted by law be offset by the 
elimination of existing costs associated with at least 10 prior 
regulations.''
    The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) has designated this IFR a 
``significant regulatory action'' under section 3(f) of E.O. 12866, 
although not economically significant under section 3(f)(1), because 
its annual effects on the economy do not exceed $100 million in any 
year of the analysis. Accordingly, the rule has been reviewed by the 
Office of Management and Budget.
    This rule is not an E.O. 14192 regulatory action because it is 
being issued with respect to an immigration-related function of the 
United States. The rule's primary direct purpose is to implement or 
interpret the immigration laws of the United States (as described in 
INA101(a)(17), 8 U.S.C. 1101(a)(17), or any other function performed by 
the U.S. Federal Government with respect to aliens. See OMB Memorandum 
M-25-20, ``Guidance Implementing Section 3 of Executive Order 14192, 
titled ``Unleashing Prosperity Through Deregulation'' (Mar. 26, 2025).
    In this section, DHS discusses several types of impacts that could 
accrue from this IFR. They are described qualitatively as DHS cannot 
make quantitative or monetized estimates of potential impacts. DHS 
welcomes public comment on the cost and benefit impacts described 
herein.
    DHS typically reviews an alien's underlying refugee determination 
prior to the final adjudication of their adjustment of status to 
permanent residence and initiates termination when warranted.\75\ 
Therefore, the impacted population are aliens with refugee status who 
entered the U.S. and have not yet adjusted status or had their 
determination reviewed. DHS has identified about 186,000 cases of 
refugees that entered the U.S. from Fiscal Year (FY) 2015 through FY 
2025 that have not adjusted status.\76\ This figure could represent the 
maximum population that could be subject to the IFR, as USCIS and ICE 
are currently working to identify particular subsets and aliens for 
requisite vetting. As it relates to potential impacts, foremost, there 
will be a change in the earnings (labor compensation) to the applicable 
aliens when their refugee status is terminated, as their work 
authorization would also be terminated immediately, which is at least 
20 days sooner than without this rule.\77\ Refugees are granted



work authorization incident to status but can file a Form I-765, 
``Application for Employment Authorization,'' under primarily the (A3) 
category, with a small number under the (A4) category applicable to 
paroled refugees. In FY 2024, for example, USCIS approved approximately 
125,000 (A3) initial employment authorization documents, which was a 
sharp increase from about 49,000 in FY 2023.\78\ This IFR shortens the 
time for a refugee to respond to a NOIT from 30 days to 10 days. 
Accordingly, this rule would shorten the amount of time that an alien 
has refugee status prior to termination, and the gap (duration, in 
working days) in earnings time due to earlier employment termination 
under the IFR would pose a change in earnings ability to the 
aliens.\79\

file for employment authorization, they would incur costs applicable 
to the burden, as well as, if applicable, direct filing fees and 
biometrics submission charges.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    For those aliens in the labor force and employed at the time of 
their employment authorization termination, the earnings impact could 
create both potential distributional effects (which are transfers) and 
costs. The extent depends on labor market factors and the individual 
characteristics of aliens and potential substitute workers. The 
distributional impacts (transfers) would be in the form of forgone 
compensation (wages and benefits). However, a portion or all of this 
forgone compensation to aliens might comprise beneficial transfers to 
U.S. citizens and others lawfully allowed to work in the United States.
    In addition, if employers are able to hire American workers to fill 
the jobs that refugees held, with relatively little labor market 
friction, the beneficial wage and benefit transfers to American workers 
would potentially pose no productivity loss or costs to employers. 
While it is possible that aliens without work authorization could 
require assistance from their social and support networks, which could 
include public entities, there could be a counterbalance; if the IFR 
process results in, or contributes to, faster removal of aliens who 
were ineligible for refugee status, there could be less of an economic 
strain on states, local government, and non-governmental organizations, 
in terms of any public assistance and resources that are currently 
provided to refugees.
    As it relates to earnings impacts, there could be tax impacts. 
Aliens who sustain earnings changes because their employment 
authorization is terminated under the IFR may generate forgone federal 
and state taxes. However, any tax losses could be partially or fully 
recovered if employers are able to easily substitute others into the 
positions the alien held. In addition, aliens can pose fiscal strains 
that could be mitigated due to the effects of this rule as a 
counterbalance of some or all of the tax losses, if there are any.
    DHS assesses that there could be labor turnover costs incurred by 
businesses employing aliens who would lose employment authorization 
under the IFR whom would not otherwise lose the authorization (i.e., if 
currently they could reaffirm their status in 30 days but not in 10 
days under this rule). Employment separations can comprise direct or 
``hard'' costs applicable to separation and replacement charges.\80\ 
The separation costs include exit interviews, severance pay, and costs 
of temporarily covering the employee's duties and functions with other 
employees, which may require overtime or temporary staffing. The 
replacement costs typically include expenses of advertising positions, 
search and agency fees, screening applicants, interviews, background 
verification, employment testing, hiring bonuses, and possible travel 
and relocation costs. Once hired, employers face additional training, 
orientation, and assessment costs.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \80\ For a description of these costs, see ``Employee Retention: 
The Real Cost of Losing an Employee,'' by Holly Bengfort, PeopleKeep 
(updated Dec. 15, 2025), at: https://www.peoplekeep.com/blog/Employee-Retention-The-Real-Cost-of-Losing-an-Employee. See also, 
``This Fixable Problem Costs U.S. Businesses $1 Trillion,'' by Shane 
McFeely and Ben Wigert, Gallup Workplace (Mar. 13, 2019) at: https://www.gallup.com/workplace/247391/fixable-problem-costs-businesses-trillion.aspx.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Second, there can be costs for productivity and possibly 
profitability due to operational and production disruptions, which can 
include errors from other employees that may temporally fill the 
position. A third cost segment, which is a type of indirect cost, can 
encompass loss of institutional knowledge, networking, and impacts to 
work culture, morale, and interpersonal relationships.
    DHS is providing a 10-day, as opposed to the current 30-day, 
timeframe to contest applicable NOITs. The NOIT will inform the alien 
the basis for termination and explain that they may submit evidence to 
contest termination, and/or request an interview. Aliens who would 
currently respond to a NOIT to attempt to reaffirm their status would 
sustain some direct costs and also opportunity costs of time applicable 
to generating and preparing responses, organizing documents and 
evidence, and participating in interviews. Under the 10-day timeframe, 
such resourcing and expenditure would likely still be incurred, but the 
timeframe would be contracted. There could be impacts and costs to 
aliens applicable to having less time to collect evidence, prepare 
documentation, and prepare their response.
    As is pertinent to the public sector, planned extensive vetting, 
case review, and reinterviews, as well as enforcement operations for 
the Federal Bureau of Investigation and ICE, in support directly or 
indirectly of this IFR, could require an increase in public resources. 
As is applicable to mailing the NOITs, DHS will utilize express 
delivery service providers, which guarantee delivery within the IFR 
timeframe, and offers tracking and confirmation of both the package's 
departure from DHS custody and its delivery to the recipient. This is 
not a significant change from current practice and DHS does not expect 
that this IFR will generate additional costs applicable to mailing the 
NOITs. USCIS will continue to expend resources on processing and review 
of the responses. However, the revised timeline may generate 
efficiencies as USCIS will be able to schedule interviews or take 
action more quickly. DHS cannot predict in advance the net effect to 
public resources and welcomes public input concerning public sector 
resources.
    DHS, however, does not and cannot assert that it knows and has 
considered every policy change that may occur at all levels and 
agencies of the U.S. government that may directly or indirectly affect 
this IFR. Therefore, there could be other impacts not currently 
described in this discussion.
    DHS cannot quantify the benefits of this IFR but believes that 
increased national security, public safety, credibility, and reduced 
fraud or misrepresentation by applicable aliens, among other concerns, 
will contribute to the safety of the American people and integrity of 
the lawful United States immigration system to the extent that the 
benefits will outweigh any costs.



Streamlining the process to terminate refugee status in cases where the 
alien is determined to not have been a refugee at the time of admission 
to the United States is consistent with the DHS mission and 
responsibilities to ensure national security and public safety and 
beneficially protects the immigration system from fraud and 
exploitation.

C. Regulatory Flexibility Act (RFA)

    The Regulatory Flexibility Act of 1980 (5 U.S.C. 601 et seq.), as 
amended by the Small Business Regulatory Enforcement Fairness Act of 
1996, requires federal agencies to consider the potential impact of 
regulations on small businesses, small governmental jurisdictions, and 
small organizations during the development of their rules. The term 
``small entities'' comprises small businesses, not-for-profit 
organizations that are independently owned and operated and are not 
dominant in their fields, and governmental jurisdictions with 
populations of less than 50,000. The RFA's regulatory flexibility 
analysis requirements apply only to those rules for which an agency is 
required to publish a general notice of proposed rulemaking pursuant to 
5 U.S.C. 553 or any other law.\81\ DHS did not issue a notice of 
proposed rulemaking for this action.

    \81\ See 5 U.S.C. 604(a).

D. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (UMRA)

    The Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (UMRA) is intended, among 
other things, to curb the practice of imposing unfunded federal 
mandates on State, local, and Tribal governments.\82\ Title II of UMRA 
requires each Federal agency to prepare a written statement assessing 
the effects of any Federal mandate in a proposed rule, or final rule 
for which USCIS published a proposed rule, which includes any Federal 
mandate that may result in a $100 million or more expenditure (adjusted 
annually for inflation) in any one year by State, local, and Tribal 
governments, in the aggregate, or by the private sector. See 2 U.S.C. 
1532(a). This rule is exempt from the written-statement requirement, 
because DHS did not publish a notice of proposed rulemaking for this 
rule.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \82\ The term ``Federal mandate'' means a Federal 
intergovernmental mandate or a Federal private sector mandate. See 2 
U.S.C. 1502(1) and 658(5) and (6).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    In addition, this rule does not exceed the $100 million expenditure 
in any one year when adjusted for inflation ($211 million in 2025 based 
on the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) \83\), and 
this rulemaking does not contain such a federal mandate as the term is 
defined under UMRA. The requirements of title II of UMRA therefore do 
not apply, thus DHS has not prepared a statement under UMRA.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

Consumers (CPI-U): U.S. city average, allitems, by month,'' https://www.bls.gov/cpi/tables/supplemental-files/historical-cpi-u-202512.pdf (last visited Aug. 18, 2026). Calculation of inflation: 
(1) calculate the average monthly CPI-U for the reference year 
(1995) and the current year (2025); (2) subtract reference year CPI-
U from current year CPI-U; (3) divide the difference of the 
reference year CPI-U and current year CPI-U by the reference year 
CPI-U; (4) multiply by 100 = [(average monthly CPI-U for 2025-
average monthly CPI-U for 1995) / (average monthly CPI-U for 1995)] 
x 100 = [(321.943-152.383) / 152.383] = (169.560/152.383) = 1.113 x 
100 = 111.3 percent = 111 percent (rounded). Calculation of 
inflation-adjusted value: $100 million in 1995 dollars x 2.11 = $211 
million in 2025 dollars.

J. National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA)

    DHS and its components analyze final actions to determine whether 
the National Environmental Policy Act (NEPA), 42 U.S.C. 4321 et seq., 
applies and, if so, what degree of analysis is required. DHS Directive 
023-01, Rev. 01``Implementing the National Environmental Policy Act'' 
(Directive 023-01) and Instruction Manual 023-01-001-01 Revision 01, 
``Implementation of the National Environmental Policy Act'' 
(Instruction Manual) \84\ established the policies and procedures that 
DHS and its components use to comply with NEPA.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \84\ The Instruction Manual contains DHS' procedures for 
implementing NEPA and was issued Nov. 6, 2014. See DHS, Office of 
the Chief Readiness Support Officer, National Environmental Policy 
Act Compliance, https://www.dhs.gov/ocrso/eed/epb/nepa (last updated 
Apr. 14, 2025).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    NEPA allows Federal agencies to establish, in their NEPA 
implementing procedures, categories of actions (``categorical 
exclusions'') that experience has shown do not, individually or 
cumulatively, have a significant effect on the human environment and, 
therefore, do not require an environmental assessment or environmental 
impact statement.\85\ The Instruction Manual, Appendix A lists the DHS 
Categorical Exclusions.\86\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \85\ See 42 U.S.C. 4336(a)(2), 4336e(1).
    \86\ See Instruction Manual, Appendix A, Table 1.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Under DHS NEPA implementing procedures, for an action to be 
categorically excluded, it must satisfy each of the following three 
conditions: (1) the entire action clearly fits within one or more of 
the categorical exclusions; (2) the action is not a piece of a larger 
action; and (3) no extraordinary circumstances exist that create the 
potential for a significant environmental effect.\87\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \87\ Instruction Manual 023-01 at V.B(2)(a)-(c).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    This IFR is strictly administrative and procedural because it is 
only amending an existing DHS regulation governing the termination of 
refugee status. DHS has reviewed this IFR and finds that no significant 
impact on the environment, or any change in environmental effect will 
result from the amendments being promulgated in this rule.
    Accordingly, DHS finds that the promulgation of this IFR's 
amendments to a current regulation clearly fits within the categorical 
exclusion A3 established in DHS's NEPA implementing procedures as an 
administrative change with no change in environmental effect, is not 
part of a larger Federal action, and does not present extraordinary 
circumstances that create the potential for a significant environmental 
effect. Therefore, these regulatory amendments are categorically 
excluded from further NEPA review.
